title: The extraordinary joy of Ethel Kennedy
summary: In her new book, "Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy," daughter Kerry Kennedy writes about a woman who maintained positivity and resilience despite numerous public and private tragedies.
story: Kerry Kennedy, the daughter of Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Skakel Kennedy, was asked to describe her mother. She replied, "Extraordinarily chic, fun, funny, fully alive."
Kerry says that most people don't know very much about her mom's life. She calls it "a story of wonder and beauty and inspiration."
But not of self-reflection. As Ethel herself said in a 2012 HBO documentary, "Ethel," "Introspection? I hate it."

She grew up in Greenwich, Connecticut, the daughter of a self-made millionaire. When she and her college roommate (who happened to be Jean Kennedy) decided that their two families should meet for a ski vacation, Ethel developed a big crush on Robert Kennedy, only to learn he was dating her sister. "Yes, he unfortunately was looking in a different direction," Kerry said.

Not for long! Robert and Ethel were married in 1950. This photo, now appearing on the cover of Kerry Kennedy's loving memoir about her mom, "Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy" (to be published Tuesday), inspired the Taylor Swift song "StarLight." "They had a truly extraordinary love story, but a real partnership," said Kerry.

Their first of 11 children was born in 1951; Kerry is number seven. In all, Ethel Kennedy was pregnant for 99 months, or more than eight years. "Yes, but my mother often would say that if she could do anything differently, she would have more children," Kerry said.
And though Ethel Kennedy grew up in a family of Republicans, she was a Democrat through-and-through.
This photo, taken the night John F. Kennedy was elected president, shows JFK, RFK and Ethel at the family compound in Hyannis Port, Massachusetts looking at the election returns.

Hyannis Port was the center for Robert and his brothers and sisters growing up. By the time Robert became his brother's attorney general, at age 35, much of the action switched to Hickory Hill, in the Washington suburbs, where Bobby and Ethel's children were included in all aspects of family life. That even meant going to the Attorney General's Office, where her father put a young Kerry on the phone with one of his deputies during a civil rights crisis.
But then, on November 22, 1963, JFK was assassinated. As Ethel said in the documentary, "It was like Daddy had lost both arms. It was six months of just blackness."

Kerry said, "My mother was the opposite. She gave him that space to be able to grieve. But she had all those children at home, and she was going to be there with us, driving the carpools, saying prayers every night."

And by 1964, Robert F. Kennedy would win the race for the U.S. Senate in New York. Just four years later, he would announce his run for the White House, in opposition to President Lyndon Johnson's support for the Viet Nam War.
Asked if Ethel were afraid for her husband, after what happened to his brother, Kerry replied, "Fear was not part of the equation for her. Would have been for me, but it wasn't for her."

When Kerry Kennedy was eight years old, after her father won the California Democratic primary, Robert F. Kennedy was felled by an assassin's bullet. Ethel Kennedy's heart was broken, and yet, Kerry said, "She was getting up the next day and forging ahead. That's how she lived her life. She was mighty."
Ethel threw herself into raising her children; and she founded what's now known as the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, dedicated to fighting oppression at home and around the world.
But she had her fair share of additional sorrows. Her son Michael died in 1997 in a skiing accident. Another son, David, died in 1984 from a drug overdose.

And then there is the controversial topic of Robert F. Kennedy Jr, who not only endorsed Donald Trump for president, but is now a member of his cabinet. Kerry said, "What was really most important to my mother, and to my father and to all of us, is our love. I love Bobby with all my heart. I just disagree with everything he says and does. My mother was like that. She had a comfort level of being on the other side of Bobby, but still being able to love him."

Kerry, who has called for her brother's resignation, says she still loves him: "Of course, I love him. But I don't think that somebody should be the Secretary of Health and Human Services who is saying we shouldn't use vaccines."

In 2014 President Obama honored Ethel Kennedy with the Medal of Freedom for her dedication to Human Rights, calling her "a force for change in her quiet, flashy, unflashy unstoppable way. As her family will tell you – and they basically occupy this half of the room – you don't mess with Ethel."
Ethel Kennedy died on October 10, 2024 at age 96.

"There was so much loss," said Kerry, "so much loss in her life. And then she came out the other side, and with this extraordinary joy. All the last years of her life she kept repeating, aren't we lucky?"

title: DOJ investigating TV networks over suspension of press pool after Trump media ban
summary: The Justice Department is investigating whether the major TV networks violated antitrust laws after they briefly suspended the TV press pool system in response to President Trump's decision to ban three news organizations from the White House.
story: The Justice Department is investigating whether the major TV networks, including CBS, violated antitrust laws after they briefly suspended the television press pool system in response to President Trump's decision last month to ban three news organizations from the White House.

"Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events," Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said in a statement provided to CBS News on Saturday. "Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

It was not immediately clear how the Justice Department was defining the move as a violation of the Sherman Act, which is a longstanding federal law that seeks to prevent monopolistic business behavior and maintain fair competition.
The New York Times was first to report the investigation. CBS News has reached out to the White House and all five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — for comment.

In mid-September, Mr. Trump announced that his administration was rescinding the White House credentials of journalists for CNN, MSNOW and Politico over what he alleged was "their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

The White House also sent letters to each of the three news outlets informing them that certain articles they had published on topics including the new White House ballroom, the ongoing war with Iran and the Republican midterm convention were threats to national security and violated standards of "professionalism and decorum" for reporters.

Following the move, the five networks that make up the TV press pool jointly announced that they would be suspending their coverage in solidarity. That suspension occurred at a critical moment in that it coincided with Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington.

In a group statement at the time, the five networks said, "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should reject a news organization because it objects to its reporting."
The TV press pool covers the president's travel and events on a rotating basis, providing video to other news organizations.

CNN, MSNOW and Politico immediately filed a lawsuit to have their access restored, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly subsequently granted a temporary restraining order against the president's ban, and their credentials were reinstated.
However, despite having their credentials restored, the White House has continued to refuse to allow CNN and Politico into the Oval Office or aboard Air Force One.
That restraining order was set to expire on Thursday, but Kelly extended it to next Tuesday while he continues to consider the case.
CBS News and CNN are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed following the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that was finalized earlier this week.

title: Vehicle driven by ICE agents in Texas hits and injures man, sheriff says
summary: The Harris County Sheriff's Office said in a statement that the incident appears to have occurred during an ICE enforcement action.
story: A vehicle driven by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents hit and injured a man in the greater Houston area on Saturday, the Harris County Sheriff's Office said.
"The incident appears to have occurred while ICE authorities were conducting an enforcement action in the area," the sheriff's office said in a statement.
During a press conference, Major McConnell of the Harris County Sheriff's special investigation bureau said the sheriff's office was called to the scene around 7:20 a.m.
ICE agents were headed south in pursuit of a wanted suspect, McConnell said, and the suspect drove west in an eastbound lane. The suspect bailed out of his vehicle and went on foot, he said.
The driver and passenger fled and ICE agents attempted to capture them both, he said. While trying to capture the passenger, the ICE agent hit him with his vehicle.
The victim was taken to a local hospital. McConnell said it appears the man has a broken leg. McConnell said the victim is a 48-year-old male and is currently in the custody of ICE at the hospital.

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday, an ICE spokesperson said that agents were "conducting a targeted enforcement operation" to arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant.
During the operation, ICE agents observed Mendoza-Cervantes and a second Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, identified as Miguel Parra-Hernandez, enter a vehicle and drive away.
According to the ICE spokesperson, when they attempted to stop the vehicle, the two subjects stopped and ran away on foot.
During the ensuing chase, Parra-Hernandez "ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck."
The ICE spokesperson said that Parra-Hernandez was taken to an area hospital with injuries believed to be non-life-threatening.
Mendoza-Cervantes escaped and remains at large, ICE said.

In its statement, ICE alleged that Mendoza-Cervantes had four prior arrests for drunken driving charges, as well as an arrest for charges of unlawful possession of a firearm. ICE did not confirm if he was convicted of any of those allegations. ICE stated that an immigration judge had issued him a final order of removal. The agency spokesperson also said that he had been previously deported twice.

title: House candidate who reported rape on campaign trail details why she came forward
summary: In the days since U.S. House candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia publicly came forward alleging she was raped over the summer while repairing a campaign sign, she says women have been reaching out to her to share their own stories.
story: In the days since U.S. House candidate Bernadette Greene-Placentia publicly came forward alleging she was raped over the summer while repairing a campaign sign, she says women have been reaching out to her to share their own stories.

"The humbling thing is that so many – hundreds and hundreds of women from around the world — have taken the time to write me and tell me their own story," Greene-Placentia told CBS News in an interview. "I would say about 70% of them have acknowledged that they never reported it, and they are thanking me for being in the public eye and talking about it and giving voice because they didn't feel like they had a voice when they went through the same thing."

Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, is facing freshman Republican Rep. Abe Hamadeh on the ballot in November in Arizona's 8th District, located in the Phoenix suburbs. The district is rated as solidly Republican by Cook Political Report.

The reported sexual assault happened amid a heated campaign season, as concerns about political violence swirl. At a rally in September, an armed man lunged at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, and at a town hall earlier this year, a man lunged and sprayed vinegar at Rep. Ilhan Omar.
Greene-Placentia, who had been a long-haul trucker, told CBS News that "we are not a well-funded campaign," and she and her staff were usually the ones putting up campaign signs or fixing them.
"I took pride in being able to, you know, do these things myself because we are a grassroots campaign, so it wasn't unusual," she said of fixing signs at all hours.

She said that a "little after midnight" one night in August, she was repairing some supplies when she was hit on the back of the head. When she regained consciousness, she said she realized she was on the ground, and a "man was on top of me, and then I felt pain down there." She said that man "climbed off," and then another man assaulted her.
"At that point, I remember I started, like, moving around and kicking," she said. "He said, 'You know, just not worth it.' And they left. I don't know how long I stayed there."
Greene-Placentia said she drove straight home, and she said she believes police have footage of her driving home.
A police report from the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office says the incident occurred on Aug. 14 between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m., and she reported the incident on Aug. 31.
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said in a statement earlier this week that it was investigating the incident but could not comment further.
Greene-Placentia said she told her husband and staff the next day, but she didn't want to talk about it at first.

Greene-Placentia said Friday that she realized she wanted to come forward while she was telling her own personal story on the trail. She said she was talking about how her father died while waiting to get care with the Department of Veterans Affairs and she found out six months later that her mother had been rationing her insulin.

"I was asking them, 'Do you think anybody's gonna fight harder than me?'" Greene-Placentia said. "And then in the back of my head, I'm like, 'Well you're telling these folks that you're gonna fight for them, but what about all the women that are victims of sexual assault? Are you not gonna fight for them? That kind of makes you a hypocrite, Bernadette.'"

Greene-Placentia's story was first published on Wednesday in the Phoenix New Times. Since then, her opponent, Hamadeh, called it a "disturbing story," and he was calling "upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law."
Greene-Placentia said that she wants to tell women who come up to her that she understands what they are going through.
"As women, we want to take responsibility for everything and blame ourselves, and that is a societal problem we've got to get away from," Greene-Placentia said.

title: Christa Pike released from hospital following botched execution, lawyers say
summary: Christa Pike survived despite being given two doses of a lethal injection.
story: Christa Pike, the woman whose execution by lethal injection was botched last month in Tennessee, has been released from the hospital and is now back in prison, according to her lawyers.
She has been transferred back to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Nashville, where she had been held before her planned execution on Sept. 30.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement Saturday. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."

Pike, 50, was given two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. One witness, a media attendee, noted she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.
Her legal team said on Tuesday that she had regained consciousness and was speaking from her hospital bed.

On Wednesday, Pike began "taking limited steps" with help, according to her team. And on Thursday, her attorneys detailed more progress, saying in a statement that she was walking "with some assistance" and her arms were "healing and regaining movement and strength." They also said that her "lungs are clear, and she has started to eat a regular diet."
Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S., according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Court filings show that Pike, then 18, tortured and killed Slemmer, slashing her with a meat cleaver and box cutter for up to an hour in a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus, with help from her boyfriend and a friend.
Pike's execution was allowed to move forward after the Supreme Court denied a last-minute effort to halt it. She was set to be the first woman executed in the state since 1820.
It's still unclear what will happen with Pike moving forward.

Pike's attorneys attended an emergency hearing in Davidson County court on Wednesday, during which they requested and were granted a decision saying Tennessee's correctional department must preserve records and other evidence of her failed lethal injection.

Her legal team has renewed its calls for Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's death sentence, pushing him to change the sentence to life in prison without parole so the state can't attempt to execute Pike a second time. This is the usual course of action after an inmate survives botched execution proceedings, her attorneys said.
However, while others have survived botched procedures before, Pike is the only known inmate in the United States' modern death penalty era to remain alive after actually receiving lethal chemicals.
"The state has made no promises that Ms. Pike will not be subject to a future execution," Ihnen, one of Pike's attorneys, said in court on Wednesday.

title: Pope says death penalty "inadmissible" amid U.S. plans to livestream execution
summary: The firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed, the U.S. Defense Department said.
story: Pope Leo XIV declared that capital punishment is "inadmissible" as the United States plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

The American pope, in a post on X marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Catholic teaching states that capital punishment attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," read the post under Leo's official handle, @Pontifex. "Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption."

The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
The decision to livestream the execution has drawn fierce criticism.

Leo's post didn't refer specifically to the planned execution in the U.S. or the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee late last month which has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, it is common for the pope's official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations like the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
However, Leo's post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was "unacceptable."

Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was "truly incomprehensible" and "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."

"The Church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent… ," Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don't know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" at the Pentagon's plans.

"In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
On Friday, President Trump said he approves of Hasan's execution by firing squad.

"He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad," Mr. Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
Mr. Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.

Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic convert, appeared to cast doubt on Friday about the livestream, telling reporters he wouldn't watch it and, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

title: Blanche, other DOJ appointees can take part in campaigns, memo says
summary: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior ​political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.
story: The Justice Department has loosened the guidelines for the attorney general and other senior political appointees, allowing them to participate in political activities.

A memo sent this week by Assistant Attorney General Jolene Ann Laurie relaxes ethics restrictions on Senate-confirmed presidential appointees such that they can speak at rallies, canvass for votes and even serve as delegates or officers of a national political party as long as those activities are conducted in their personal capacities.
The guidance applies to the attorney general, the deputy attorney general, assistant attorneys general, the FBI director, U.S. attorneys and others.
Former Attorney General Pam Bondi had loosened the regulations somewhat during her tenure by allowing political appointees to attend rallies and fundraisers. The new memo goes a step further.

It specifically states that presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Justice Department employees are exempt from the more stringent guidelines imposed on some other DOJ employees, such as administrative law judges and those in the Criminal Division.

Attorney General Todd Blanche addressed the Republican midterm convention in September and attended a rally for a North Carolina Republican Senate candidate, drawing criticism that he violated long-standing Justice Department norms intended to keep politics independent from the law.
"I am not in any way violating any rule or law," Blanche said about his appearances at these events, adding they were done in his personal capacity.
These moves come after the Biden-era Justice Department clamped down on appointees' political activities.
"Non-career appointees may not attend any partisan political events, even in their personal capacities," a 2024 memo said, continuing a policy instituted two years earlier.
The 2024 memo also said that appointees should "avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable."
PBS News was first to report on the new guidelines.

title: Pentagon's plan to livestream execution sparks backlash
summary: "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," said GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.
story: Washington — The revelation that the Pentagon plans to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has sparked intense pushback, with one Republican senator calling it "disgusting" and critics warning it could inspire more acts of terrorism.

On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed CBS News' reporting that the Dec. 3 execution will be livestreamed. Hegseth told Real America's Voice the execution would be public "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth recommended, and President Trump approved, a plan to use an Army firing squad.
"Death penalty through firing squad, and he deserves it," Mr. Trump said during an unrelated White House event on Friday.
In an interview Friday night in Syracuse, New York, with WSTM-TV, President Trump said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, "but I understand that decision."
"I guess they want to have it serve as an example, and I understand that very well," the president added.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, called the decision "beyond disgusting." Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth, but is now expressing his regret in doing so.

"Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting," Tillis wrote on X. "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America."
Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia wrote on X, "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that."
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah urged Hegseth to reconsider.

"Seneca warned that Rome's bloody spectacles corrupted the people who watched them," he said on X. "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.  Secretary Hegseth's plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider."
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said publicly executing someone is "medieval."

"That's disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions?" Murphy said on CNN. "I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval. It's frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups. And the fact that the United States is doing it — I just learned this, that is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That's what America has become?"
Ned Price, who was the State Department's spokesman during the Biden administration, said a public and livestreamed execution will create more "radicalized zealots."

"You can take it from those of us who've spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause," Price wrote on X. "Or take it from AQ and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth's proposal.  Either way, it's hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America's image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable."

Alonzo Lunsford, a former U.S. Army sergeant who was shot seven times during the Fort Hood shooting but survived, said he supports the gunman's execution by firing squad. But Lunsford said this execution is "not something you should view for entertainment purposes."
"To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief," he told BBC Radio.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, issued a statement Friday morning urging the Pentagon to reconsider.

"In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" the archbishop said, citing Romans 12:17. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
Conservative talk show host Erick Erickson, who supports the death penalty, also said a public, livestreamed execution of Hasan will give him the "platform for martyrdom he wants."

"Hasan is a paraplegic, confined to a wheelchair," Erickson wrote. "The public imagery of a firing squad killing a man sitting in a chair because he cannot stand is going to undermine support for the death penalty. A society that increasingly finds ways to sympathize with the villains will do so here. This also gives Nidal Hasan the platform for martyrdom he wants. They'll be passing out the livestream video in the Middle East to inspire more terrorists to shoot up Americans to celebrate the glory of the martyrdom of Nidal Hasan."

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News that the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."
"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said.
Corn said "turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."
Despite Lunsford's concerns about the livestream, the former U.S. Army sergeant said he'll be there for the execution.

"I'm going to be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude, you failed, I'm still here,'" he told the BBC.
The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place 90 years ago in 1936. That's when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky. The execution reportedly drew a crowd of about 20,000.

Hegseth's announcement comes amid efforts from Democrats and Republican Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach him. A vote on his impeachment was delayed by House Speaker Mike Johnson's decision to cancel votes a day early ahead of the midterms.

Eleanor  Watson and 
                                                  
                                  Joe  Walsh
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: 3 men found guilty in murders of American, Australian surfers in Mexico
summary: A local judge has found three men guilty of murdering two Australian brothers and their American friend in Baja California, Mexico, in April 2024.
story: A local judge on Friday found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.

The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N" were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.

Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them," CBS News' partner network BBC News reported. Debra Robinson and her husband, Martin Robinson, were at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said, BBC reported.

The three friends traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N."

During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9 mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.

The state prosecutor's office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and "instigated one of her companions to rob them," which was carried out the following day.

The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims' cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to "aggravated robbery with violence" and "vehicle theft with violence" in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General's Office requested for each defendant the "exemplary sentence" of 210 years in prison.

title: Trump picks "loyal" Katie Zacharia as next White House press secretary
summary: "I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary," President Trump said.
story: Washington — President Trump on Friday announced conservative commentator Katie Zacharia will be the next White House press secretary, praising her "unblemished record of support."

Zacharia, a California native, briefly worked for the Department of Homeland Security as a spokesperson earlier this year, and currently works as a senior communications adviser for Truth Social, the president's social media site. She also assisted the president on the campaign trail, he said.

"She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," the president wrote on Truth Social. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA! I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration."
The president wished her luck. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia was offered the role.

The position has been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left in late August. The White House James S. Brady Press Briefing Room hasn't hosted a briefing for the press since Sept. 3, when Vice President JD Vance addressed reporters and took questions.
In a social media post, Zacharia said "serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime."

"The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," she said in the post. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out. Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting."
Zacharia, who lives in California, completed her undergraduate and law degrees at Pepperdine University in Malibu, according to her LinkedIn.

Earlier this year, Zacharia wrote an op-ed for the New York Post about her experience wearing a "Make America Great Again" hat to her local gym. She said the owner of the gym ultimately asked her to stop wearing it.
"I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," she wrote. "This is raw, unfiltered intolerance. Freedom of speech doesn't evaporate at the gym door."
"The First Amendment has no 'discomfort' clause," she added, although the First Amendment protects against government censorship of speech, not private businesses.

title: Book excerpt: "Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy"
summary: Kerry Kennedy writes of her mother's inspiring example, from before and after the assassination of her father, Robert F. Kennedy.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Ethel Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy were married nearly 18 years, and had 11 children together, before he was felled by an assassin's bullet in June 1968. In her memoir, "Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy" (to be published Oct. 13 by HarperOne), daughter Kerry Kennedy writes of her mother's inspiring example, from before and after the murder of her father.
Read an excerpt below, and don't miss Rita Braver's conversation with Kerry Kennedy on "CBS Sunday Morning" October 11!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.
The Funeral Train ("We'll Cry Later")

The line outside St. Patrick's Cathedral, where Daddy lay in state, was a mile long. One hundred thousand mourners passed by his coffin. Family and friends took turns holding vigil. The first time I witnessed that public outpouring of grief was when I accompanied Mum, along with my siblings, to a special service the night before the funeral. Mum's face, swathed in a black veil, was composed, almost serene, as we knelt to pray. The singer Andy Williams, a close friend of Mum and Daddy, sang "Ave Maria" a cappella, his resonant tenor echoing through the cathedral. I was thinking that Mary and all her angels were in the very room with us. Mum, Grandma Rose, and our aunts told us that Daddy was in Heaven and happy to be with Uncle Jack, his eldest brother, Joe, and his sister Kick. I could picture that lovely reunion. I was eight years old, and as a child had such a strong sense of Heaven as a physical place that when I flew in an airplane I chose the window seat so I could try to find Heaven in the clouds. Mum also believed Heaven was real, and she felt the full presence of God when she prayed. Her faith kept her going. It lifted us all through those awful days.

[The next day] we were on the funeral train taking Daddy from New York to Washington, D.C., for the burial. Twenty-one rail cars carried hundreds of friends and family members on that slow, final journey. I looked out the windows, and all along the tracks people were lined up to wave or had their heads bowed in mourning. Some were in suits, some in denim overalls, a lot of women and girls in pastel summer dresses. There were Black and white people all out in force, sometimes mixed together, though it depended on which town we were passing through. There were people in military uniforms and young men with long hair and scraggly beards. There were a lot of nuns and priests, and people crossing themselves and crying.

Part of the time, I stood in the back, with the casket. I liked being in that car because no one spoke; it was very quiet and still, except for the rhythmic hum of people I loved repeating Hail Marys and the Lord's Prayer.

When I walked through the train it was like a dream: All of our family, all of Daddy's and Mum's friends from across the country, filled the seats. I thought this must be what Heaven is like—all our friends, all together, all at once. Looking out the windows of that train at people holding handkerchiefs and American flags, and then being inside with all those friends, it felt as if waves of loss and tenderness were washing over me. In the midst of horror, there was such love and intimacy.

At the center of it all was my mother. She walked up and down the aisle, car after car, greeting old friends, comforting them in their grief, even as her own grief must have been overwhelming. "I haven't seen you in so long," she told one passenger. "Thanks for coming." She patted the back of another who was bent over in sorrow. "We'll cry later," she said.

My mother endured more tragedy in her lifetime than anyone should. But her spirit proved indomitable. All through the funeral I had been watching Mum closely and absorbing the lesson that one way to conquer despair is to focus on other people's needs. And to keep moving, always keep moving.

Ethel Kennedy quickly became a beloved figure in the United States and across the globe. In magazine polls in the years to come, she was often voted the most admired woman in America. She seemed to have sailed through grief with her ever-present social grace and aplomb. That was only part of the story, though—the public side. Behind the scenes was a tale much more complex and, in many ways, more inspiring.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed Dec. 3, email states
summary: Nidal Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
story: An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, 2026, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.
Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday that the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
CBS Texas has reached out to Fort Hood for comment and was directed to Army headquarters.

In addition to the 13 people Hasan killed on Nov. 5, 2009, 32 others were injured. Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.
The last military execution took place 65 years ago, when the Army executed Pvt. John Bennett by hanging after he was convicted of rape and the attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.
The last execution by firing squad happened during World War II, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was put to death in France for desertion.

Hasan, now 56, was an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shootings. He had served two decades in the Army. Witnesses described hearing Hasan shout "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down when police returned fire.
Since his conviction, Hasan has been on death row at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.
Why a firing squad?

According to Army regulation 190-55, military executions can only be approved by the president. A 2019 revision removed the term "lethal injection" from this regulation and left the method up to the secretary of the Army's designation. According to the guidelines, the method is recommended to the secretary by the provost marshal general.

According to this order, the prisoner is informed of the president's decision in person by the commandant, who is accompanied by a chaplain and, if available, a defense attorney. After the notification, the prisoner becomes a "condemned prisoner."
The victims

Family members of those who died were notified of the planned execution before the announcement was made. They, along with survivors, were asked if they wanted to attend. The group, bonded in tragedy, has been intertwined over the last 17 years. This is what many hope will be the final chapter in the tragedy.
Below are the names of those who died.
Lt. Col. Juanita Warman, 55
Maj. Libardo Eduardo Caraveo, 52

title: Terminal in Riyadh airport hit again, a day after deadly strike killed 12
summary: The strike on King Khalid International Airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
story: A passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was attacked again on Sunday, one day after a deadly strike on the Riyadh airport killed at least 12 people, including a U.S. citizen, and wounded hundreds of others.
The second attack comes as Yemen's Houthi group said they carried out at least four operations targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh since Saturday.
Saudi's civil aviation authority said the latest Riyadh airport attack caused injuries and that damage assessments are underway.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that the attacks are in response to "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people," CBS News partner BBC News reported. He claimed Saudi Arabia launched more than 120 airstrikes in the past 24 hours in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen.

The Houthis said their other targets included the Shugadam gas facility, which belongs to Saudi's national petroleum and natural gas company Aramco, the Tanajib oil refinery, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, the BBC reported.
Saudi's civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on King Fahd Airport.
There were no immediate details about the latest strike at King Khalid Airport, which hit the same complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights.

Saturday's strike at the airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

The airport remains closed on Sunday and Saudi Arabia moved Riyadh schools online amid the Houthis' latest threat. Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Earlier on Saturday, the Houthies threatened new attacks on the kingdom's airports, except for the holy sites of Mecca and Medina, warning passengers not to travel.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Saree wrote on X.
He urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously."
On Sunday, the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.
The attack on Riyadh's airport on Saturday drew condemnation from the United Nations and world leaders, including President Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.
A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks by Iran's proxies are "pushing the region into a spiral of violence."
"They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes," she wrote on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned "in the strongest possible terms" the attack on King Khalid Airport and extended his condolences.

"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," he said in a statement shared on X. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East—one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region.

The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the 309 people injured, some in serious condition.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera News television.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Sunday that one of its citizens died after being wounded in the attack on the Riyadh airport a day earlier.

"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today. We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased," the embassy wrote in a statement posted on X.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The airport has no military facilities.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
