title: India's "Cockroach Party" leaders released from detention
summary: Three leaders of India's Cockroach Janata Party, a youth movement, were released Sunday, a day after they were detained ahead of protests against a contentious revision of voter lists.
story: Leaders of the Cockroach Janata Party, an Indian youth movement, were released Sunday, a day after they were detained ahead of protests against a contentious revision of voter lists. The movement is demanding the resignation of the country's election chief.

The three leaders — Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka — were freed on condition that they commit "no breach of peace for one year," Ratna Singh, the movement's legal director, said in a social media post. It was unclear what the condition meant or whether it would restrict their participation in protests.
Police had boarded the leaders' flight from Mumbai after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday and took them into custody as they prepared to lead a demonstration in New Delhi.

Authorities have launched a sweeping security crackdown in the capital, detaining more than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition lawmakers. Train services to the capital were canceled, metro stations closed and mobile internet suspended in parts of the city.
Most of those detained were released late Saturday, police said.
After his release, Dipke called Prime Minister Narendra Modi "an embarrassment to India."
"Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully," he wrote on X.

title: At least 12 killed, more than 300 hurt in strike on Saudi airport, officials say
summary: At least 12 people, including one American, were killed and 309 others injured in a strike Saturday​ on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
story: At least 12 people, including one American, were killed and 309 others injured in a strike Saturday on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi officials.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said those killed included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis and one person each from Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Those injured were receiving treatment at several hospitals, officials said in a social media post. Several people were in critical condition.
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the airport, which is the country's main international airport.

A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. The attack was the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh — and it marked the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
The Saudi kingdom has faced an extraordinary series of assaults on the new front in the Iran war that has opened up involving the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
President Trump said earlier Saturday he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

"We may. We're gonna look at it," Mr. Trump told reporters when asked about the possibility. "We just found out about the recent attack [on the airport]. So we'll make a decision — we move very quickly."

"The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.
A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."

The Houthis have not yet claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike. However, the Houthis did claim attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. In Saturday's strike, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
In a statement posted to social media, Hans Grundberg, United Nations special envoy to Yemen, called Saturday's strike a "dangerous escalation" that poses "a grave threat to regional security."
Riyadh airport operations have been suspended

Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.
Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry, hours after the latest one, was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.

Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told The Associated Press and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.

Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged on the ground, with no passengers on board.

title: Trump says Ukraine needs new president, blames Zelenskyy for diesel prices
summary: President Trump's criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy comes after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people, including three children, in Ukraine.
story: President Trump said Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting the current leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia.

"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump told reporters as he was leaving the White House for a trip to Tennessee.
He also blamed Ukraine's recent strikes on Russian oil refineries for contributing to high diesel prices before the midterm election, despite the ongoing war in Iran.
"He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Mr. Trump said.
Mr. Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, Russia's invasion of Ukraine "would have never started."
"There was no reason that the war with Ukraine and Russia started," he said. "It started due to incompetence."

Zelenskyy, Mr. Trump said, has "lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukraine's foreign minister said Saturday that Zelenskyy had the backing of the Ukrainian people and deserved support.

"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said of Zelenskyy in a post on X. "Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support."
The American president's comments came hours after Zelenskyy offered pointed criticism of a new diesel deal between the U.S. and Russia. He said the deal would help bankroll Moscow's war in Ukraine.

According to Mr. Trump's announcement on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Mr. Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.
The Treasury Department announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
"It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

Former Vice President Mike Pence blasted the deal on social media, saying it "makes no sense and is a betrayal of the legacy and leadership of the late Senator Lindsey Graham," who was a fierce Ukraine supporter. He added that Mr. Trump should "rescind the deal immediately."

"America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin's war machine," Pence said in the post. "Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration.   Putin doesn't want peace. Putin wants Ukraine. I have no doubt that if Putin overruns Ukraine, it will only be a matter of time until Russia's military crosses a border that our troops will have to deal with him."
Russian strikes kill at least 20 in Ukraine
Meanwhile, Russian strikes killed at least 20 people, including three children, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, officials said on Saturday.
Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the regional military administration, said Saturday. At least 18 people were wounded.
Missiles also struck Kyiv in a daytime attack Saturday. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said four people were wounded.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.
He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities," adding that "different signals are needed."

title: Man attacked by tiger in England after entering enclosure at wildlife park
summary: The incident occurred at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster, police said.
story: A man sustained serious injuries Saturday after entering the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England, police said.

The incident occurred at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster at about 1:35 p.m., South Yorkshire Police said in a statement. The tigers remained inside the enclosure and there was no danger to the wider public, the force said.
The Yorkshire Ambulance Service said it dispatched two ambulances, an air ambulance and a doctor to attend the scene. Authorities didn't immediately release information about the victim's injuries.
"We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,'' the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its "Land of the Tigers" attraction opening in 2011.

The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or playing in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

Visitors to several zoos and wildlife parks around the world have tried to enter tiger enclosures. A woman was caught in 2024 jumping over a fence and taunting a tiger at the Cohanzick Zoo in New Jersey. In 2016, a zookeeper was fatally attacked by a Malayan tiger at a Florida zoo when she entered the enclosure for the tigers' night house, a medical examiner's investigation found.

Several years earlier, in 2012, a man jumped from an area near the monorail in the Bronx Zoo over two fences, including an electrified one, in one bound to get into the tiger enclosure, police said. He was severely injured in what appeared to be a suicide attempt, police said.

title: India detains thousands of "Cockroach" movement youth protesters in crackdown
summary: The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people.
story: Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters on Saturday.

India's youth "Cockroach" movement had sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.

The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.

Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi's party, dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchic elements." "Their flop show has been completely demolished," Patra said.
A large-scale crackdown

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement, Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas, with police briefly detaining some of them.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights?" said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"

The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi's government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world's largest democracy.
Opposition leaders accuse government of curbing dissent
The latest crackdown renewed criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police.

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

title: Pope says death penalty "inadmissible" amid U.S. plans to livestream execution
summary: The firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, will be livestreamed, the U.S. Defense Department said.
story: Pope Leo XIV declared that capital punishment is "inadmissible" as the United States plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

The American pope, in a post on X marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Catholic teaching states that capital punishment attacks the inherent dignity of a human being.

"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," read the post under Leo's official handle, @Pontifex. "Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption."

The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.
The decision to livestream the execution has drawn fierce criticism.

Leo's post didn't refer specifically to the planned execution in the U.S. or the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee late last month which has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, it is common for the pope's official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations like the World Day Against the Death Penalty.
However, Leo's post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was "unacceptable."

Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was "truly incomprehensible" and "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle."

"The Church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent… ," Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don't know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."
The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" at the Pentagon's plans.

"In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
On Friday, President Trump said he approves of Hasan's execution by firing squad.

"He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad," Mr. Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
Mr. Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.

Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic convert, appeared to cast doubt on Friday about the livestream, telling reporters he wouldn't watch it and, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

Pope Leo XIV

title: Abbas delays Palestinian elections to 2027, marking 20 years without a vote
summary: Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats.
story: President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.

Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.

The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.

The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.

The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.

Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.

The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.

Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.

Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.

"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

title: 3 men found guilty in murders of American, Australian surfers in Mexico
summary: A local judge has found three men guilty of murdering two Australian brothers and their American friend in Baja California, Mexico, in April 2024.
story: A local judge on Friday found three men guilty of the murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend in April 2024 in the Mexican state of Baja California.

The trial for the triple homicide that shocked Mexico and drew international attention concluded Friday after Judge Raúl Hernández in the coastal city of Ensenada ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, alias "El Kekas," Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N" were responsible for the murders of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson and American Carter Redd Rhoad.
The defendants, who had been in custody for more than two years, were also found guilty of armed robbery and armed carjacking.

Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom the murders of her sons had taken "the future we had imagined with them," CBS News' partner network BBC News reported. Debra Robinson and her husband, Martin Robinson, were at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said, BBC reported.

The three friends traveled to Baja California in April 2024 to surf, but shortly after arriving in the town of Punta San Jose, about 50 miles from Ensenada, they were reported missing. Their bodies were found on May 3 in a well.
García, identified as the perpetrator of the murders, was arrested in May 2024 in connection to the case, along with his ex-partner Ary Gisell Silva Raya, Irineo Francisco "N" and Ángel Jesús "N."

During the monthlong trial, chilling details of the brutal crime were revealed. Silva Raya testified last month during a hearing that García confessed to her that he arrived at the tent where the foreigners were staying with a 9 mm pistol.
Upon seeing him, they began throwing their belongings to prevent him from attacking them, and one of them begged for his life, which the assailant ignored, she said.

The state prosecutor's office reported that Silva Raya arrived in Punta San Jose on April 27, 2024, where she met the three foreigners and "instigated one of her companions to rob them," which was carried out the following day.

The woman, who was found in possession of one of the victims' cellphones, was sentenced in November 2025 to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to "aggravated robbery with violence" and "vehicle theft with violence" in an expedited proceeding. However, García and his two accomplices decided to go to trial.
The judge will announce the final sentence on Oct. 16. The Baja California State Attorney General's Office requested for each defendant the "exemplary sentence" of 210 years in prison.

title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge Navi Pillay
summary: Nobel Peace Prize 2026 was awarded to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a former judge on the International Criminal Court, drawing a quick, angry rebuke from Israel.
story: The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 was awarded Friday to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born former judge with the International Criminal Court who went on to become the United Nations human rights chief and is still serving with the U.N.'s other judicial body, the International Court of Justice. She also led a U.N. inquiry last year that accused Israel of genocide in the Gaza Strip, and Israel was quick to condemn her receiving the honor on Friday.

The Nobel Committee said it was honoring Pillay "for her efforts to promote peace and international law," and that awarding the prize to someone with her body of work on international justice was a message to those seeking to undermine international law institutions.

The South African-born former United Nations human rights chief, who is 85, was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
"This is definitely a message to those who are undermining the international system and institutions," Frydnes said.

"The system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack," he said, noting what the committee saw as a shift "towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice."

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has come under fire from Israel and the Trump administration in recent years, with the U.S. imposing sanctions against the U.N. court last year after it issued an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump accused the court of "illegitimate and baseless actions targeting America and our close ally Israel."
The ICC condemned the U.S. sanctions against its staff and said they were intended to "harm (the Court's) independent and impartial judicial work."

Pillay served as an ICC judge from 2003 until 2008, when she resigned to take on the role of United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She was the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that said last year it had concluded Israel's actions in Gaza amounted to genocide. Israel dismissed the report as "scandalous."

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge for the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is separate to the ICC, in the case of Gambia v. Myanmar, in which Myanmar's ruling military junta stands accused of genocide over its treatment of the nation's Rohingya Muslim minority in the western state of Rakhine.

Frydnes said the committee wasn't immediately able to reach Pillay Friday to tell her she had been awarded the prize, adding from the podium that if she was watching and saw a call coming in from a Norwegian phone number, to "please pick up."

She soon appeared in a video posted on social media by the head of Amnesty International, being applauded by well-wishers at the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were put on trial for their crimes against humanity after World War II.

"Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom... when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award," Pillay said. "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack ... This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."

"If you clap a little bit louder I may share this prize with Trump," she quipped, drawing laughs from the crowd. She said that when she was informed that she had been awarded the prize, she first thought "it must be a joke," and that as a "lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this thing."

She noted that she was lauded by the Nobel committee for her courage, which she questioned, saying: "You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's an impartial decision you make."
Israel condemns Pillay's honor, U.S. further sanctions ICC

The Israeli Foreign Ministry blasted the Nobel committee for awarding the prize to Pillay on Friday, saying in a statement posted online that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
It condemned the committee for awarding her as "the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."

A separate statement posted on the X account of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the Nobel committee had "lost its moral compass. It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state."

The Trump administration, hours later, announced further sanctions against the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the ICC a "threat to U.S. sovereignty" and said the new measures were deemed necessary to ensure the court, which the U.S. has never been a state party to, can never prosecute a U.S. national.

He said the new sanctions would "ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," adding: "We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."

The ICC has never prosecuted or indicted a U.S. national, but it has investigated the actions of U.S. forces abroad, in countries where it does have jurisdiction, including Afghanistan, and it could theoretically seek to prosecute Americans.

According to Human Rights Watch, there are "limited situations in which the ICC has jurisdiction over the nationals of countries, such as the U.S., that have not joined the Rome Statute. This includes when a citizen of a non-member country commits war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide on the territory of an ICC member country. That's why U.S. citizens may be subject to the court's jurisdiction as it investigates alleged grave crimes that took place in Afghanistan."
Nobel prize history

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman "who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness."

Machado gave President Trump, who has long said he deserves the prize, her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: The Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for "bold and inventive" works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Education activist Malala Yousafzai is the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate; she won at 17 in 2014.

The United States is the most-credited country, with 24 awards naming U.S. institutions or individuals, ahead of the United Kingdom (13) and Switzerland (11). No laureate listed as American has won since then-President Barack Obama was awarded in 2009.

The prize has gone unawarded on 19 occasions, most of them during the world wars. In 1948, the year Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, no prize was awarded; he had been nominated 12 times and never won.
In 1939, a Swedish member of parliament nominated Adolf Hitler, then withdrew the nomination, saying it was never meant seriously.

title: 'Reagan' star Lesley-Anne Down relives 3 terrifying brushes with death: ‘I should have been killed’
summary: Lesley-Anne Down recalls three harrowing brushes with danger, including a chilling link to the Moors murders and a terrifying fake taxi escape.
story: The producer shared the lesson he learned from Ronald Reagan that he has tried to apply to his own life.
Lesley-Anne Down believes she's already used up three of her nine lives.
The actress, who takes on the Iron Lady opposite Dennis Quaid in "Reagan," has shown plenty of steel off-screen, recalling "three times in my life when I should have been killed by other people."
For Down, known for her roles in "North and South" and "Upstairs, Downstairs," the unsettling experiences began when she was just 10 years old.
MORGAN FAIRCHILD SAYS TWO MEN ONCE ABDUCTED HER OFF NYC STREET AS BYSTANDERS LAUGHED
Actress Lesley-Anne Down plays former U.K. Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in the biopic "Reagan." (Rawhide Pictures)

"I remember there was a little girl, one of a number of children who were murdered and buried on the moors in England," the British star told Fox News Digital. "There was a little girl who had dark hair and blue eyes and was my age, 10. Her name was Leslie Ann Downey. My mother got phone calls when this little girl's identity was announced."

"It wasn't me, of course," said Down. "But it certainly freaked her out. Leslie Ann Downey was about six months younger than me. It turned out there were two people, a man and a woman. Ian Brady and Myra Hindley. They were the killers."
Lesley Ann Downey, age 10, one of the children murdered by Ian Brady and Myra Hindley, is shown in a photo. (Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

Brady and Hindley murdered five children between 1963 and 1965, with several of their victims buried on Saddleworth Moor in northern England, according to The Associated Press. The case became known as the Moors murders.
WATCH: ‘REAGAN’ PRODUCER SHARES WHAT HE LEARNED FROM RESEARCHING RONALD REAGAN

Hindley and Brady were arrested in 1965 and later convicted of murders connected to the case. The five victims were Downey, Pauline Reade, John Kilbride, Keith Bennett and Edward Evans, who ranged in age from 10 to 17. Bennett's body has never been found.
Ian Brady and Myra Hindley were found guilty of murder in Chester, England, on May 6, 1966. Both were sentenced to life imprisonment. (Bettmann Archive)
According to accounts of the case, Downey was abducted after Hindley asked her to help carry packages to a car.
Hindley died in 2002 while serving a life sentence. Brady died in a psychiatric hospital in 2017.

Floral tributes overlook Saddleworth Moor in Saddleworth, United Kingdom, where the body of missing Keith Bennett may be buried. Bennett was abducted by moors murderers Ian Brady and Myra Hindley on June 16, 1964, and they never disclosed his burial location. (Getty Images)
The case frightened Down’s family. But it wouldn’t be the last time danger came close to home.

"A year later, my mother and I were coming back from the launderette with the washing," Down said. "I ran ahead. I left the washing, I left my mother and just ran ahead. I ran uphill and then over a footbridge. As I ran over the footbridge, a man came from the other side. He's walking towards me. He stops in the middle of the footbridge and says, 'Hello.' He then was going to put me in his car."
Harrison Ford and Lesley-Anne Down on the set of "Hanover Street," written and directed by Peter Hyams. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"He told me he needed a babysitter, and he would call my parents when we got to his house," Down said. "I remember having one foot in the car. Seeing my mother broke the spell. Then he was gone. But I still remember that horrible feeling swooping in before my mother came."

English actress Lesley-Anne Down took on the role of Margaret Thatcher in the 2024 biopic "Reagan." (BSR Agency)
Years later, when Down was 18, she ordered a taxi. But when a car pulled up in the countryside, she climbed in and quickly noticed something was wrong.

"As soon as he's driving away, I'm already feeling that horrible feeling," Down said. "I looked around and there were no radios or anything, like a taxi is supposed to have. So I said, 'Could you pull over, please?' He said, 'Oh no, we don't need to pull over. We'll be there soon.'"
Patrick Swayze and Lesley-Anne Down appear in the TV miniseries "North and South," circa 1985. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
Down said she decided to jump from the moving car.
Lesley-Anne Down poses for a portrait in New York circa 1980. (Getty Images)

"I opened the door and threw myself out of the 25-mile an hour car," she said. "I fell onto the curb in a puddle. I was covered in blood. There was nobody around. What did he do? He pulled the car door shut and drove off at top speed. I didn't freeze up because I couldn't. That feeling was familiar to me. I've been through it."

Down, now 72, earned a Golden Globe nomination for her role opposite Patrick Swayze in "North and South." She also starred opposite Peter Sellers in "The Pink Panther Strikes Again" and Harrison Ford in "Hanover Street." She later appeared on the soap opera "The Bold and the Beautiful."
Lesley-Anne Down as Madeline Fabray LaMotte Main in the TV miniseries 'North and South,' 1985. (Getty Images)
When asked what advice she would give to women pursuing a career in Hollywood, Down had a warning: "Never go anywhere alone."

"Always have your agent or your publicist with you at all times," she said. "Even if they have to be on the phone a lot and out in the lobby, just always have somebody with you at all times as you chase your dreams."

"I made a decision many, many years ago, actually about 2012, that I wanted out," Down said. "I was in a position where I didn't have to. Things were very good. And I was fortunate to have all my eggs in a basket and make a choice."
Lesley-Anne Down attends the 6,000th episode of "The Bold and the Beautiful" at CBS Television City in Los Angeles on Feb. 7, 2011. (FilmMagic)
Down has since moved from California to Georgia. She also said she has no regrets about turning down two opportunities to play a Bond girl.
Sean Connery and Lesley-Anne Down in a scene from the 1979 film "The Great Train Robbery." (Getty Images)

"I guess my thought process was maybe a little old-fashioned, but being a Bond girl didn't really resonate with me," she explained. "Being a Bond girl was skimpy clothing, pretty face, not much dialogue, no acting involved, kissing James at the end in a spacecraft or whatever. I thought if I became a Bond girl, then I'd be a Bond girl for life. I didn't want that for myself."
The opportunity to play Thatcher came "out of the blue," Down said. She accepted the role and said she was grateful for the experience.
Lesley Anne-Down attends The Hollywood Show held at the Westin LAX Hotel in Los Angeles on Feb. 10, 2018. (WireImage)
"She loved and believed in England and the English people," Down said. "Her counterpart, Mr. Reagan, also believed and loved the American people."

Down said leaders should "encompass what Thatcher and Reagan both believed," including doing "anything and everything they can for the longevity and success of the nation."

For Down, taking on the role of Thatcher became another unexpected chapter in a life that has repeatedly taken surprising turns. But these days, the actress is content with where those turns have taken her.

title: Elon Musk's mom Maye nearly turned down SI Swimsuit cover over 'wrinkles and cellulite'
summary: Maye Musk nearly turned down her Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover over wrinkle fears, but a phone call from her daughter changed everything.
story: Author Maye Musk joins Fox & Friends to discuss her new memoir "Timeless." She shares her story of escaping a toxic marriage, raising three children as a single mother and finding career success after 50.
Maye Musk nearly passed on the chance to make a splash in Sports Illustrated Swimsuit because she worried about looking "wrinkly" in the iconic magazine.

The Canadian-born, South African-raised model made history in 2022 as the oldest Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover model at 74. Martha Stewart later broke the record at 81 in 2023. Now, Musk is looking back at the milestone and her journey from a single mother of three to a sought-after model in her new book, "Timeless."

"At my age, you have wrinkles and cellulite on your arms and on your thighs, so I prefer to wear long sleeves," the mother of tech mogul Elon Musk told Fox News Digital. "So, the idea of wearing a swimsuit was very uncomfortable. But then my daughter called me. I told her they were going to be shooting in Belize. She instantly said, 'You've got to go. Belize is beautiful.' So, I did. I took a chance."
MAYE MUSK DEFENDS SYDNEY SWEENEY'S NUDE SPORTS AD AND RECALLS 12-YEAR PATH TO CITIZENSHIP

Canadian-South African model Maye Musk arrives for the screening of the film "Asteroid City" during the 76th edition of the Cannes Film Festival in Cannes, on May 23, 2023. Musk has written a new book, "Timeless." (Patricia De Melo Moreira/AFP via Getty Images)

In the book, Musk wrote, "I was still 73. My skin showed the signs of my weight having cycled up and down so many times in my life, including for each of my pregnancies. I'm wrinkly and I have cellulite. Swimsuit model?"
Despite her worries, Musk said she felt at ease when she began posing for photographer Yu Tsai. She even wore colorful two-pieces for the occasion.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
Maye Musk is seen here posing for the 2022 Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue cover on Jan. 29, 2022, in Belize (Yu Tsai/Sports Illustrated via Contour RA by Getty Images)

"It was very unusual," she said with a laugh. "I've been told all of my life that I'm not a swimsuit model. When you think of swimsuit models, you think of the Victoria's Secret models. Those are really special body shapes. So it was a challenge for me. But as I say, you have to take a chance in life. And I knew they're not going to publish ugly photos. At one point, I felt so at ease that I even started dancing with the local people. I was in awe of exploring a new country, a new culture. That's what I love doing. And I got to celebrate me."
WATCH: MAYE MUSK DISCUSSES RAISING ELON MUSK, ESCAPING TOXIC MARRIAGE IN NEW MEMOIR ‘TIMELESS’
Looking back, Musk said she wonders why she was so nervous.

"When women go to the beach, they wrap a towel around themselves," she said. "But men, they could be obese, and they're still strutting in Speedos with such confidence. We really have to make a change. And if any man insults your body, well, they can get lost. There's always going to be somebody who feels the need to trash on you. It's not fair. But it's all about embracing who you are and not apologizing for that."
Maye Musk's book "Timeless: The Art of Reinvention and Resilience at Any Age" is available now. (Harper Wave)
Musk didn't undergo a makeover to appear younger for the cover. Her signature silver hair remained untouched.
Maye Musk attends the launch of the 2025 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit issue at Hard Rock Hotel New York on May 15, 2025, in New York City. (Getty Images for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit)

"Why do I need to color my hair?" Musk said. "You have to do the roots every four weeks, and I used to do them myself. Your hair then becomes very brittle because it's so damaged. And it grows out. And then I decided to cut my hair short. Soon after, I had four billboards in Times Square. I didn't feel like a granny. I felt fashionable."
It wasn't the first time Musk took a chance on a modeling gig.

From left: Christie Brinkley, Maye Musk, Brooks Nader, Kate Love, Kate Upton and Lily Aldridge attend the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Celebration of the 2024 Issue Release and 60th Anniversary with Swimsuit Island in Hollywood, Florida, on May 17, 2024. (Getty Images for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit)
In her book, Musk describes a phone call she received from her agent: "Tomorrow, you pose naked for the cover of TIME magazine. You're the only model they want and they won't budge."
Musk had never done a nude shoot because, as she wrote, "nobody had ever asked."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Maye Musk, an author and dietician, also has campaigns with high-profiled brands like CoverGirl and Dior Beauty. (Fadil Berisha)
Before stripping down, Musk sought advice from her children.

"I picked up the phone to dial Elon first, then stopped myself," Musk wrote. "I already knew what he would say: 'Absolutely not.' He was not the kind of son who wanted his mother naked on magazine covers. Not prudish, but definitely more conservative when it came to nudity. So I called Tosca. I wasn't too surprised to find that she was not in love with the idea, either. 'You never do naked!' she said. Her instinct was protective, not wanting me to risk an uncomfortable experience."
Maye Musk and Elon Musk attend the 2022 Met Gala celebrating "In America: An Anthology of Fashion" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 2, 2022, in New York City. (Getty Images)

"Finally, I called Kimbal," she wrote. "Of my three children, he is the most relaxed and free-spirited. (He met his current wife at Burning Man.) He had a completely different perspective. ‘It’s TIME magazine. It’s journalism,’ he said. ‘Not some nudie magazine. It’ll be tasteful. You have nothing to worry about. Do it.’"
Musk told Fox News Digital it was important for her to get her children's approval before posing nude.
Maye Musk walks the runway at the Philipp Plein fashion show during Milan Fashion Week Womenswear Fall/Winter 2023/2024 on Feb. 25, 2023, in Milan, Italy. (Getty Images)
"Well, would you want your mother naked on the front cover of a magazine?" she said.

"But it was Kimbal who encouraged me. He said it would be tasteful. He's always been a free spirit. And I trust him. When I arrived for the photoshoot, they were very careful with me. You have a makeup artist who has to go through your whole body. Then they did my hair and very plain makeup. Then they sat me with a mirror in front of me, so I could see exactly what the photographer sees."
From left: Kimbal Musk, his mother Maye Musk and his wife Christiana Musk attend the Kering Foundation Caring For Women Dinner in New York City. (Getty Images)

"The photographer came in for the shoot, and maybe five minutes later, it was over," she said. "It was really quick and very respectful. They immediately brought a robe for me. I got changed and went home. That's all there was to it."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Maye Musk attends the Sports Illustrated Swim Issue Launch Party at the Hard Rock Hotel on May 16, 2024, in New York. (WWD via Getty Images)

For Musk, aging with confidence isn't just about embracing wrinkles and silver hair. The longtime dietitian also believes that taking care of your health plays an important role in feeling your best at any age.
Maye Musk attends the Juzui FW25 Collection show at The Glasshouse in New York City on Feb. 7, 2025. (Getty Images for Juzui)

"It gets harder to lose weight as you get older," Musk said. "With my patients, I always tell them to plan ahead. If you get hungry, there's no salad next to you. There's a donut. Also, only eat when you're hungry. And when you are hungry, make sure there is healthy food around, no desserts or chocolates. And if my patient didn't take the journey seriously, I would tell them, 'You can't come anymore.'"
From left: Tosca Musk and her mother Maye Maye Musk attend the "Downton Abbey: The Grand Finale" New York premiere at Jazz at Lincoln Center on Sept. 8, 2025. (WireImage)

"Even 10 pounds can make you feel uncomfortable," she said. "Everything is tight and you don't have confidence. You have to track your food intake. If a patient goes off what I recommended, they need to explain why. You need to hold yourself accountable if you want to make smarter choices for your health."
Maye Musk attends the launch of the 2022 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit issue and debut of Pay With Change at Hard Rock Hotel New York on May 19, 2022. (Getty Images)
Musk said each decade of her life has been better than the last. At 78, she's happily embracing aging and hopes other women will do the same.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Maye Musk visits "Fox & Friends" at Fox News Channel Studios in New York City on Sept. 18, 2026. (Getty Images)

"When my mom was 86, she moved from South Africa to Canada and started all over," Musk said. "She was an artist. When she was nearing 90, her hands weren't strong enough to do the wood carvings she loved. So, by 94, she started doing computer art. My older sister taught her. She died at 98. But she always remained curious and busy. She was always exploring."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

From left: Maye Musk, Christen Harper, Hailey Clauson and Georgina Burke attend the Swimsuit on Location event hosted by Sports Illustrated Swimsuit at Hard Rock Seminole in Hollywood, Florida, on May 21, 2022. (Getty Images for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit)

"You're never too old to start again," Musk said. "And don't worry about the wrinkles. A man doesn't care if he gets wrinkles. He still has his confidence. When you get insecure, you become less attractive. I didn't do anything to my face because I wanted to frown and have expression. But also, don't mix with people who make you feel insecure. They're not your friends. And there will be people who will push you down. You can't stay down. You just have to get up and show your talents, who you are."

title: Prince Edward told girlfriend he wanted 'two wives' before marrying royal family's 'secret weapon': memoir
summary: Ruthie Henshall claims in her memoir that Prince Edward once told her he wished he could have two wives before marrying Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh.
story: Royal historian Hugo Vickers, who wrote a new book on the late monarch, explains how the Queen Mother favored another suitor, but Queen Elizabeth ultimately chose Prince Philip.
Before Prince Edward married his royal family's "secret weapon," he once told an ex-girlfriend he wished he could have two wives, according to her new memoir.

Years earlier, the youngest son of the late Queen Elizabeth II dated actress Ruthie Henshall from 1988 to 1993. The West End star recently opened up about their romance in her memoir "The Showgirl and the Prince."

"Ruth, I couldn't put you through the job," Henshall recalled Edward telling her. "If I could, I would have two wives. One for the job, and one whom I loved, because you would never want to subject the woman you love to the job."
QUEEN ELIZABETH’S MOTHER WANTED HER TO MARRY ANOTHER MAN BEFORE PRINCE PHILIP: AUTHOR
Prince Edward's former flame, actress Ruthie Henshall, has written a memoir about their past romance. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images; David M. Benett/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Henshall, 59, and Edward, 62, for comment. A Buckingham Palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital the palace doesn't comment on books.

The pair first met in 1988 while Henshall was starring in "Cats" and Edward was working as a production assistant for Andrew Lloyd Webber's Really Useful Theatre Company. Henshall recalled making a beeline for the young prince when he arrived at the theater, playfully welcoming him "to the litter." A romance blossomed.
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"The Showgirl and the Prince" by Ruthie Henshall is available now. (Macmillan Publishers)
As their relationship grew more serious, Henshall said the realities of royal life began to set in.
WATCH: WHY QUEEN ELIZABETH REJECTED HER MOTHER'S PREFERRED MATCH: AUTHOR

"Honestly, this type of thinking is very standard for royal men throughout history," royal commentator Amanda Matta told Fox News Digital. "It's why royal mistresses were so common. For most of history, official marriages have been strategic and political arrangements. But the royals are still people, and they need intimacy and companionship like anyone else."
"Edward and Sophie have been married for over 25 years though and seem genuinely well-matched," Matta added.
Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh and Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh attend Day 2 of the Royal Windsor Horse Show in Home Park at Windsor Castle in Windsor, England, on May 2, 2024. (Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital it's easy to see why the prince was drawn to Henshall.
Actress Ruthie Henshall poses at a photocall for the Broadway musical "She Loves Me," date unknown. (PA Images via Getty Images)

"Ruthie Henshall has been a renowned theatre actress for several decades and Edward loved that world," he explained. "I personally remember working with the National Youth Music Theatre of which Edward was president, so Ruthie would have been his ideal partner at the time."

"The relationship went on for quite a while, and she was very nervous meeting the royal family, especially the queen," Turner said. "She forgot to curtsy to her. She also saw first-hand how the royal family operated with all their high jinks behind the scenes. I feel, although she felt deeply fond of Edward, she realized she could not marry him and still have her beloved career, which was her main passion."
Prince Edward during the wedding of Prince Andrew and Sarah Ferguson on July 23, 1986, in London. (WireImage)
In the book, Henshall wrote that, at least initially, she believed love might be enough to overcome the rigid expectations of marrying into the royal family.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Ruthie Henshall, as Marguerite, and Julian Ovenden, as Armand, perform in "Marguerite" at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in London. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"Of course, I had spotted some etiquette dilemmas, but typically I'd just assumed that I'd be able to break the rules," Henshall wrote. "That an exception would be made for me. I knew how to be a good girl, but I also knew that the possibility of me going out on a wild night and flashing my boobs in public was quite high. So, there were times when I felt torn about it all, but as far as I was concerned, I just wanted him."
Matta suggested Henshall would have adapted to royal life rather than challenged its traditions.
Diana, Princess of Wales, Prince Charles (left) and Prince Edward (right) visit Wanganui Collegiate in Wanganui, New Zealand, during the Royal Tour of New Zealand on April 22, 1983. (Getty Images)

"I don't think Henshall would have shaken up the institution very much," Matta said. "Growing up British, she would have understood the monarchy and grasped the weight of its traditions in a way a true outsider or foreigner might not. In that sense, she's similar to Edward himself. He has a big personality and a real love of the art world, but he's also deeply dutiful."
Ruthie Henshall is seen here performing on stage. (Redferns)
"I suspect that, if she'd married him, she would have adapted to the role rather than reinvented it. That may have even meant giving up her career, as Sophie later had to do."
Henshall wrote that she even turned to Sarah Ferguson, who was then married to the former Prince Andrew, for guidance.
Sarah Ferguson and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor are seen here on their wedding day in 1986. (Derek Hudson/Getty Images)
"One time when I was pining for Edward, I remember saying to Sarah, 'Would I ever be allowed to marry him?'" Henshall wrote.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sarah Ferguson, later Duchess of York, is surrounded by press photographers as she arrives for work in Mayfair, London, on March 3, 1986, shortly after the announcement of her engagement to Prince Andrew. (David Levenson/Getty Images)

"She probably knew there wasn't a chance in hell, but still kindly said she didn't know. Later, in her memoir, she described how she wanted to make any other woman coming into the royal family feel comfortable. And she absolutely did that. She made it her mission. So, I think I got the best side of her. And I was grateful to her on many occasions."

As Henshall's career continued to rise, she realized that she and Edward came from different worlds — worlds that were too different. Unwilling to give up her career for royal life, Henshall knew their relationship wasn't going to work.
Prince Edward is seen here in London, date unknown. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"We had wanted to be together," Henshall wrote. "We had tried desperately to make it work. But it seemed impossible because of who he was, and what I wanted to do in my career. There was this push–pull going on all the time, and we'd reached a point of no return."
Host Ruthie Henshall performs on stage during "Magic at the Musicals" at the Royal Albert Hall in London on May 4, 2017. (John Phillips/Getty Images)
"... I fell in love with him, and it wasn't because he was a prince. ... But at times, it was only too obvious that we came from different worlds."
Despite the breakup, Turner suggested Edward and Henshall remained close.
Ruthie Henshall attends The Olivier Awards with Mastercard at the Royal Opera House on April 3, 2016, in London, England. (Getty Images)
"As far as I know, their great friendship has remained through the decades," Turner said.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The newly-wed British royal couple Prince Edward and Sophie Rhys-Jones greet wellwishers on their way from Windsor Castle after their wedding ceremony on June 19, 1999. The royal couple took a brief ride through the historic town of Windsor. (AFP via Getty Images)
In 1999, Edward married Sophie, who later gave up her public relations career to become a full-time working royal. The couple have two children: Lady Louise, 22, and James, Earl of Wessex, 18.

Edward and Sophie decided not to use prince and princess titles for their children, allowing them to choose whether to use those titles and His or Her Royal Highness (HRH) styling when they turned 18, People magazine reported. Neither has chosen to do so.

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, James, Earl of Wessex and Lady Louise Windsor watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace following the coronation of King Charles III and Queen Camilla at Westminster Abbey in London, England, on May 6, 2023. (Getty Images)

Over the years, Sophie has earned a reputation as one of the royal family's most dedicated and reliable members. She has taken on additional royal duties as King Charles oversees a slimmed-down monarchy and has largely avoided public scandal.

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh and Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh attend The Royal British Legion's 80th Anniversary of D-Day Service of Remembrance at the National Memorial Arboretum in Alrewas, England, on June 6, 2024. (Getty Images)
"Prince Edward is married to the characterful, dependable, hardworking and personable Duchess Sophie," royal broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital.

"She is also viewed as the royal family's 'secret weapon.' She really is a huge asset to King Charles and the institution. Behind the scenes, she is putting duty above all else. She's also applauded for her personal patronages. Edward and Sophie are a great match."
Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, departs after attending a bingo night at The Royal Hospital Chelsea in London on April 29, 2025. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Matta suggested Edward ultimately found in Sophie the qualities he once believed he would need two different women to provide.

Duchess Sophie and Prince Edward depart Soufriere by boat on Day 6 of their Platinum Jubilee Royal Tour of the Caribbean on April 27, 2022, in Soufriere, Saint Lucia. (Getty Images)
"If anything, she ended up being everything he once thought he'd have to look for in different places!" Matta said.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Happy Days' star Anson Williams says he had to create a second career because sitcom pay wasn't enough
summary: Anson Williams reveals how conversations with David Cassidy and Barry Williams inspired him to pitch a musical act on the iconic sitcom.
story: ‘Happy Days’ star Anson Williams recalled how the sitcom was facing cancelation before it ‘exploded’ and became the number one most-watched show in America.
When playing Potsie Weber on "Happy Days" didn't pay well enough, actor Anson Williams came up with a side hustle: a music career.
In a recent interview on the "Still Here Hollywood Podcast," the 77-year-old actor revealed the singing sideline was simply a matter of 1970s economics.

"On 'Happy Days' we didn't have the same salaries they have today. Not even close," he said. "Nine hundred dollars an episode, $1,200 an episode. It was fine back then, but...it's not a lifetime of earnings there."

Williams said that after speaking to "Partridge Family" star David Cassidy and Barry Williams, of "The Brady Bunch," about how much money they were making by taking their singing acts off the show, he thought to himself, "Wait a minute. I sing. If I can convince Garry to put a band on the show, maybe I can get booked, and maybe I can get some extra income."
Williams shared he pitched the idea for him to sing on the show in order to make more money. (Michael Buckner/Penske Media via Getty Images)
‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS

After speaking with the show's creator, Garry Marshall, about the possibility of putting together a band to perform at Arnold's, the burger joint where Fonzie held court, the legendary director gave him a chance. Marshall told him he would have to pick a song and sing it to a bulldog, telling him, "If you're good, I get laughs. If you're bad, I get laughs. You're going to sing the bulldog."

"So I do it and then the letters start coming in, and he goes 'The people like it. The people like it.' He goes, 'We'll do more. You're in charge of it though,'" Williams recalled. "Then I got a major agent for that and started getting booked at state fairs for 10 years."
Williams added that his idea to sing on the show "started this whole career" that ended up being better for him monetarily, and was "just a whole other life experience."

After finding success as a musician as well as an actor, Williams said that Marshall approached him to express how proud he was of the actor, telling him, "You found an opportunity, and you're helping the show."
Williams previously shared with Fox News Digital that the show was on the verge of being cancelled. (ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

During an interview with Fox News Digital in March 2024, Williams revealed that while the show started as a hit with audiences, landing in the top 15 or 20, it slid down to 48th place at one point and was "on the verge of getting canceled."

"And Garry Marshall and Jerry Paris, our director, thought, ‘What if we changed the whole tone? What if we make it a live audience sitcom?’" Williams recalled. "So, half the season, one camera. The next season, one camera. The next season — two and a half in — they switch it to live audience. And the chemistry of the cast, the writing, was magic. That's the year we went to No. 1 in the world. That's when we exploded."

When the show became a huge success, Williams recalled Marshall advising him and his young co-stars to use their platforms for good, telling them to take the spotlight they found themselves in and "shine it on people that deserve it."

Following his time on "Happy Days," Williams pivoted to working more as a writer and director. He directed episodes of "Beverly Hills, 90210," "Sabrina the Teenage Witch," "Lizzie McGuire," "Charmed," "The Secret Life of an American Teenager" and more.

title: Michael Douglas' wildest Hollywood confessions: From A-list actress bite to Julia Roberts clash
summary: Michael Douglas alleges a confrontation with Julia Roberts, secret affairs and a cocaine-fueled evening with O.J. Simpson in his new memoir.
story: In his memoir, ‘One Helluva Ride,’ the actor admitted he had an affair with his ‘Basic Instinct’ co-star, Jeanne Tripplehorn. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
Michael Douglas is pulling back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes.

In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor-producer also opens up about secret affairs; heavy cocaine and alcohol use; a "rehab or divorce" ultimatum from his first wife, Diandra; and the painful family struggles that followed him from childhood into fatherhood.

Douglas details his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment and the Stage 4 cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality.
Michael Douglas's memoir, "One Helluva Ride," was released Oct. 6.  (Getty Images)
Here are the top ten bombshells:
MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET
An A-list actress bit him during casting dinner
Debra Winger allegedly bit Michael Douglas in the 1980s. (Getty Images)
In the book, Douglas recalled he and filmmakers were trying to convince Debra Winger to star as Joan Wilder in "Romancing the Stone," but the meeting took an odd turn.

"We took Debra to dinner and, once again, it was an epic meal. Any time you have dinner with Jack or Danny, it’s a riot. … But the real goal of the dinner was to get Debra on board to make Romancing the Stone, and no matter how hard we tried, she would not give us an answer, one way or the other. We were stuck in limbo.
MICHAEL DOUGLAS ADMITS HE ALMOST LEFT HIS WIFE FOR HIS 'BASIC INSTINCT' CO-STAR AFTER AFFAIR

"Stories had filtered back that Debra was delivering an incredible performance in Terms of Endearment, but also that she was difficult during shooting and had huge, blow-out fights with Shirley MacLaine.

"We all left the restaurant and were walking down the street when, the way somebody might punch you in the arm as you part company, Debra leaned over and bit me. I mean, she really bit me. Jesus, I had a whole set of teeth marks dug into my arm. We still had no answer from her, but that bite sealed the deal for me. No, thank you!"
MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES
Douglas said he later reenacted the moment for Fox executives, telling them, "She bit me. Hard. Look at the teeth marks in my arm."
Although the studio pushed back because Winger was a major star, Douglas held his ground. Winger ultimately did not join the project, and Kathleen Turner was cast in the role.
Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Winger for comment.
Douglas confronted Julia Roberts over his teenage son
Michael Douglas said he once snapped at Julia Roberts while drunk.  (Getty Images)
Douglas experienced another tense moment involving Julia Roberts at a Golden Globes party.

Douglas was at the event with his son Cameron, who was about 13 at the time. In the book, Douglas alleges that Roberts had her arm around Cameron and was "kind of nuzzling him." Douglas, who admits he was drunk, claims Cameron looked stunned.
BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG
"I told her, ‘Take your hands off my son and take that Golden Globe and stick it where the sun don’t shine,’" he wrote.
Douglas later apologized to Roberts and her boyfriend at the time, Kiefer Sutherland.
BRAD PITT ADMITS HE BEGAN DRINKING AGAIN AFTER YEARS OF SOBRIETY
"I sent Julia roses with an apology for my behavior, and then, back in the production office, I apologized to her and Kiefer in person," he wrote.
Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Roberts for comment.
Douglas reveals secret affair with Lee Purcell
Lee Purcell and Michael Douglas had a secret affair in the 1970s. (Getty Images)
While filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas says he and his married co-star Lee Purcell became lovers.

"As filming progressed, my relationship with Lee changed and we became lovers," he wrote. "Our intimate relationship was complicated by the fact that she was married, and we had to keep it a secret from the cast, crew, the people in the town we were filming in, and of course her husband. It was a passionate affair that lasted through filming."

Purcell told Fox News Digital, "This story came as a complete surprise to me. I have fond memories of Michael and our time together. However, our recall appears to differ. First, I remember the process of searching for his character of Adam after having already been hired by Steve McQueen for the role of Jerri Jo. Secondly, we had a strictly professional relationship during filming. The personal one came much later."
