Years later, while making "Romancing the Stone," Douglas also admits he had an affair with screenwriter Diane Thomas, who wrote the film. He says he and his first wife, Diandra, were both involved in extramarital relationships as their marriage deteriorated.
Diandra gave him a ‘rehab or divorce’ ultimatum
In the midst of his substance abuse and infidelity, Douglas said his first marriage to Diandra Luker eventually came to a head at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel.
After Diandra initially declined to stay with him at the hotel, Douglas called a woman he had been seeing. The woman came to his room, where they had drinks.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Douglas says Diandra unexpectedly returned, obtained a key from the front desk and walked in on them.
Michael Douglas and Diandra Luker married in 1977. (Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
"She gave me an ultimatum: ‘Rehab or divorce,’" he writes.

"The indiscretion, the drugs, the booze. I was in a constant state of temporary pleasure or temporary escape," he writes. "In my heart, I knew that I was heading down a very bad road at a very high speed, but I was trying my best to compartmentalize."
Douglas entered the Sierra Tucson rehabilitation clinic in Arizona in 1992 for treatment for alcohol and substance abuse.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Douglas denies being a sex addict
Douglas says his rehab stay was later exploited by a tabloid.

He claims two fellow patients sold information about the program to a publication and then left treatment. According to Douglas, the story transformed his treatment for alcohol and drug abuse into a sensational headline portraying him as a sex addict.

"The story that was printed was utter bulls—," Douglas writes. "I had made mistakes, had moments I wasn’t proud of, made choices I wouldn’t have if I wasn’t high, but I was never a f---ing sex addict."
Douglas says the story damaged his reputation and continued to follow him in interviews for decades.
Douglas recalls partying with O.J. Simpson
Michael Douglas claims he once partied with O.J. Simpson. (Getty Images)
Douglas also writes about an encounter with O.J. Simpson and Rolling Stone co-founder Jann Wenner.

Douglas says he and Wenner encountered Simpson at a "Saturday Night Live" after-party. Wenner invited Simpson back to his apartment, where Simpson allegedly pulled out a rolled dollar bill and offered them cocaine.
"Jann and I were looking at each other — Are we really doing this with O.J. Simpson?" Douglas writes.
He also claims cocaine was readily available throughout Hollywood. Douglas says that at one major talent agency, a valet could allegedly replace a $100 bill left in a car with a packet of cocaine.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Wenner for comment.
Douglas describes a private evening with Princess Diana
Diana, Princess of Wales, talks to American actor Michael Douglas at the London premiere of the film "Wall Street" April 28, 1988. British actor Terence Stamp is in the center. (Getty Images)
Douglas writes that he spent a private evening with Princess Diana at a London screening of "Wall Street."
He says they sat beside each other during the film, with their hands occasionally touching on the shared armrest. Afterward, they spent time together at a private dinner away from the cameras.
"The truth was simple: she was in an unhappy marriage and wanted a different life," he writes.
He does not claim they had a romantic relationship, but describes their time together as "very special."
He recalls growing up afraid of Kirk Douglas
Actor Kirk Douglas and actor Michael Douglas in 2011 (Getty Images)
Douglas describes his father, Hollywood icon Kirk Douglas, as a powerful, but volatile presence.
"Kirk Douglas was my father, a flawed man with a ferocious temper and a burning ambition," he writes.
Douglas says his father’s behavior left him and his brother Joel frightened. He recalls Kirk saying, "I yell and scream because I care," while Douglas writes that Joel endured more of the abuse.
Douglas’ cancer was misdiagnosed for nine months
Douglas says doctors initially treated his persistent throat pain as an infection and prescribed multiple rounds of antibiotics.
A Canadian specialist eventually discovered a subtle swelling at the back of his tongue. A biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma.
"It’s stage IV cancer," the doctor told him, according to Douglas, who says the tumor was the size of a walnut.

Douglas writes that three doctors had missed the cancer and that he had been given the wrong diagnosis for nine months. He feared surgery would require removing part of his tongue and jaw, potentially ending his acting career.
His doctors publicly referred to the disease as throat cancer rather than tongue cancer because they feared reports about possible disfigurement would become sensationalized.
Douglas once tried to kidnap Cameron and force him into rehab
Douglas also describes the darkest years of his son Cameron’s addiction.
"When he was really strung out in New York, I decided I was going to kidnap him and force him into rehab," he wrote.

Douglas said that Cameron was addicted to cocaine and heroin, dealt methamphetamine and carried a Glock for protection. During one incident, Cameron flashed the weapon at a drugstore and was nearly shot by police.
Cameron Douglas and Michael Douglas attend the 2024 Vanity Fair Oscar Party at the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts March 10, 2024, in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
At one point, Douglas says he arranged for two large men to help abduct Cameron and force him into rehab.
"When we came back, I asked to hold the leash. Cam figured it out. He looked at me, like, ‘Dad, how could you?’ Like I had broken his heart. Again."
Cameron realized what was happening and resisted, so Douglas threw the plan out of the window.

Cameron later served seven years in prison after a federal drug case. Douglas wrote that his son’s heroin relapse behind bars led a judge to add 4½ to his sentence, and Cameron also spent two years in solitary confinement.

title: Zachary Levi says Texas gives him the ‘freedom’ he couldn’t find in California
summary: Zachary Levi says he traded California for Texas "freedom" and values that are "more aligned with mine." The actor is starring in the new Western remake "Angel and the Badman."
story: "Angel and the Badman" star Zachary Levi explains why he believes Texas’ values align more closely with his own after leaving California behind.
Zachary Levi believes Texas offered him the kind of freedom and shared values that he no longer felt he had in his home state of California.
In 2017, the 45-year-old actor, who is starring in the new Western movie "Angel and the Badman," left Los Angeles behind and moved to a ranch outside Austin.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital alongside his "Angel and the Badman" co-stars, Neal McDonough and Meg Fraser, as well as the film's director, Julio Quintana, Levi reflected on trading the Golden State for the Lone Star State, noting that the "great state of Texas" is a "much easier place to live than a lot of the other places that I have lived."
'FRIDAY NIGHT LIGHTS' STAR ADRIANNE PALICKI SAYS TEXAS GAVE HER SOMETHING HOLLYWOOD COULDN'T
Zachary Levi shared that he found the freedom to "live the life that I'm meant to go live" in Texas after leaving California. (Getty Images)
"I love California. It's a beautiful state," he said. "Unfortunately, I think it's got a lot of issues and I don't see those going anywhere."

"Whereas in Texas, I think that their values are more aligned with mine," he continued. "I appreciate that I don't have to pay state income tax and there's liberty. There's the liberty to go do what I want to go do, which is, like, go buy a bunch of land and build a movie studio."
NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

"You can be a crazy person and go do that," Levi added. "If Walt Disney tried to go build Disneyland in California today, I don't think it would ever get done, you know, so it gives me the freedom to go live the life that I believe that I'm meant to go live."

Levi is currently building Wyldwood Studios, a $100 million film and lifestyle campus on his 75-acre property in Bastrop County outside Austin. Designed as a hybrid production hub and creative retreat, the multiphase project pairs soundstages and production offices with housing and wellness spaces. Wyldwood is expected to open its first two soundstages in 2027.
WATCH: ZACHARY LEVI SAYS TEXAS GAVE HIM THE FREEDOM HE COULDN'T FIND IN CALIFORNIA
The "Chuck" alum previously told Fox News Digital that the inspiration to build Wyldwood was rooted in his longstanding desire to rethink how the entertainment industry operates from the inside out.

"Ever since I started working in Hollywood and I saw how broken it all was, I felt very compelled by God to go build a better Hollywood — like a new United Artists kind of studio — where it's owned and operated by the artists, where we can cut out all the middlemen, where we all can do really well, build a community," Levi said.

"And then not just a place to work," he continued. "People can live there, and kids can go to school there. And we have an organic farm, and, like, all of the things that I think everybody really wants these days."
Levi is starring in the Western remake "Angel and the Badman." (Angel Studios )

Levi's latest project, "Angel and the Badman," which was produced by Angel Studios, is a remake of the classic 1947 Western of the same name that starred John Wayne, Gail Russell, Harry Carey and Bruce Cabot.

The official plot synopsis for the remake reads, "When feared outlaw Quirt Evans staggers onto a rancher's land with a bullet in his back, he expects a quick death, not mercy. But Penny, the rancher's daughter, offers him a chance at something he’s never had: a life beyond violence. However, the past doesn’t forgive. With the marshal closing in and an outlaw gang ready to burn the ranch to the ground, Quirt must decide what kind of man he’ll be when the world demands blood."

Levi stepped into Wayne's original role as Quirt Evans (the Badman) while Fraser plays Penny (the Angel) and McDonough portrays the marshal. "Angel and the Badman" also stars Tommy Lee Jones as the outlaw gang leader Laredo.
WATCH: NEAL MCDONOUGH SAYS YOUNG PEOPLE NEED TO SEE ‘THE BAD GUY GETS WHAT HE DESERVES’
While speaking with Fox News Digital, McDonough explained how he believes "Angel and the Badman" conveys an important message for the young people of today.

"I think nowadays — with the temptation of social media and what we look at and what we hear and what we listen to — who do we look up to as heroes anymore?" he said. "Especially for the younger generation, it's really hard for them."

"The younger generation who don't really know Westerns so well, to go to a film like ‘Angel and the Badman,’ you see, ‘OK, the bad guy gets what he deserves in the end,’" McDonough continued. "Where in modern day, the bad guy sometimes gets to go scot-free and that's tough to really learn from as a kid. What do you learn from that as a young adult?"

"So films like this are important because it tells us, you should be trying to do the right thing," he added. "You should redeem yourself and not do the dumb things that you used to do. Try to be a better person, try to give glory to Him, try and do the right thing for your family. I love doing films like these because they do exactly that, and thank goodness for Angel Studios."
Neal McDonough is pictured in a scene from "Angel and the Badman." (Angel Studios )
Quintana said he believed that the story’s redemptive themes feel especially relevant in a social media era when public mistakes can quickly become permanent scandals.

"In modern culture, in some ways, we actually have the inverse situation where it seems like we're always — you make one public mistake, and it's like your life is ruined," he said. "Our media outlets thrive on downfall and self-destruction and things like that. And I think this is a good reminder that actually what's really inspiring is people making mistakes and ultimately making the sacrifices to make amends and try to claw their way back up and try to be better, because we don't really see the redemptive side of a public downfall. Nowadays, we only see the dark side."

McDonough shared that he personally resonates with redemptive storytelling after his past struggles with substance abuse issues. During a 2025 interview with Fox News Digital, the "Band of Brothers" star explained that he gave up alcohol in 2016 after realizing he had to make his life about serving God, "rather than serving me." He also credited his wife of over 22 years, Ruvé, with giving him the motivation he needed to quit drinking as he recalled, "She grabbed me and says, it's us or the bottle, you choose," and he "never looked back."
Reflecting on "Angel and the Badman's" message of redemption, McDonough admitted, "I think that we all do things that we are not proud of at times."
WATCH: ‘ANGEL AND THE BADMAN’ STAR ZACHARY LEVI SAYS REDEMPTION STORIES APPLY TO EVERYONE

"We all make mistakes," he continued. "None of us are perfect. We all sin, we all do dumb things, but every once in a while, you get called out and something might happen to make you think, ‘Hmm, maybe I should be a better dad. Maybe I should be a better husband. Maybe I should be better coworker. I need to stop doing that thing.’"

"Years ago, I stopped drinking because it took me off my game, and it just wasn't keeping me focused to do His work," McDonough remembered. "And ever since then, I focused so hard on doing His work and giving glory to Him and everything that I do. So we all have to overcome these things and that's redemption. And ‘Angel and the Badman,’ boy, you know, Quirt Evans has to go through that."

"It's that redemptive quality that Westerns have more than any other films," he added. "They keep it simple. There's a good guy, there's a bad guy. Good guy's gonna win, but he has to overcome something because the bad guy couldn't. And that's what we did in ‘Angel and the Badman.’"

Neal McDonough, Zachary Levi, Meg Fraser and Julio Quintana attend the "Angel and the Badman" world premiere on Oct. 1, 2026, in Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Sam Wasson/Getty Images for Angel Studios)
Levi told Fox News Digital that he also believed that the movie's message was universal.

"I love a good redemption story," he said. "It's one of the most classic stories that you can tell, and if you can tell it within a classic genre like a Western that has a little bit of all of these subcategories of action-adventure and romance and drama and comedy and heart and charm and all of those things woven into one beautifully shot and directed story — then you get to tell a story that I believe applies to everyone."

"Because everyone knows deep down inside of them, they either have been redeemed or are in need of redemption," Levi continued. "It's a human story. It's a human story. So those are the ones that I like to tell the most."

title: James Bond legend Roger Moore's son calls out TikTok culture, Hollywood's recycled comic book movies
summary: Geoffrey Moore stars in spy thriller "Knightfall" and shares why Hollywood needs stronger stories over big-budget spectacle and recycled comics.
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
Forget bigger explosions — Geoffrey Moore says Hollywood needs better stories.

The son of the late James Bond legend Roger Moore told Fox News Digital that today’s films have become too reliant on recycled comic book material and big-budget spectacle, while originality and meaningful dialogue have taken a back seat.

"I think that today, it's too much TikTok," the actor told Fox News Digital. "A person will have a conversation with you, and it's the conversation that he read or heard on TikTok, as opposed to actually having read Hemingway and knows what he's talking about."
GABRIEL BASSO SAYS SOCIAL MEDIA HAS TURNED PEOPLE INTO VOYEURS OBSESSED WITH STRANGERS' LIVES: 'IT'S WEIRD'
Geoffrey Moore, son of late James Bond icon Roger Moore, is starring in the British spy film "Knightfall." (Saban Films)

"I think it's important that the art of storytelling maintains the culture," Moore said. "There's just too many studio executive heads deciding what's right, as opposed to what people want to hear or people should hear and see."

Moore stars in the British spy thriller "Knightfall," which has its share of guns and fight scenes. However, he said the film doesn't rely on over-the-top action to keep audiences hooked and instead leans on a strong storyline and sharp dialogue.
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital that today's Hollywood films are too lengthy and rely heavily on comic book franchises. (Saban Films)
"I would like to see more culture in films, as opposed to the regurgitation of these comics," Moore said.
WATCH: BOND GIRL ALISON PAPWORTH REVEALS HER HOPE FOR THE NEXT 007

"And everything's so negative. Oh, my goodness. It's like, you need to have a certain budget with helicopters flying upside down. But the storyline has to be strong. Good dialogue, good storywriting are key. You don't have to have constant action to keep the person's attention going. You also need action in the storyline, in the words."
Moore also believes "Knightfall" has something else working in its favor in the social media era: It doesn't overstay its welcome.
Geoffrey Moore attends the London premiere of "Knightfall" at Cine Lumiere in London, England, on Sept. 13, 2026. (Alan Chapman/Dave Benett/WireImage)
The actor said the film was deliberately kept short, acknowledging that today's audiences may not have the patience to sit through a lengthy saga.

"Knightfall" tells the tale of Charles Knight, a former spy catcher who must work with his estranged daughter to avert a homeland security bloodbath and survive a terrifying home invasion. Geoffrey Moore plays Hugh. (Saban Films)

"You can't sit through a three-hour movie," he argued. "You can imagine today, it's just everyone on the treadmill. You need that right amount of length before someone starts asking, 'When is it over?' That's the direction I would take with today's films."
For Moore, "Knightfall" also marks a full-circle moment.
Roger Moore's 4-year-old son Geoffrey watches from the edge of the set on Aug. 11, 1970. (Getty Images)

The actor grew up immersed in the entertainment business as the son of one of Hollywood's most famous spies. Now, decades later, he's stepping in front of the camera as a spy himself at roughly the same age his father was when he made his final James Bond film.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital he was eager to help boost the British film industry with his new movie. (Saban Films)

"I have not been an actor all my life, even though I did start as a child actor," Moore said. "My second womb was the soundstage. But just because you're related to someone in the entertainment industry, it doesn't make me a part of the entertainment industry or even an actor. But this time, it just felt right. It wasn't forced. And also, it's never too late. I mean, yes, go figure, it's a spy film, but there's a twist. And really, it's never too late."

Moore was six years old when his father filmed his 007 debut, "Live and Let Die," which was released in 1973. The Telegraph reported that Moore was present for all of his father's Bond films and the famous stunts that came with them. Once the director yelled "cut," the patriarch would look at his son and ask if he wanted to get ice cream.
British actor Roger Moore walks through London Airport with his son Geoffrey, 6, and daughter Deborah, 8, on Aug. 2, 1972, before leaving for a short holiday in Rome, Italy. (Getty Images)

"Look, I've been on enough film sets to know how laborious it can be," Moore said. "It's a demanding schedule and you mustn't break your ankle. But I've never had a big role where I'm doing a lot of running around. I have to say on some mornings when I wake up, if you've ever been horseback riding, you recognize muscles you never knew you had. I'm doing all of this running around and going, 'Oh my goodness, I thought I was fit!'"
Geoffrey Moore, 60, is marking his first acting role in 33 years with "Knightfall," The Telegraph reported. (Saban Films)

"I was never like, 'I'm looking for a job in front of the camera,'" Moore continued. "It just felt right. And I was intrigued. It's an independent British film and very few films aren't dictated by executive heads. This isn't a regurgitation of another franchise where they're spending lots of money. Here, the conditions were harsh. It was physically demanding. Rewrites are happening on the day. It was back to back."
"The food was good, considering this wasn't a multimillion production," he said. "And if the money is good, that'll get your attention."
Geoffrey Moore attends the Rosewood Munich grand opening on Oct. 25, 2023, in Munich, Germany. (Getty Images for Rosewood Munich)
Moore said the key to making it in the movie-making business is simple: don't take yourself too seriously.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Geoffrey Moore attended the "Spectre" premiere after party at the British Museum on Oct. 26, 2015. (GC Images)

"If an actor shows up on the set and doesn't understand the importance of the production, what each person does, then they're in the wrong business," he said. "It's a team effort. Everyone is as important. You're nothing without the guy who knows how to keep you in focus. If you make something look good, it's usually not that easy. And to be a film star, you have to be a good actor. There's no such thing as an ignorant person who can act."
Despite following in his father's footsteps by playing a spy, Moore isn't campaigning to become the next James Bond.
English actor Roger Moore poses for a portrait in London, England, on July 20, 1979. Moore portrayed James Bond in the Bond series. (Getty Images)

"I think the next James Bond should be someone who can carry the decade, a reflection of the times," Moore said. "When it comes to who's the next Bond, it's really who depicts the times, who is relevant to today, whether it be a tall person, a short person, someone who doesn't know how to tie a tie or who doesn't know how to read because he's on TikTok the whole time. Who knows who they'll choose."
Geoffrey Moore told Fox News Digital he's not looking to follow in his father's footsteps and play 007. (Saban Films)

"I think they know what they'll be doing. They're not just handing it over to Amazon, that was basically a delivery service, and now they're in the film business. Who they ultimately choose is someone relevant to the times. And I think that's the key to Bond."

Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the James Bond franchise in 2025 after forming a joint venture with longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli. The transaction closed March 24, 2025, with Amazon MGM Studios, Wilson and Broccoli remaining co-owners of the franchise.
Geoffrey Moore looks at a double-breasted mohair dinner suit believed to have been made for Sir Roger Moore in "The Spy Who Loved Me" in 1977. (PA Images via Getty Images)
Several actors have been linked to the role, including Paul Mescal, Jacob Elordi, Jack O'Connell, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Sir Roger Moore, who starred as James Bond, died on May 23, 2017, at the age of 89. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

The next installment will be the 26th film in the official Bond series, which began with "Dr. No" in 1962. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct, with "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight writing the screenplay.
As Moore looks ahead to making more films, there's one piece of advice from his late father, who died in 2017 at age 89, that he hasn't forgotten.
"Make sure you get paid," he joked.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Knightfall" is available now. (Saban Films)
"Knightfall" is available on digital and on demand.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Silent inflammation could be damaging your body — and 5 habits may help keep it in check
summary: Jim LaValle reveals how the gut-immune-brain interface drives chronic inflammation, and why stress, blood sugar and environmental toxins play key roles.
story: Clinical pharmacist Jim LaValle breaks down how diet, stress, medications, blood sugar, environmental exposures and even overtraining may contribute to inflammation — and why the gut-brain connection matters.

Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but when it becomes chronic, it can pose a health threat, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Over time, chronic inflammation can contribute to rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.
Keeping the condition in check can help protect healthy tissues and support overall health, experts say.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
Jim LaValle, a clinical pharmacist and metabolic medicine expert based in Texas, told Fox News Digital that inflammation can be influenced by a variety of factors beyond injury or infection.
Inflammation is a natural immune response that helps protect the body from injury and infection, but chronic inflammation can damage healthy tissues and contribute to serious diseases. (iStock)

LaValle first pointed to the gut-immune-brain connection — the communication between gut microbes, the immune system and the central nervous system — as one pathway that can influence the body's inflammatory response.
Beyond gut health, he said several everyday lifestyle factors can play a role in preventing chronic inflammation.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
No. 1: Manage stress
Managing stress and anxiety can help support the gut-brain connection and keep inflammation in check, according to LaValle.
He pointed to cortisol, a hormone released in response to stress, which he said can "wreak havoc on your chemistry" when levels remain elevated.
Stress can "wreak havoc on your chemistry," the expert warned. (iStock)
Chronic stress can also affect the intestinal barrier, potentially allowing substances that would normally remain inside the gut to pass through more easily, LaValle said.
This increased intestinal permeability is sometimes called "leaky gut."
ZERO SUGAR, MORE PROBLEMS? STUDY REVEALS SURPRISING GUT HEALTH EFFECTS
"So, it turns out that if I'm stressed out a lot, I can be more prone to irritable bowel," LaValle said, as stress can trigger or worsen digestive symptoms in some people.
No. 2: Watch for food triggers
Diets high in sugar, fat and ultraprocessed foods can also affect gut health.
Paying attention to which foods trigger certain symptoms may help identify potential food sensitivities or intolerances, LaValle noted.
Paying attention to what kinds of food trigger certain reactions or sensitivities may help signal what is causing inflammation in the body. (iStock)
Symptoms such as bloating, rashes or discomfort after eating certain foods may signal a food-related reaction, although they can have other causes.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Certain medications, including antibiotics, may also alter the gut microbiome, but their effects vary depending on the drug and the individual, the expert said.
No. 3: Keep blood sugar in check
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation, according to LaValle.
Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels is another important factor in managing inflammation. (iStock)
LaValle noted that conditions such as diabetes and insulin resistance are often associated with chronic inflammation.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Research suggests that GLP-1 medications, commonly prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity, may have anti-inflammatory effects, while scientists are investigating other potential benefits beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
No. 4: Be aware of environmental exposures
The "exposome," or the environmental exposures people experience throughout their lives, can influence inflammation and the risk of chronic disease, according to the National Institutes of Health.
Microplastics could trigger inflammation signaling, according to the expert. (iStock)

LaValle pointed to emerging research on how environmental exposures — including "forever chemicals," microplastics, metals and pesticides — may affect weight, blood sugar regulation and other aspects of health.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"A lot of us don't think about that kind of impact on our health and how that could trigger inflammation signaling," he added.
No. 5: Don’t over-train
Regular exercise supports overall health, but intense workouts without adequate recovery time can put additional stress on the body, LaValle cautioned.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"You’re not getting a good enough recovery," he said. "You’re training hard. And, in fact, you might be training hard every day to lower that cortisol, but you're not getting good recovery. And that could lead to silent inflammatory signaling as well."
Anyone who is concerned about chronic inflammation or is experiencing persistent symptoms should consult a doctor to determine the underlying cause and appropriate treatment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Stomach-turning sexually transmitted infection is on the rise, and standard medicines are failing
summary: Shigella bacteria are becoming harder to treat as drug-resistant strains rise, and doctors warn Americans should be concerned but not panicked.
story: Speaking to Fox News Digital, Lenox Hill Hospital internist Michael Aziz discusses the increase in antibiotic-resistant shigella cases and explains why patients experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms should seek medical attention before taking over-the-counter medications.
A highly contagious gut infection that can spread during sex is becoming harder to treat as antibiotic-resistant strains become more common.

An April report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tracked nearly 17,000 shigella samples, which causes shigellosis that can bring on diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, collected between 2011 and 2023.

In 2023, 8.5% of shigella samples with resistance data were classified as extensively drug-resistant, or XDR — resistant to all five antibiotics in the CDC’s definition — compared with none from 2011 to 2015.
The findings point to a growing resistance problem, not a surge in overall infections, noted Dr. Tyler Evans, a California-based infectious disease physician and CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance.
HIGHLY CONTAGIOUS STOMACH BUG SPREADS FAST, HITTING CERTAIN PATIENTS HARDEST
"The infection is not surging. The bacteria are changing," Evans told Fox News Digital. "Case counts can hold steady while the treatment options quietly disappear."
The percentage of Shigella isolates classified as extensively drug-resistant rose to 8.5% in 2023, according to the CDC. (Leonie Asendorpf/picture alliance via Getty Images)
There is no FDA-approved oral antibiotic for XDR shigella, he said.
Shigella bacteria can spread when tiny amounts of stool reach someone's mouth, including through contaminated food or water, unwashed hands or sexual activity.
DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES
"Shigella is not considered to be a typical sexually transmitted infection," Dr. Andi Toufexis, a Texas-based family medicine physician who specializes in sexual health, told Fox News Digital.
"However, this gastrointestinal bacteria can be spread through sex when one partner comes into contact with the other's fecal matter."
Most patients with extensively drug-resistant Shigella in the CDC analysis were adult men. (iStock)
Shigella is not new, and sexual transmission has been documented since the 1970s, Toufexis said. What is changing is the growing share of tested samples classified as XDR.
MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The CDC report found that most people with XDR shigella were adult men. Sexual exposure data were not routinely collected, so the report could not establish exactly how each infection was contracted. But previous research has found sexual contact among men who have sex with men as an important transmission route.

Eighty-six percent of XDR patients were men with a median age of 41, and of those with a known HIV status, nearly half were living with HIV, Evans noted. People experiencing homelessness and those with weakened immune systems may also face heightened risks, he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Children younger than 5 are especially likely to get shigella, according to the CDC, and many outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to childcare and schools. Earlier U.S. outbreaks primarily affected children and involved strains that were susceptible to antibiotics.
Washing hands before preparing food can help reduce the spread of Shigella.

According to the CDC report, 37.6% of patients with hospitalization data were hospitalized for the antibiotic-resistant infection. The CDC reported no deaths among the XDR cases analyzed and said infections may be undercounted because not all positive specimens were cultured or tested for resistance. Most patients with available travel histories reported no recent international travel, though travel information was missing for many.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans said Americans should be "concerned, not panicked" about the infection.
Most shigella infections resolve on their own, Toufexis added, but severe illness may need treatment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dr. Michael Aziz, an internist at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York City and author of "The Perfect 10 Diet" and "The Ageless Revolution," urged people who suspect shigella to seek medical advice before taking antidiarrheal medicine such as Imodium.
"You want to flush out the bacteria, you want to get it out of your system," Aziz told Fox News Digital.
Experts advise people with Shigella not to take antidiarrheal medicines such as Imodium, which can slow the gut.

To reduce the chance of infection, doctors recommend washing hands, genitals and the anal area before and after sex, using condoms or dental dams and cleaning sex toys after each use. If you or a partner has diarrhea, avoid sex and wait at least two weeks after symptoms end before resuming, Toufexis said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Feeling better does not always mean that an infection is completely gone," she said.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: One type of sleep linked to dramatically lower risk of dementia, Parkinson's and 81 other diseases
summary: Greater REM sleep was linked to 80% lower Parkinson's risk and 46% lower dementia risk in a major study of over 95,000 adults tracked for years.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of ‘The Sleepdemic Solution,’ confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
Not all stages of sleep are equal in terms of benefits for the brain.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown.
Additionally, greater amounts of deep sleep were associated with lower risks of seven conditions.
THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS

That’s according to a study of 95,559 adults who wore wrist accelerometers continuously for seven consecutive days and nights. Researchers in China used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity.
They then looked at health records to assess associations with more than 1,000 diseases over a nearly nine-year follow-up period.
Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown. (iStock)
Greater REM sleep was associated with a significantly lower risk of several diseases, including Parkinson’s (80% lower relative risk), dementia (46% lower risk) and heart failure (26% lower risk).
Greater deep sleep was associated with lower risks of seven conditions, including Type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS

Sleep duration was also found to be highly linked to disease outcome. Six to eight hours per night was found to be the "sweet spot" associated with the lowest risk for 69 diseases. In contrast, sleeping fewer than five hours per night was linked to an increased risk of 37 health conditions.

The study also found that greater night-to-night sleep irregularity and more wakefulness during the night were associated with higher risks of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders.
The findings were published Sept. 17 in the journal PLOS Medicine.
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, a sleep expert noted. (iStock)

"I think what is important is the total duration of sleep, and the percentage that REM takes up," Oki Ishikawa, M.D., pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine expert at Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital, told Fox News Digital.
"The average percentage of REM sleep in this study population was about 20%, and generally 20-25% is considered normal per sleep cycle."
5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS
Ishikawa, who was not involved in the study, said he does not believe that a higher amount of REM sleep alone will necessarily lower the risk.

"Normal sleep pattern and duration are associated with aspects like maintenance of good immune function and memory, so I think the important message here is to try and get a sufficient amount of sleep in general," Ishikawa sai.
Researchers used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity. (iStock)
Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, according to Dr. Chelsie Rohrscheib, head sleep expert at Wesper, a sleep analysis company in New York.

"Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, dementia and heart failure can begin affecting sleep years before they are diagnosed," Rohrscheib, who also was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
"At the same time, poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
The researchers noted some limitations of the study. Because it was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that increasing REM or deep sleep directly prevents disease.
"Sleep was measured for only one week using a wrist device, which is less accurate than a clinical sleep study for identifying sleep stages," Rohrscheib said.
"Poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways," an expert said. (iStock)
"Some health information was collected years earlier, medications that can affect sleep were not fully considered and some medical diagnoses may have been missed."

As the participants were all from the UK Biobank, the study population was also less diverse and generally healthier than the overall population, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone, Rohrscheib noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Overall, changes in sleep may provide important clues about underlying health, but this study cannot determine whether poor sleep is a cause, an early symptom or both," she concluded.
Rohrscheib also cautioned that while wrist-worn sleep trackers are generally good at estimating sleep stages, they are not 100% accurate.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Without a formal in-lab sleep study, it's impossible to know how much time the participants spent in REM and other sleep stages," she said.
More research is needed to determine whether increasing REM or deep sleep can help prevent certain diseases, the researchers said.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."
Future studies could also explore whether the relationship between sleep stages and disease risk varies by age, sex, overall health and other individual characteristics.

Both experts recommended following general sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining an optimal environment (dark, cool and quiet), keeping a consistent sleep schedule and avoiding sleep-disrupting substances such as alcohol and caffeine.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If you have other sleep pathologies like sleep apnea … treating that would be a great way to optimize the amount of REM sleep," Ishikawa advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While it can be difficult to measure REM sleep without a wearable, he said the best gauge is whether one feels refreshed upon waking and doesn’t feel sleepy during the day.
"If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

title: Man loses 15 stubborn pounds after age 50 without giving up pizza or donuts
summary: Carl Daikeler lost 15 pounds by swapping breakfast for a 250-calorie shake and eating a big salad for lunch, then enjoying total dinner freedom.
story: Carl Daikeler, CEO and founder of BODi, shares how a simple breakfast, a hearty lunch, and the freedom to eat what he wants for dinner helped him lose 15 pounds and get into the best shape of his life at 63.
Maintaining weight loss in midlife doesn’t necessarily require strict dietary bans or extreme fasting protocols.
Carl Daikeler, co-founder and CEO of the fitness and nutrition company BODi, says a simple routine earlier in the day has helped him manage his weight while allowing more freedom at dinner.
Los Angeles-based Daikeler, 63, who has led the health brand formerly known as Beachbody for 28 years, openly admits that he doesn't have an affinity for healthy foods.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG
"I eat like a third-grader, okay? Pizza's a food group," Daikeler joked in an interview with Fox News Digital.
"I'm just constantly trying to figure out how can I hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of those diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."
The fitness CEO said he maintains long-term weight loss without strict dieting by eating structured, high-nutrient meals during the day to allow total freedom at dinner. (iStock)

When Daikeler turned 57, he found himself unable to lose 15 pounds he had gained around his waistline. Rather than adopting a strict diet, he adjusted two specific meals during the day while leaving his evening schedule unrestricted, he shared.
For breakfast, Daikeler replaced standard options with a nutrient-dense shake containing protein, fiber, prebiotics, probiotics and greens, totaling roughly 250 calories.
NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS
"I got rid of breakfast, or I changed my breakfast to this shake that we've got called Shakeology," Daikeler said. "I put some spinach in there and I put a banana in there."
For lunch, Daikeler prepares a large salad loaded with baby spinach, carrots and chicken, mixed with toppings that mask the taste of the greens.
Replacing traditional breakfast with a 250-calorie nutrient shake provides essential greens, fiber and protein without requiring major cooking or dietary overhauls. (iStock)
"I hide it with some cheese, some nuts, some sliced strawberries, and it's delicious, and I put chicken in there ... I don't feel like I'm eating a bowl of vegetables, but I am."
By keeping breakfast and lunch relatively structured, Daikeler gives himself more flexibility at dinner.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
He does, however, follow a single guideline regarding alcohol intake. "I'm careful not to drink too much," he said.
"Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner."
"Once I did that — Shakeology for breakfast, a big salad for lunch, total freedom for dinner, limited alcohol — the 15 pounds just got wiped out. And it stayed off."
Daikeler warns that overly restrictive nutrition plans are usually difficult to stick with long-term, leading many to abandon their health goals entirely.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If you're trying to be too restrictive, I don't think that's life," he said. "The whole point is living ... So if it's too restrictive, it's going to break."

Instead of completely banning indulgence foods, Daikeler recommends using portion control and mindfulness to enjoy without overeating.
The expert said he focuses on smaller portions rather than cutting favorite foods like pizza out entirely. (iStock)

"I love pizza. But I've learned that I can enjoy pizza without eating the whole pizza," he said. "I like doughnuts. I've learned that I can have literally a quarter of a doughnut and be like, that was delicious. But I get no additional satisfaction by eating the whole doughnut."

For Daikeler, that balance is part of a broader focus on "health span" — prioritizing quality of life and the ability to stay active as he ages.

"Health span versus lifespan is all about quality of life," he said. "I'm all for longevity, but it's really about quality of life — a way to live and enjoy life that is balanced with maximizing your time on earth."

While Daikeler said this approach has worked for him, weight-loss strategies are not one-size-fits-all.

According to the National Institutes of Health, different eating plans can support weight loss, but the most effective approach depends on a person's individual health needs, preferences and ability to maintain the habits long-term. Individuals are generally advised to consult a doctor or registered dietitian for personalized guidance.

title: Parkinson's patients may protect memory and movement with one simple habit
summary: A University of Cincinnati study links weekly physical activity to slower cognitive decline and motor function loss in Parkinson's disease patients.
story: Dr. Bhavya Shah and Parkinson's patient Bud Leavell explain a groundbreaking focused ultrasound therapy. The non-invasive procedure uses MRI guidance to target brain areas, instantly stopping severe tremors.
Weekly physical activity could help to slow down disease progression in Parkinson’s patients, a new study found.
The research, led by the University of Cincinnati, included 294 patients with mild-to-moderate Parkinson's disease. Their average age was 66.
The participants reported their weekly physical activity via questionnaires.
ALAN ALDA REVEALS UNEXPECTED WEAPON IN HIS BATTLE AGAINST PARKINSON'S DISEASE
Physical activity was assessed through structured interviews covering moderate and vigorous activities at work, at home and during recreation.
Examples of moderate activity included brisk walking, light swimming, doubles tennis and household activities such as washing windows, vacuuming or mowing the lawn, the study release stated.
Weekly physical activity could help to slow down disease progression in Parkinson’s patients, a new study found. (iStock)
Vigorous activity included pursuits like jogging, fast bicycling, team sports and singles tennis, along with shoveling and carrying heavy loads.
Participants were divided into three groups based on their amount of weekly physical activity — up to four hours, four to eight hours and more than eight hours.
PARKINSON'S IS BECOMING MORE COMMON; HERE ARE 5 THINGS EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW
The researchers then monitored the participants’ cognitive health for up to five years and their motor function for up to seven years.

Each additional hour of physical activity per week was linked to slightly slower declines in memory, thinking and movement abilities over time, even after accounting for factors such as age, sex, education, weight and disease severity.
Physical activity was assessed through structured interviews covering moderate and vigorous activities at work, at home and during recreation. (iStock)
Patients who were physically active for four to eight hours per week experienced slower declines in memory and thinking abilities than those who exercised less than four hours.
Exercise duration above eight hours per week did not appear to provide additional benefits for memory and thinking.
The study was published Oct. 7 in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.
PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARSLONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT

"Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen, leading to disability and a loss of independence," study author Dong-Woo Ryu, M.D., Ph.D., of the University of Cincinnati and The Catholic University of Korea, said in the press release.

"Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."
"While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time."
Ryu pointed out that the potential benefits of physical activity for Parkinson’s patients may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time.
"While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time," he said.
"Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen, leading to disability and a loss of independence," a study author said. (iStock)
The researchers cautioned that most participants had relatively strong thinking and memory skills when the study began, so additional research is needed to confirm the findings.

"Exercise has well-established benefits for physical fitness and mobility, along with potential benefits for brain health through mechanisms that are not yet fully understood," Dr. Vibhash Sharma, a neurologist at UT Southwestern in Dallas, Texas, who specializes in Parkinson’s disease and other movement disorders, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"These findings further emphasize the importance of regular physical activity in managing Parkinson’s disease."
One of the strengths of the study is that patients were followed over several years, with assessments of both motor and cognitive function, noted Sharma, who was not involved in the research.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The study did have some limitations, the researchers acknowledged.
Because the study was observational, it could not establish whether exercise directly slows Parkinson's disease progression.
Because participants reported their own physical activity, they may not have accurately remembered how much they exercised. (iStock)
Also, as participants reported their own physical activity, they may not have accurately remembered how much they exercised.
The participants were all located at a single location and were primarily White, which could limit the generalizability of the results, the researchers noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"It is also possible that patients with inherently slower-progressing disease are more likely to remain physically active," Sharma added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Randomized studies are needed to confirm whether exercise directly slows cognitive or motor decline, according to the researchers.
The study was supported by a grant from the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.

title: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in record-breaking feat
summary: DonnaJean Wilde held an abdominal plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games, smashing her own Guinness world record by nearly 30 minutes.
story: DonnaJean Wilde broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah and beating her previous time by nearly 30 minutes.
A 61-year-old Canadian grandmother broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours.
DonnaJean Wilde accomplished the feat at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah on Oct. 4, breaking her own record by nearly 30 minutes, Storyful reported.
Wilde’s plank began at 3:03 p.m. and ended at 8:03 p.m., with several judges rotating in and out of shifts during that period, a spokesperson for the World Senior Games told Storyful.
FITNESS INFLUENCER SAYS ONE SIMPLE HABIT CAN HELP ANYONE GET BACK IN SHAPE

Her previous record of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds was set on March 21, 2004, at the Canadian high school where she once served as vice principal, according to the Guinness Book of World Records.
"To successfully achieve the record, the challenger’s forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times," Guinness states.
The feat occurred at the Huntsman World Senior Games Oct. 4 in Utah, where DonnaJean Wilde broke her own record by nearly 30 minutes, according to Storyful. (WorldSeniorGames via Storyful)
"The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout," it also says.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
"My elbows hurt pretty bad," Wilde said after completing the previous record.
"I was so worried about losing my form, and I think that’s why my quads hurt because I was just really tense."
A woman in her early 60s has broken her own planking record by nearly 30 minutes. (iStock)
She shared with Guinness that the first two hours "went by quickly," but the next two hours were much more difficult.
"The last hour was the most challenging, just to stay focused and keep my form," she said.

During the last 30 minutes, she said she focused on "breathing, staying calm and not shaking."

Wilde first added planking to her daily routine years ago after breaking her wrist because she could perform the exercise while wearing a cast.
"I realized that I could read and do things when I was planking and fell in love with it," she said, according to the report.
Wilde shared some advice for others aiming to hold extended planks.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Keep trying and keep practicing. When you have to read or work on your computer, just get on the floor and do it on the floor."
Wilde has 12 grandchildren, according to Guinness.

Her new record is pending review and approval by Guinness.

title: Doctor reveals 4 hidden health risks of spending too much time indoors
summary: A Nature & Health Alliance survey finds nearly half of Americans spend under two hours outdoors weekly, fueling burnout, brain fog and belly fat.
story: Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax."
Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey from the Nature & Health Alliance involving researchers at Texas A&M University.
Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors.
In his book, "Indoor Epidemic," he discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims the remedy is a simple 7% outdoor prescription.
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

"Many people don't realize that they're inhibited from feeling as good as they can, because they're exhausted even after a full night's sleep," La Puma told Fox News Digital. "They need coffee to feel normal. They crash at 2 in the afternoon. They're wired at night. They can't go to sleep, but their labs are normal."
"And they come into the office saying, ‘Why do I feel so exhausted?’ It's the four Bs," he said.
Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey. (iStock)
The ‘4 Bs’ caused by too much indoor time
Outdoor light can be many times brighter than typical indoor lighting, La Puma noted, making it a powerful signal for setting the body’s internal clock, or circadian rhythm.
"If you don't set your body clock, your body doesn't know what time it is, and it just goes to sleep whenever you can get to sleep instead of on time," he told Fox News Digital.
Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and author of "Indoor Epidemic," has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors. (John La Puma)
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES
Getting bright outdoor light soon after waking can help synchronize the body's sleep-wake cycle and support the natural rise in melatonin later in the evening, according to La Puma.
He recommends spending about 10 minutes outdoors within the first hour of waking, without sunglasses.
La Puma uses the term "ultraprocessed time" to describe hours lost to screens, scrolling and other digital distractions.
"Ultraprocessed time is kind of like ultraprocessed food," he said. "It’s not nutritious. It’s synthetic. It’s artificial. It’s ubiquitous."
The doctor discusses how humans spend about 93% of our lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims that a simple 7% outdoor prescription can fix it. (iStock)
That includes time spent endlessly scrolling, he said, which can seem to simply "evaporate."
La Puma argues that a person’s environment can contribute to burnout, rather than viewing it solely as a matter of willpower.
AMERICA'S NATIONAL PARKS COULD ADD YEARS TO YOUR LIFE — HERE'S HOW THEY BOOST HEALTH

Spending excessive time indoors can lead to an overload of screen exposure, he said, as people often turn to the same devices for work, entertainment and relaxation. He noted that the body may not interpret screen time as true rest or escape.
"And equally important, no horizon. We are horizon-deprived as a species because indoors, we can't see more than 20 feet in front of us," La Puma said.
"Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air."
To combat burnout, he recommends getting up and going to the window and looking outside for a minute every hour.

"It relaxes your eyes, relaxes the muscles around your temples, reduces headache if you have it, improves energy and reduces fatigue," he said. "That's the beginning of being able to reverse burnout."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Simply going outside during the workday can help to reverse burnout, LaPuma said.
"Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air."
People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, La Puma said, particularly in poorly ventilated spaces where carbon dioxide can build up.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Indoor CO₂ levels can climb above 1,000 parts per million in poorly ventilated spaces, and some research has linked elevated levels with reduced cognitive performance.
"So it's not that you're just making bad decisions in the afternoons — there's a biologic reason for it," La Puma said.
People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, the doctor said. (iStock)
"What you need to do is cross-ventilate, but that's tough to do in an office or conference room."

The doctor said that getting outdoors gives the eyes a chance to focus at greater distances while providing a break from potentially stuffy indoor air. The EPA notes that concentrations of some pollutants can be two to five times higher indoors than outdoors.
When someone’s body clock is out of sync, it can disrupt the body’s normal cortisol rhythm, La Puma said.

Cortisol, often called the stress hormone, naturally rises and falls throughout the day. Research has linked altered cortisol activity with greater abdominal and visceral fat, although the relationship is complex.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Again, the way to improve your metabolism is to get daylight at the right time, in the right place, for the right duration — early in the morning especially," La Puma advised.
"This will give you a bump in cortisol, which you want early in the morning to feel awake, and then it drops appropriately."
The 17-minute dose
Most people spend about an hour outdoors each day as they walk from the car to the office, for example — but that's what La Puma calls "incidental time," not "biologically active time."
"Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning when you have your 10 minutes outdoors to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised. (iStock)
To combat the four Bs, he recommends spending "intentional time" outdoors, "in a blue or green space," for a minimum effective dose of 17 minutes a day.
"Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning … to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who live in a big city and can’t see the sky, La Puma recommends looking at a distant rooftop, or looking through an open window when going outside isn’t possible. The goal is to focus beyond the confines of an indoor space.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"So 17 minutes a day is the minimum effective dose — that's all it takes to begin to bend the curve on the four Bs," he said.
"You can turn those minutes into medicine."

title: Diet soda vs water: Study reveals which beverage is better for weight loss
summary: A two-year randomized trial found that diet drinks with aspartame, sucralose and acesulfame potassium matched water for weight loss outcomes.
story: Pop’s Social co-founders Sam Sachs and Ali Greenberg demonstrate how to make a dirty soda on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’
Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial.
The study, led by the University of Liverpool, England, included 493 participants ranging from 18 to 65 years old, all of whom had a body mass index (BMI) between 27 and 35 (overweight or obese).
Half of them received 22.3 ounces of water each day, and the other half received the same amount of soda with non-nutritive sweeteners (about two cans) for a 104-week period.
YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS

The group assigned to NNS drinks could choose from a variety of diet sodas, low-calorie fruit drinks and flavored waters. The primary sweeteners used were aspartame, acesulfame potassium and sucralose.
After two years, people drinking diet beverages had lost about 10.6 pounds, while those drinking water lost about 8.2 pounds.
Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial. (iStock)
People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated.
Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, but there was no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK
Additionally, total cholesterol remained within the healthy range in both groups.
The findings were published in the British Journal of Nutrition.
People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated. (iStock)
"The study does not show that diet beverages themselves caused the weight loss," Alix Turoff, a registered dietitian in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
"Everyone in the study was participating in a structured weight-management program that included nutrition counseling, behavioral support and physical activity recommendations."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Turoff, who was not involved in the study, noted that the main value of including diet beverages comes down to substitution, "not that these beverages have a magical metabolic effect."
Notably, the study compared diet beverages with water — rather than with sugar-sweetened drinks — making it a test of whether the sugar substitutes themselves appeared to hinder weight loss efforts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If someone normally drinks 250 calories of regular soda and switches to zero-calorie soda, then they’re saving calories," she added.
The dietitian emphasized that these findings don’t mean water and diet soda are nutritionally identical.
Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, but there was no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water. (iStock)

"The study did not find significant between-group differences in hunger or sugar intake at the end of the trial, which is relevant because one common concern is that artificial sweeteners may increase appetite or lead to compensatory eating," Turoff said.

"I would still recommend water as the primary hydration choice, but I don’t think people need to be afraid of diet drinks because they think they will automatically prevent fat loss or cause weight gain."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

There were some limitations with the research, including that it was conducted at one location in England. Race and ethnicity data were not collected, which limits the generalizability of the findings.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Only 220 of the 493 participants who started treatment completed the 104-week assessment. The second-year extension was also voluntary, meaning those who continued may have been more motivated or more likely to stick with the program, Turoff noted.
While the trial was funded by the American Beverage Association, the study authors stated that the association did not participate in the study design, data analysis or interpretation of the results.

title: People on weight-loss drugs report fingernails falling off as researchers uncover surprising link
summary: Nail discoloration was reported by 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% of non-users, while scalp inflammation accompanied hair loss in most medication users studied.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel analyzes study findings on 'Fox Report.'
People taking GLP-1 medications for obesity or diabetes experience nail detachment and hair loss at significantly higher rates than people with similar overall health who do not take GLP-1s.
That's according to research presented Oct. 1 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, Austria.

Two studies evaluated 575 users of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) drugs and a control group of 1,329 non-users, all of whom had type 2 diabetes, obesity or both. Participants were recruited across France, the U.S, Brazil and Mexico.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS

In the primary study examining nail health, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail detachment compared with 9% of non-users. Discoloration of the nails affected 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% in the control group.
Overall, two-thirds of GLP-1 users (66%) reported experiencing at least one nail disorder, compared with 53% of the control group.

People taking GLP-1 medications for obesity or diabetes experience nail detachment and hair loss at significantly higher rates than people with similar overall health who did not take GLP-1s. (iStock)
Researchers found that weight loss alone did not explain the difference.
Even when researchers looked only at people who lost weight, those taking GLP-1s were still more likely to have these problems.
After adjusting for existing dermatological conditions and nutritional deficiencies, nail detachment and discoloration remained two to three times more frequent among the medication group.
Two-thirds (66%) of GLP-1 users experienced at least one nail issue, with nail discoloration affecting 46% of drug users compared to 17% of controls. (iStock)

"Until now, nail changes associated with GLP-1 therapies had essentially been anecdotal," study author Dr. Charles Taïeb, a clinical dermatologist at Necker University Hospital in Paris, said in a press release.
"Our findings show a clear association, but they also underline an important point: Not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself."
POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER
In another study evaluating hair and scalp conditions among the same group of participants, 50% of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss compared with 34% of the control group.

After starting treatment, 26% of GLP-1 users reported hair loss or thinning, compared with 12% of those not taking the drugs. Loss of hair volume was also more common, affecting 42% of GLP-1 users compared with 19% of those not taking them, the study found.
Patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists were more than four times as likely to report nail detachment compared to non-users with similar medical profiles. (iStock)

Scalp redness was reported around three times as frequently in GLP-1 users, and hair loss among users was typically accompanied by inflammatory scalp symptoms such as itching, scaling or redness, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"This suggests that what is happening on the scalp may go beyond the classical shedding seen after rapid weight loss and involve an inflammatory component," said study author Dr. Bruno Halioua, a Paris dermatologist, in the release.
"Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Halioua stated that patients experiencing these symptoms should consult a physician rather than stopping their medication, noting that the changes are typically not serious enough to warrant discontinuing treatment.
Half of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss, while 42% experienced reduced hair volume or density in a study. (iStock)

The authors emphasized that because both studies relied on patient-reported data and looked at them at a single point in time, the findings only show associations and cannot prove that the medications caused these effects.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Roughly half of the GLP-1 users surveyed reported having nail issues prior to starting treatment.
The research team is planning further studies to determine when these changes occur, what may be causing them and whether they go away over time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

title: Shingles rates fall off a cliff among some Americans as researchers reveal likely reason
summary: Epic Research analyzed 85 million health records and found shingles rates dropped 62% among younger adults eligible for childhood chickenpox vaccination.
story: Neurologist Dr. Ajeet Sodhi breaks down research linking the shingles vaccine to a reduced risk of dementia, while stressing that the findings show an association, not proof that the vaccine treats dementia.
Shingles rates have dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s.
That’s according to a major study led by Epic Research, which analyzed the electronic health records of more than 85 million adults.
The biggest drop was between people born from 1991 to 1995 and those born from 1996 to 2000.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS

"Shingles is caused by a virus that is harbored in the peripheral nerves — varicella-zoster, the same virus that causes chickenpox — which can remain dormant and later reactivate, particularly during stress or other decreased immune responses, resulting in a shingles risk," Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, told Fox News Digital.
Shingles rates dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s. (iStock)
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease.
The study period was between January 2017 and June 2026, with the findings published on Oct. 2, 2026.
CANCER VACCINE PREVENTS DEADLY MELANOMA FROM RETURNING OR SPREADING IN LANDMARK TRIAL

Overall, shingles was found to be much more common in older adults. About 182 out of every 10,000 people born between 1968 and 1975 were diagnosed with the condition, compared with just seven out of every 10,000 born between 2006 and 2008.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Shingles diagnoses rise steeply with age, but the newer signal is a sharp drop that begins with people who were eligible for the childhood chickenpox vaccine in the mid-1990s," study author Kersten Bartelt, a research clinician in Verona, Wisconsin, told Fox News Digital.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease. (iStock)

If the trend continues as vaccinated groups grow older, it would suggest that childhood chickenpox vaccination could offer a lasting benefit in reducing shingles, "which is something continued follow-up and research will clarify," Bartelt added.

Siegel agreed that this data aligns with previous research showing that by preventing the initial infection via the chickenpox vaccine ("or causing a very mild version of a live virus vaccine") the risk of shingles is significantly reduced.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
He noted that the vaccine uses a weakened form of the virus, which is much less likely to reactivate later in life and cause shingles.
There were some limitations of the study, including that the researchers did not determine whether individual patients had actually received the varicella vaccination during childhood.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"This is a descriptive, observational study, so it shows associations rather than cause and effect," Bartelt said.
Healthcare disruption due to the COVID pandemic in 2020-2021 could have also affected diagnosis rates and skewed the results, the researchers noted.

A doctor noted that while people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk. (iStock)
Future studies are needed to confirm a link between childhood vaccination histories and long-term shingles outcomes.

"People should continue to follow established vaccine recommendations and talk with their clinician about the shingles vaccine when they're eligible," Bartelt advised. "It's also a reminder that shingles can occur in younger adults, so anyone with a painful, blistering rash should seek timely evaluation."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, Siegel said he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends shingles vaccination for adults 50 and older, as well as certain immunocompromised adults 19 and older, including people who previously received the varicella vaccine.
