title: Fort Hood shooter's firing squad could usher in new era of executions across US, expert says
summary: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan's firing squad execution could pave the way for more states to adopt the method, a death penalty expert says.
story: Fordham Law death penalty expert Deborah Denno calls firing squad quicker and more certain than other methods but warns recent South Carolina case produced a ‘troublesome outcome.’ A smooth execution in Fort Hood could set the tone going forward.

The planned firing squad execution of the Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan could clear the road for more executions by gunfire across the United States, according to a leading death penalty expert, who says the method could gain traction if the military's upcoming execution goes smoothly.

"I think it's highly likely that if firing squad is successful here and successful in quotes because we still don't always know what a person is going through, but let's say it's a very quick execution, that it seems conceivable that it would be used on other inmates as well," Fordham Law Professor Deborah Denno, a leading expert on capital punishment, told Fox News Digital.
In recent years, Idaho, Utah and South Carolina have been among the states to embrace the firing squad as a potential means of execution as lethal injections fall out of favor.
TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE
Hasan is currently imprisoned in the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. (Bell County Sheriff's Office via Getty Images)

The Trump administration announced earlier this week that Hasan will be executed by firing squad. He had been sentenced to death in 2013 after a 2009 mass shooting at the Army base killed 13 people and wounded 32 others.
The Pentagon confirmed to Fox News Digital on Thursday that authorities plan to livestream the sentence when it's carried out on Dec. 3.
FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD
"The firing squad is considered to be more certain," Denno explained. "It's considered to be quicker, and it's also considered to be the, what I call the least inhumane method of execution."
The state's death chamber in Columbia, S.C. with the electric chair, right, and a firing squad chair, left. (South Carolina Department of Corrections via AP)
Condemned prisoners who face the firing squad are believed to suffer less pain than those who receive lethal injections or other methods of capital punishment, she said.
People with excellent aim are also more abundant and better trained than executioners in other methods, she said.

"We have an endless supply of people who are experts in shooting, either professionally, because they're a police officer, corrections officer, or something like that," she said. "But we also have people are who are excellent, superb markspeople too, because that's a hobby or whatever. So this is, it's not difficult finding somebody who's willing to do this."

According to the Army, the last U.S. military execution was that of Pvt. John A. Bennett on April 13, 1961, at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. He was hanged after being convicted of rape and attempted murder.
Previously, Denno has said that the firing squad is the most humane and effective means of execution, with relatively few hiccups throughout American history.
TENNESSEE DEATH ROW INMATE SURVIVES 2 LETHAL INJECTION DOSES IN FAILED EXECUTION ATTEMPT

In recent years, the firing squad has returned to favor in some states that still use capital punishment over concerns including the limited availability of lethal injection drugs and their reliability.
Christa Gail Pike is seen during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Last week, a death row inmate in Tennessee survived two doses of pentobarbital — becoming the first person in the modern era to survive a lethal injection attempt and raising new questions about whether they should remain a viable means of execution.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS
Christa Pike, 50, is recovering after the injections failed to kill her last week. She had been sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville.
An undated portrait photograph of Colleen Slemmer provided by her mother. (May Martinez/Special to the News Sentinel)
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Firing squads have had far fewer controversies throughout American history, Denno said. Until recently, there had only been two incidents — in 1877 and again in 1951.
"Of course there haven't been that many firing squad executions, but otherwise, given everything about the firing squad, these shooters should not be missing their target," she said.
That was until last year, when questions arose surrounding the South Carolina execution of 42-year-old double murderer Mikal Mahdi, she said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Mahdi killed two people in 2004. They were a store clerk named Christopher Boggs, whom Mahdi shot in the head while he was checking his ID, and off-duty officer James Myers, who was shot eight times and burned outside his own home.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
Mikal Mahdi, 41, is set to be executed on April 11 at 6 p.m. at a prison in Columbia. (South Carolina Department of Corrections via AP)
The death row inmate had the option to choose lethal injection, electric chair or firing squad, and took the latter.
SEND US A TIP
But after his execution, his lawyers raised concerns that none of the three bullets fired struck him in the heart as intended, prompting concerns that the cop-killer had been retaliated against.
GOT A TIP?

"The shooters missed the intended target area and the evidence indicates that he was struck by only two bullets, not the prescribed three," said Dr. Jonathan Arden, a forensic pathologist hired by Mahdi's defense. "Consequently, the nature of the internal injuries from the gunshot wounds resulted in a more prolonged death process."
Orangeburg Department of Public Safety Capt. James Myers, 56, was violently murdered by Mikal Mahdi on July 18, 2004, at a shed on his property. (SC Law Enforcement Officers Hall of Fame)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
The executioners in Mahdi's case have not been publicly identified, but Denno said that they were presumably experienced shooters.

"This seems to be a really troublesome outcome, so it's just something to pay attention to on December 3," she said.

title: Delaware neighborhood on edge after masked men with apparent weapons knock on doors of homes
summary: Home security footage shows a masked man in a tactical vest carrying what appeared to be a rifle knocking on doors in a New Castle County neighborhood.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

New Castle County police are investigating reports of masked individuals knocking on residents' doors while allegedly carrying what appeared to be weapons. (New Castle County Police)

title: Toxicology reports reveal same controlled substances in 2 Ole Miss students found dead: court docs
summary: Court documents reveal identical controlled substances in both University of Mississippi students' systems allegedly linked to an Oxford vape store purchase.
story: Fox News correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on the toxicology results that were revealed in a federal court filing suggesting a possible link between a local Oxford, Mississippi, store and the deaths of two Ole Miss students.
The same three substances were present in the bloodstreams of two recently deceased University of Mississippi students, according to federal court documents obtained by Fox News Digital.

Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, both had mitragynine and the Schedule I controlled substances MGM-15 and MGPI present in their bloodstreams, according to toxicology reports revealed in a court filing reviewed by Fox News Digital.
The revelations come ahead of the public release of the full toxicology report.

The three substances, according to the document, are all found in Smax-Mango Breeze pills, which investigators determined Hamilton and Strang had in their possession at the time of their Sept. 21 deaths in Oxford.
KRATOM INDUSTRY WARNS SYNTHETIC OPIOIDS SHOULD NOT BE CALLED 'KRATOM'
Robert Strang and Aidan Hamilton in a split image provided by their families. (Strang family, Kathleen Hamilton/Facebook)
"During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations," Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said in a September statement.
Specifically, officers found packages of Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15 with price tags reading $39.99, each with a black smudge on the first 9, at both sites.

Law enforcement officers arrested 51-year-old Yahya Mohamed Mosleh and his son, 18-year-old Islam Mohamed Mosleh, on charges connected to a narcotics investigation involving an Oxford tobacco shop, Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store.
The men are facing federal drug charges after investigators say they traced purchases made by Strang and Hamilton at the store before their deaths, according to court documents.
VAPE STORE CLERKS NEAR OLE MISS CAMPUS, JAILED FACING DRUG CHARGES

A package of Smax Pseudo-DHM tablets, a synthetic kratom-derived product, that authorities say was found near Aidan Hamilton when paramedics arrived. (U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi)

According to court documents, agents made a controlled purchase from Yahya Mosleh, who allegedly sold them a product hidden in a locked container that had been "banned by local ordinance for more than 4 years."

Shortly after the purchase, agents obtained a search warrant and conducted a search of the store where they found "the same Smax Mango Breeze MGM-15 – with the exact same packaging, exact same ingredients and exact same price tag, of $39.99 with a smudge on the 9."

After testing the substances in a lab, agents determined the products contained Schedule I controlled substances – MGM-15 and MGPI. Furthermore, Strang's and Hamilton's bank records show they both made purchases at Puffs on the same date, according to the court documents.

"There is also probable cause to believe these drugs caused two overdose deaths in Oxford, Mississippi. The Government proved that there was probable cause that the laboratory-tested drugs taken by the two overdose victims were the same type of drugs that were seized from the Moslehs during a court-authorized search warrant," the court documents read.
POLICE NEAR OLE MISS RESPOND TO SUSPECTED OVERDOSE, SAY 'NOT STUDENT-RELATED'
The shocking deaths of two Ole Miss students have reverberated across campus. (Kelsie Cairns/Fox News Digital)

The court documents also note that Mosleh made the sale of the products to a confidential informant after Strang's and Hamilton's deaths, even warning the informant that people had been dying from the product.

"As the purchase was being made, Yahya Mosleh even told the informant that people were dying from similar products and to be careful. He additionally attempted to conceal his sale when other third parties entered the store, only completing it to the informant when those parties had exited," the documents state.
Yahya Mosleh will remain in custody pending trial after a federal judge found him to be "a flight risk with ties to another country," according to the court documents.

Islam Mosleh will be released on a $20,000 unsecured bond with conditions that include a curfew and location monitoring, according to the documents.

The owner of Puffs was indicted by a state grand jury in Lafayette County, Mississippi, for distribution of a controlled substance years ago. However, he absconded and investigators believe he is now running the store remotely from Egypt, according to the documents.
Fox News Digital contacted the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi for additional information.
Fox News Digital's Adam Sabes and Bradford Betz contributed to this report.

title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital, returned to prison after botched execution, attorneys say
summary: Christa Pike is back at prison after surviving a botched lethal injection, but her attorneys say she still struggles with arm injuries and memory problems.
story: Anesthesiologist Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from a hospital and returned to prison after surviving a botched lethal injection that left her with serious medical complications, her attorneys announced.

Pike, who survived two doses of the execution drug pentobarbital Sept. 30, is back at the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years, according to a joint statement from her legal team.
"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been housed for more than 30 years," the statement read.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."
CHRISTA PIKE NOW CONSCIOUS AND TALKING AFTER SURVIVING 2 DOSES OF LETHAL INJECTION DRUG
Christa Gail Pike appears remotely from Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation for her hearing in Knox County Criminal Court in Knoxville, Tenn., Aug. 11, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)

The statement was issued by attorneys Stephen Ferrell and Luke Ihnen of Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee and Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason of the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender.
The attorneys did not disclose when Pike was discharged or whether she has recovered from complications they previously described, including pneumonia, a blood clot and injuries to her arms.
Ferrell told BBC Radio 4 Thursday that Pike had begun walking around her hospital room but continued to struggle with injuries to her arms and memory problems.
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEY SAYS SHE'S 'UP AND WALKING' MORE THAN A WEEK AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION

Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tenn., Sept. 30, 2026. Pike had not been declared dead when witnesses were asked to leave the room they were in. (Denny Simmons/The Tennessean/USA Today Network via Imagn Images)

"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured, and she's not able to use them very much," Ferrell said. "She is up and walking for the first time today but just around the room, not very far."
Pike's attorneys said they believed she was brain-dead Monday evening before she unexpectedly regained consciousness the following morning.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville.
LETHAL INJECTION SURVIVOR CHRISTA PIKE'S FORMER SATANIST BOYFRIEND COULD BE RELEASED IN 5 YEARS
Christa Gail Pike during her trial for the murder of Colleen A. Slemmer March 18, 1996, in Knox County Criminal Court. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
The failed execution has prompted legal action, and a Tennessee judge ordered the state Department of Correction to preserve physical and electronic evidence related to the execution attempt.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has halted executions for the remainder of 2026. It remains unclear whether the state will seek to carry out Pike's death sentence.
Fox News Digital's Mike Ruiz contributed to this report.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Letitia James faces new push to boot her from Cornell rape probe over alleged bias: court documents
summary: A defense lawyer argues New York Attorney General Letitia James prejudged the Cornell University rape case and asks Tompkins County court to remove her.
story: Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn joins Lawrence Jones to analyze a controversial Cornell University sexual assault accusation. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten defends his decision not to charge the students, citing a lack of evidence. The panel debates the legal implications of New York Attorney General Letitia James's public social media comments.

A lawyer representing one of the men accused in a lawsuit of raping Cornell University's "Jane Doe" has formally requested that New York Attorney General Letitia James be removed from the criminal investigation, alleging she is biased and prejudged the case before being appointed as special prosecutor.

Teny Geragos, daughter of prominent criminal defense attorney Mark Geragos, filed a motion Thursday in Tompkins County court arguing that James' previous public statements in support of the accuser have "prejudiced grand jurors."
The motion cited a social media post made by James Sept. 28, the same day local prosecutor Matthew Van Houten announced he would be reopening the case.

"What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers," James wrote. "To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you."

Defense attorney Teny Geragos, appearing the Manhattan Federal Courthouse July 2, 2025, filed a motion on behalf of her client on Oct. 8, 2026, arguing that New York Attorney General Letitia James should be removed as special prosecutor in the Cornell University rape probe. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images)
CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE
Geragos argued that this showed James believed the seven men in the fraternity who were named in a prior lawsuit were guilty "despite not having examined a shred of evidence" up to that point.

"The public cannot, and should not, have any confidence in the investigation or charging decisions of someone who has clearly prejudged the guilt of individuals who the law presumes are innocent," Geragos wrote in the filing. "The AG should be removed."

She also accused New York Gov. Kathy Hochul of selecting James because of her "prejudicial public statements" about the case, arguing that the governor expects the investigation to produce a particular outcome.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James during a news conference in New York Oct. 2, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS
When reached for comment, a spokesperson for Hochul referred Fox News Digital to the governor's answer to a reporter's question about James' social media post at an Oct. 2 press conference.

"I will answer that. I have every confidence in our attorney general to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That's exactly what's going to happen in this case," Hochul said.
The attorney general's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
Geragos' motion comes days after another one of the men named in the lawsuit filed a request in Albany State Supreme Court seeking James' removal, also citing alleged bias.

The former Cornell student at the center of the investigation filed the lawsuit in September, accusing seven former Chi Phi fraternity members of drugging and raping her on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and into the next morning.
The fraternity house at the center of a rape allegation stands on the campus of Cornell University Oct. 8, 2026, in Ithaca, N.Y. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In the lawsuit, she alleges she arrived at the frat house already intoxicated, after which the men pressured her into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated.
The fraternity was suspended Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe reported sexual assault allegations to campus police, according to Doe's civil complaint.

Van Houten, who initially declined to pursue charges, has said Doe's November 2024 sworn statement did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang-raped and, instead, described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual."

title: Nine people killed in Pennsylvania shooting; suspected gunman found dead: report
summary: Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah called the Perry Street mass shooting the worst crime he has encountered in nearly three decades of law enforcement.
story: Erie police SWAT officers breached a home where nine people died. Investigators determined a suspect died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound before arrival. No gunshots were fired by officers during the response.
Authorities said nine people died in a Pennsylvania shooting Friday night, including a 45-year-old suspected gunman who reportedly died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Two young children and a woman who was eight months pregnant were among the eight victims killed, Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah revealed during a news conference Saturday.
Eight of the nine deceased, including the suspected shooter, were related, while the remaining victim was a family friend, Lorah said.
POLICE REVEAL NEW DETAILS ABOUT GUNMAN, 5 VICTIMS KILLED IN RURAL MICHIGAN SHOOTING RAMPAGE
Multiple people were killed in a shooting along Perry Street in Erie, Pa., Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, authorities said. (Google Maps)

Lorah said the ShotSpotter alert was triggered at approximately 4:53 p.m. by two gunshots in the 700 block of Perry Street. Officers arrived approximately three minutes later and discovered two women, ages 51 and 37, dead outside the residence.

Investigators reviewing Ring doorbell footage from a neighboring home determined that the two women appeared distressed as they sought help from neighbors and pounded on a door. The recording captured what investigators believe were muffled gunshots inside the residence before the suspect emerged and fatally shot both women, Lorah said.
One of the women was a family friend, while the other was a sister-in-law of one of the victims, according to Lorah. Neither woman lived at the home.
Lorah clarified Saturday that sounds some witnesses may have mistaken for additional gunfire during the police response came from flash-bang devices and chemical munitions deployed by SWAT officers.

"I want to be candid with our community. This is one of the most difficult and heartbreaking scenes our officers and investigators have ever encountered. The loss of life is devastating, and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing," Lorah said, according to FOX8.

During Saturday's update, Lorah said officers discovered a 5-year-old boy and a 22-month-old girl on the first floor of the home. Four additional victims — a 24-year-old woman, a 44-year-old woman, a 19-year-old man and a 21-year-old man — were found on the second floor and in a stairwell.
The suspected gunman was found dead on the second floor from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, with a .40-caliber handgun recovered on his person. Lorah said the gun was registered to the suspect.
Investigators believe all eight victims were killed, and the gunman died before officers arrived, Lorah said. All the victims found inside the residence lived there.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro issued a statement confirming the number killed during the incident while offering support to victims' families.

"I’ve spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration’s full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians," Shapiro wrote in a post on X Saturday morning.
"My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community."
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro confirmed nine people died in the mass shooting. (Jessica Kourkounis/Getty Images/File)

"It's a horrific scene," Lorah told the station. "There was a large loss of life inside that residence and outside that residence. … I can tell you that this is a tragic, tragic situation."Lorah defended the police response Saturday, explaining that officers initially had no way of knowing whether the suspect remained inside, had escaped or was holding anyone hostage.
He said officers heard no gunfire, screams or other signs of life coming from the residence. Police deployed drones and a robot to assess the interior before entering the home.

Lorah emphasized that obtaining a search warrant did not delay officers from entering the residence and that they would have gone inside immediately if they had detected signs someone was in imminent danger.
MULTIPLE PEOPLE KILLED IN SHOOTING AT IDAHO IN-N-OUT RESTAURANT, SUSPECT DEAD
Erie police responded to the 700 block of Perry Street Oct. 9, 2026, after reports of a shooting. (Erie Police Department)
The city of Erie issued a statement about the shooting, saying the incident resulted in "multiple deaths" and confirming that there was no ongoing threat to the public.
"We understand that this news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained," the city said.

"Our thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones and everyone impacted by tonight's tragedy," the statement continued. "We will continue working closely with our Erie Police Dept, and will provide updates as soon as verified information becomes available."

Erie Mayor Daria Devlin said Saturday the city is coordinating with crisis services, healthcare providers and schools to provide trauma support to families, students and residents affected by the shooting.
Erie police responded to reports of gunfire Friday evening before discovering multiple victims. (Erie Police Department)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The department's Criminal Investigations Division continues to investigate the shooting.

title: Philadelphia police officer killed, partner shot 12 times in ambush; suspect found hiding in tree
summary: Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber, a 40-year-old father of two, was killed. His partner was shot 12 times after the officers were ambushed while responding to an armed man.
story: An official confirms charges have been brought against a defendant for disarming an officer. The case involves two law enforcement officers who were shot, leaving one deceased, while nine other officers were not struck.
A Philadelphia police officer died Saturday after he and his partner were ambushed and shot multiple times while responding to a report of an armed man in the western part of the city.

Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner identified the suspect as 35-year-old Eric Lewis, who has a criminal record dating back to 2012, according to Pennsylvania court records reviewed by Fox News Digital.
A municipal labor union also identified Lewis as an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department.

Krasner outlined a series of charges stemming from the shooting, including attempted murder, attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault and gun offenses. Prosecutors identified at least 11 potential victims, including the two officers who were shot and nine additional people who were fired upon.
CONNECTICUT POLICE OFFICERS SHOT, SUSPECT KILLED AFTER ATTEMPTED ARREST SPARKS HECTIC CHASE
Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel identified the officer who died as Shane Seiber, a 40-year-old father who spent 10 years on the force.
He leaves behind his wife and his two children, a 7-year-old son and a 3-year-old daughter.

Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel, pictured here May 8, 2025, gave an update on the officers shot while responding to a call in the western part of the city Oct. 10, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"He fought valiantly, but he lost his life today," Bethel said at a morning news conference. "His wife was able to be by his side before he passed, as well as his family."

Lewis was found guilty of theft and receiving stolen property in 2012 and gun-related offenses and simple assault in 2013, receiving probation in both cases, according to court records. In 2018, Lewis pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct involving fighting and was again sentenced to probation.
Court records also show Lewis was cited for three traffic violations in 2024, including driving without headlights, failing to provide proof of insurance and windshield-related violations.

District Council 33, a labor union representing Philadelphia municipal workers, identified Lewis as one of its members and an employee of the Philadelphia Water Department in a Facebook statement addressing the shooting.The union condemned the violence, expressed condolences to Seiber's family and wished the surviving officer a full recovery. District Council 33 also said it would cooperate with authorities as the case proceeds.
During a news conference, Mayor Cherelle Parker said Seiber "paid the ultimate price while sacrificing his own life to protect and serve our city."

Parker also announced plans to seek legislation expanding Pennsylvania's involuntary commitment laws to cover substance use disorders and other mental or behavioral health conditions. She said she would work with Gov. Josh Shapiro, the state legislature and Attorney General Dave Sunday on the proposal.
The Philadelphia police officers were shot a total of 15 times, according to officials. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images/File)
CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED

Krasner said investigators had not determined whether mental health or substance use played a role in the shooting. Krasner also declined to discuss the suspect's motive, citing the ongoing investigation and sensitivity toward the victims' families.The mayor also referenced the deaths of nine people in Erie, Pennsylvania, saying the tragedy underscored the need to revisit existing laws. Parker acknowledged that investigators had not determined whether mental health or substance use played a role in the Erie deaths.
Parker separately ordered city flags to remain at half-staff until sunset on the day of Seiber's interment.

Gov. Shapiro said in a social media post that he and his wife were praying for Seiber's loved ones and the Philadelphia Police Department. He also ordered all U.S. and state flags to be flown at half-staff.

Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., also mourned Seiber's death, offering prayers for his family, the Philadelphia Police Department and the wounded officer. McCormick said Philadelphia had lost a hero whose sacrifice would not be forgotten.
The two Philadelphia police officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center. (Al Bello/Getty Images/File)
Rep. Mike Kelly, R-Pa., separately offered prayers for the Erie community and the families affected by Friday night's tragedy.

The other officer, a 33-year-old father of five children, was shot 12 times and was initially in critical condition. After going into surgery, Bethel said, he is now in stable condition but is "not out of the woods yet."
Just after 12:20 a.m., the officers responded to a report of a man with a gun on a porch, Bethel said.
About 30 minutes later, the officers arrived at the address and came under "significant gunfire" once they were on the porch.
Shortly after shots were fired, Bethel said, additional officers and a SWAT team found the original responding officers on the porch with gunshot wounds.
After running away, the suspect fired at two additional officers, Bethel said.
Krasner outlined nine additional counts of attempted murder and attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer involving the nine other people who were fired upon.
A SWAT team was able to locate the suspect in a tree and take him into custody.
Krasner said Lewis remained in custody without serious injuries and was expected to appear for a preliminary arraignment and bail hearing.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lewis was found with two handguns and a shotgun, Bethel said. One of the handguns belonged to one of the officers who had been shot.

title: Discarded trash uncaps 41-year-old murder case in ritzy seaside resort town, authorities say
summary: A Rhode Island investigator trailed William Morton to a concert and seized a water bottle that allegedly links him to a 1985 Newport murder.
story: On Oct. 6, William ‘Billy’ Morton was arrested and charged with first-degree murder for allegedly killing Hillary Hellewell in 1985 in Newport, Rhode Island.
After sitting cold for more than 40 years, a Rhode Island murder case may have been solved with the recovery of a discarded water bottle in a theater.
On Oct. 6, William "Billy" Morton was arrested and charged with first-degree murder for allegedly killing Hillary Hellewell in Newport in 1985.
After four decades, investigators used new DNA technology that allegedly links 61-year-old Morton to the crime.
Hillary Hellewell was found dead in Newport, R.I., May 19, 1985. (Getty Images)
DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON
Since her death, investigators had slowly uncovered clues that suggested Morton might be a suspect. But they needed some of his DNA to confirm the connection.
So, in late August, an investigator followed Morton to a Heart tribute band concert at a Rhode Island theater, court records show.
FIANCÉE STICKS BY ACCUSED SERIAL RAPIST AS SPECIAL AGENTS DEFEND TAILING HIM FOR RESTAURANT DNA STAKEOUT

Morton bought popcorn and bottled water for himself and his fiancée, investigators said. But when the couple left the concert early and Morton didn’t pick up his trash, an investigator collected it as potential evidence.
DNA recovered from his water bottle was used to confirm the match to DNA found on Hellewell’s body, according to court documents.
William "Billy" Morton was convicted in 1987 of a violent sexual assault in Newport, 45 days after Hellewell's death.  (Visions of America/Joseph Sohm/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT
Morton was taken into custody Oct. 6 and is being held without bond.
The killing
On May 19, 1985, the body of 22-year-old Hellewell was found in Newport, Rhode Island, by two brothers — 17 and 20 — who were on their way to work at 4:15 a.m.
Hellewell’s body was lying on a sidewalk along Anthony Street. She was wearing white painter’s pants, a sweater and socks but no shoes.
Her pulseless body was mostly "cold to the touch," with some areas still "slightly warm" when officers arrived, Morton’s arrest warrant shows.
She died from asphyxia due to strangulation, a medical examiner reported. Her cause of death was homicide.
KILLER UNDONE BY DECADES-OLD THREADS — GLOVE, TOWEL AND SHIRT STITCH TOGETHER COLD CASE JUSTICE
Investigators found a blood stain on the back of Hellewell’s white pants,and a "heavily soiled" blue T-shirt near her head, the arrest warrant shows.
Swabs taken from an internal exam of Hellewell’s body revealed spermatozoa, indicating sexual contact, the warrant shows.
She was identified the next day when she was reported missing.
Boats make their way through the harbor in Newport, R.I. (Reuters/Brian Snyder)
Friends and family told investigators that she’d attended a gathering with friends in Newport the night before. Everyone there drank alcohol, investigators were told.
Investigators learned that Hellewell had offered to walk home with one of her male friends, who’d become overly intoxicated.
He made it home. She did not.
The next day, he was still so intoxicated he couldn’t give many details to police.

The men, who were close to Hellewell at the time of her death, were ruled out as being "potential donors" of the sperm, according to court records. But Newport Police were never able to develop a viable suspect.
At the time of Hellewell's murder, DNA evidence was collected and preserved.
Resurrecting a cold case
The case was reviewed by state officials in 2004. They hoped new advancements in DNA technology could help.
During that review, DNA profiles for Hellewell and the suspect were entered into the FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) database.
Then, in 2023, the Rhode Island Attorney General's office formed the Cold Case Unit (CCU), and Hellewell’s case went under review again.
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha's office worked with the Newport Police Department with help from the Smithfield Police Department. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
With recent breakthroughs in technology used to evaluate DNA, the evidence was sent to a private lab.
That work brought a new lead into sharp focus. Suddenly, Morton was a suspect.

Investigators pinpointed Morton’s family line through the DNA found on Hellewell’s body. They later found Morton had been convicted in 1987 of a violent sexual assault in Newport 45 days after Hellewell's death. The assault took place a couple miles from where Hellewell’s body was found, court records show.
Morton was sentenced to 20 years in prison. He spent seven years behind bars and served out the remainder of his sentence on probation.
Date night DNA discovery
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
After the new DNA evaluation, investigators collected evidence and conducted interviews. New clues led them to Morton.
They began to watch and trail him.

On Aug. 21, Michael Nayor, a senior cold case investigator with the Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General, followed Morton and his fiancée, the arrest warrant shows. They pulled into a Burger King before heading to a theater in Woonsocket, Rhode Island.

The investigator purchased a ticket to a show by Bad Animals, a Heart tribute band, and followed the couple inside. He watched as Morton bought popcorn and two bottled waters, the arrest warrant shows.

Naylor watched Morton sip his water throughout the show. And when he set the bottle on the seat next to him, Naylor took note, the warrant shows.
SEND US A TIP
When Morton and his fiancée left early, the bottle of water was left behind. Naylor seized it and submitted it for DNA testing.
GOT A TIP?

The DNA profile from the water bottle "is consistent with the previously reported partial profiles" from the sperm stain on Hellewell’s pants and a stain on the blue shirt found near her body, according to the Rhode Island Department of Health.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

On Oct. 6, officers from multiple agencies visited Morton’s home at about 7 a.m. as he was leaving for his job as service technician at a Volkswagen dealership. He was charged with first-degree murder in the Rhode Island District Court Second Division.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
The case will go to a grand jury, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha said. A status conference is scheduled for Oct. 20.

title: Sally Yates' Cornell review of alleged gang rape could scrutinize crucial police interview, attorney says
summary: Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity case faces fresh scrutiny as Sally Yates examines a key police interview prosecutors never fully received.
story: Attorney Scott Iseman examines what Sally Yates could uncover in Cornell's rape case review, including a key police interview prosecutors never received in full.

A key campus police interview that local prosecutors say they never received in full before initially declining to bring charges in the Cornell University alleged rape case could face fresh scrutiny as former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates reviews the Ivy League school's handling of the allegations.

Yates, who served as deputy attorney general during the Obama administration, has been tapped by Cornell's trustees to conduct a sweeping independent review of the October 2024 allegations involving members of its Chi Phi fraternity after the university's own investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions.

The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, told Cornell University Police during a November 2024 interview, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," according to a transcript obtained by CBS News.
She also described later sexual activity as coercive and said she had been "completely and totally incapacitated."
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, however, said his office reviewed a six-page sworn statement that described Doe's participation in the sexual activity and drug use as voluntary and consensual.
Van Houten said his office did not initially receive the complete interview and told CBS News last week that the information in the fuller interview "changes the landscape for me."

Former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates (right) is reviewing Cornell University's handling of sexual assault allegations involving members of its Chi Phi fraternity, whose house is pictured at left. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images; Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Scott Iseman, a New York attorney who has represented students accused of campus sexual misconduct, said Yates could review Doe's full police interview and compare it with her sworn statement, later testimony and other evidence gathered during Cornell's investigation.
"Those full recorded interviews, I can tell you from experience, have a treasure trove of information that are really, really important to exactly what happened," Iseman said.
"It wouldn't surprise me if there was additional information in there that would have changed the trajectory of this case because that happens all the time."
The apparent differences between Doe's full interview and her shorter sworn statement could be particularly significant, Iseman said.
"Law enforcement is supposed to make sure that all salient facts are included in that sworn statement," he said.

Cornell said its police department provided prosecutors with Doe's sworn statement and a Snapchat screenshot in 2024, describing the evidence-sharing process as standard protocol when a possible crime has occurred.

Iseman cautioned that he had not reviewed the complete interview, which has not been made publicly available, and could not determine whether any omitted information was material. It remains unclear why the full interview was not initially provided to Van Houten's office. Fox News Digital reached out to Cornell University Police and the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office for clarification.

Cornell said Yates and her team will have access to relevant records, case files, university personnel and leadership as they review the school's response, under its original Title IX investigation, which determines whether students violated university sexual misconduct policies rather than criminal law.

Beyond the police interview, Iseman said Yates could identify witnesses who were never questioned, overlooked text messages or social media evidence and other information that did not emerge during Cornell's original investigation.
"There's a lot that potentially she could uncover," Iseman said.
But he cautioned against assuming Cornell mishandled the allegations.
"It may have all been done very appropriately by Cornell. We don't know yet," he said.
CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE
Former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates is reviewing Cornell University's handling of the allegations. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)
Cornell has defended its handling of the allegations, pointing to an extensive investigation that included more than 50 interviews and 12 days of disciplinary hearings.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said two of the seven accused students were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before discipline could be imposed and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.
Cornell said both the accuser and accused students had opportunities to review evidence, testify and challenge the findings through an appeals process.

Yates was brought in after the case erupted into a national firestorm following Doe's Sept. 16 lawsuit, which laid out graphic allegations that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her during a night involving alcohol, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024.
The allegations have since sparked protests on campus while New York Attorney General Letitia James' office is conducting a separate criminal investigation.
The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.

Yates' investigation extends beyond the Chi Phi case to examine how Cornell handles sexual misconduct allegations across campus, including its oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.

Her team at the law firm of King & Spalding will also assess Cornell's practices against federal and state laws and examine whether the university followed its own procedures in responding to the Chi Phi allegations.
Any new or previously overlooked evidence identified during the review could potentially be shared with James' office, Iseman said, though Yates herself has no authority to bring charges.
BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

Thousands of Cornell University students and others from the Cornell community fill Ho Plaza for the Justice for Survivors protest hosted by twenty student organizations Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. (Matt Burkhartt/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Her findings could also lead to recommendations for improving Cornell's procedures, even if the university is found to have followed its existing rules. Cornell said Yates will report her findings and recommendations to a special committee of its Board of Trustees, which intends to share the results with the university community.
Yates has tackled explosive misconduct allegations before.
Her 2022 investigation into women's professional soccer exposed widespread sexual harassment, coercion and abuse by coaches, along with failures by league officials to act on complaints.

What began as an investigation into individual coaches exposed much wider problems across women's soccer, prompting a series of recommendations for sweeping reforms that U.S. Soccer subsequently pledged to implement.
The Cornell case also highlights a wider debate over the legal protections available to students accused of serious sexual misconduct, even as universities have the power to expel them.

John R. Grasso, a Rhode Island criminal defense attorney and former police officer who has represented accused students for two decades, argued that campus disciplinary proceedings can carry life-altering consequences without offering the same legal protections available in criminal court.
"When I defend a student on campus, we don't have any right to discovery. We can't compel the production of anything," Grasso said.
He said those limitations can make it difficult for attorneys to obtain potentially important text messages, photographs and other evidence that might support an accused student's defense.

Grasso also described the difficult choice students can face when university disciplinary proceedings and criminal investigations overlap: participating in campus proceedings and potentially making statements that could affect a criminal case or remaining silent and risking disciplinary consequences.
"I have a right to remain silent, but if I don't participate, I'm getting found responsible," he said, describing the dilemma he has encountered representing students.
The now-shuttered Chi Phi fraternity house at 107 Edgemoor Lane in Ithaca, NY., Oct. 6, 2026.  (Richard Beetham for Fox News Digital)

Grasso said the consequences of campus sexual misconduct allegations can extend far beyond disciplinary hearings, describing students whose education, reputations and emotional well-being have suffered even when they were ultimately cleared.
"Bad things happen to the accused the minute a complaint is filed against them on campus. Really bad things," he said.

"Just because the allegations are salacious or dramatic does not mean that's what happened," Iseman said. "So, people need to keep an open mind."

title: Ohio dog park shooting over Trump argument could end with two self-defense claims or none: legal expert
summary: Both men in the Ohio dog park shootout over Donald Trump could claim self-defense or neither could, a legal expert says, creating a rare puzzle.
story: Emmanuel ‘Mike’ Mathews, 81, and David Mattai, 55, got into a shootout at an Ohio dog park April 21 after arguing about President Donald Trump, according to authorities.

A shootout sparked by an argument over President Donald Trump at an Ohio dog park could end with a jury finding that both men acted in self-defense or that neither did, a legal expert told Fox News Digital.
Emmanuel "Mike" Mathews, 81, was charged with felonious assault for shooting David Mattai, 55, April 21 at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, according to authorities.
Mathews has pleaded not guilty.
Case Western Reserve University law professor Michael Benza said, under Ohio law, defendants lose the right to claim self-defense if they helped ignite the confrontation that led to the shooting.
Emmanuel Mathews faces charges in a shooting at an Ohio dog park. (Geauga County Sheriff's Office)
VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE
Since both men allegedly took part in the escalation, he said, the case presents a unique legal puzzle.
"They could both be found at fault, which means neither of them would get self-defense," Benza told Fox News Digital.
Since self-defense relies heavily on subjective fear and perceived danger, Benza said, "It's also possible both get self-defense."
Competing accounts
Mathews' attorney, Ian Friedman, said the encounter began as an argument, which turned physical in the park before ending in gunfire in the park’s parking lot.
"Mr. Mathews was attempting to leave," Friedman told Fox News Digital. "He was attempting to keep himself safe."
Friedman said it started when Mattai, who overheard Mathews talking to an eyewitness about Trump, disagreed with Mathews' view that Trump is one of the country's greatest presidents.

Bainbridge Township Patrolman Friedrich Kaufmann testified at Mathews’ May 5 preliminary hearing in Chardon Municipal Court that, after that initial argument, Mattai drove away, then returned to the park about five minutes later.
David Mattai faces charges in a shooting at an Ohio dog park. (Geauga County Sheriff's Office)
FLORIDA MEN WIELDING HATCHET AND MACHETE CLASH IN PUBLIX PARKING LOT, POLICE SAY
Mathews was still sitting at a picnic table with his dog when Mattai returned.
Mathews gathered his belongings and began walking toward his vehicle, but after crossing to the other side of a park fence, an exchange of insults between the pair caused a physical confrontation.
GUN-WIELDING COUPLE IN VIRAL BLM STANDOFF GOT FIREPOWER — AND 'A VOICE' — BACK AFTER LEGAL SAGA

Friedman said Mattai grabbed Mathews by the hair and pulled him into the fence. Mathews also reported being headbutted. Mattai denied the headbutt allegation, but Friedman said an injury below Mathews' eye supports that account.
After the physical altercation, both men retreated toward their vehicles after witness Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, reportedly stepped in to defuse the situation.
The dog park at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, Ohio. (Google Maps)
OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO
Mathews got into his vehicle and allegedly placed a .45-caliber gun on his dashboard, when Mattai, who stood in the parking area after loading his dog in his vehicle, saw the weapon.

The men allegedly exchanged words before Mathews fired once. Mattai retrieved a 9 mm Taurus handgun from inside his Hyundai, then fired six shots "almost contemporaneously" near Mathews' head and body, according to Friedman.
"We believe that Mattai was turning to retrieve his gun and coming back to aim at Mathews when the bullet struck the lower right portion of his back," Friedman added.
Mathews was not injured in the gunfire exchange, but Mattai's return fire hit Mathews' vehicle at least four times.
Mattai previously told The New York Times he did not physically touch Mathews after seeing Mathews’ weapon and fired back in fear of his own safety.
Mattai’s wife, Sally Mattai, told the Times her husband almost died after suffering a severe gunshot wound to his lower back that damaged his spine and required two separate emergency surgeries.
Mattai's attorney, Ryan Fisher, said he believes public opinions have convoluted the case and created confusion.
"There are a great deal of differing opinions of what went on in the dog park that day," Fisher told Fox News Digital.
Fisher's response did not address the defense's claims about the gun or the timing of the shots.
Geauga County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Mattai Aug. 5. He’s facing misdemeanor charges of assault and disorderly conduct.
'You can't be the first one to draw the gun'
Benza said introducing a gun changes the legal footing of a physical scuffle, but he emphasized that the order of events greatly matter.

"You go from, OK, we're hitting each other. ... Physically, punches are being thrown. Now you've pulled a weapon. You have now escalated this fight, which then justifies me escalating my response by then pulling my own gun and defending myself," he said.
"But you can't be the first one to draw the gun."
Ohio law removes the duty to retreat when someone is lawfully in a location. Friedman said that since Mathews was legally allowed to be at the park, he had no obligation to flee.
"He certainly had no duty to retreat," Friedman said. "Had he done anything different from what he did do in those seconds, he may not be here to talk about it today."
Political challenges
Friedman said, although the argument began over politics, his client acted out of fear for his safety, not political retaliation.
"This was never about a political dispute for Mr. Mathews," he said.
Benza, however, said the county’s politics could potentially complicate seating a jury, regardless of why the incident happened.
"In Geauga County, where this happened, it is a very Republican-dominated county," Benza said.
"The one defendant may be concerned that he will end up with jurors who are very pro-Republican or pro-Trump, which would create his concerns about a fair jury.
"The other defendant may want a pro-Trump jury because they would be so, well, he got what he deserved or something to that effect."
President Donald Trump listens as a reporter asks a question in the Oval Office of the White House Aug. 27, 2026, in Washington. (Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP)

The case may come down to a jury deciding whether Mathews had a genuine, reasonable fear for his life when he was accused of shooting Mattai.

Friedman predicted the evidence would show Mathews should never have been arrested, while Fisher said the case is "going to have to be flushed out by the jury in the upcoming trial."

title: Texas think tank accuses Houston parent coalition of using 'socialist' tactics to push radical agenda
summary: The Texas Public Policy Foundation accuses a Houston education coalition of using socialist-aligned tactics to push radical policies in HISD schools.
story: As the Houston Independent School District reports academic gains following a state takeover, critics and conservative researchers clash over the district’s future and testing policies.
Education policy experts are warning against a Houston education advocacy coalition, accusing the group of using socialist-aligned tactics to push radical policies in public schools.

The Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF( warned that Community Voices for Public Education (CVPE) — which it said presents itself as a grassroots group of parents, teachers and community members — acts as a front for teachers' unions and far-left organizations working to preserve the status quo.

"There are several policies that they're advocating for which are questionable at best, but very harmful," Kate Bierly, campaign director for TPPF's Next Generation Texas Campaign, told Fox News Digital.
WATCHDOG REPORT EXPOSES TEACHERS UNION 'POLITICAL MACHINE' FUNNELING MORE THAN $1 BILLION TO LIBERAL CAUSES

Community Voices for Public Education (CVPE), a local advocacy group in Houston, uses tactics similarly employed by far-left groups like the Democratic Socialists of America in opposition to a state takeover of the Houston Independent School District and pushes for radical reform policies, according to the Texas Public Policy Foundation. (Getty Images)

CVPE has been an outspoken opponent of the state's 2023 takeover of the Houston Independent School District (HISD), Texas's largest school district. The Texas Education Agency (TEA) intervened following years of academic underperformance at select campuses — a move that drew sharp accusations of political overreach from critics.

State metrics, however, show noticeable academic gains since the intervention. Reading and math scores on the State of Texas Assessments of Academic Readiness (STAAR) improved among grades 3 through 8 over the past three school years, while the number of A- and B-rated campuses in HISD jumped from 93 to 197.
SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'
Demonstrators hold a Democratic Socialists of America banner ahead of a Rent Guidelines Board vote at El Museo del Barrio in New York on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"F-rated campuses went from 56 to five, and the whole district moved from a C rating to a B rating," Bierly said. "The results were amazing. But from this, several critics emerged ... suggesting destructive replacement policies. One of the main groups behind these proposals is CVPE."

The local group, Bierly said, uses tactics similar to those employed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which has gained traction in recent years as a political force with the election of several DSA-endorsed candidates across various levels of government.
DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

HISD presides over 274 schools and 184,109 students. Historically the largest school district in Texas, despite some fluctuations in recent years after COVID, the district has touted academic progress across all grades and subjects and "more than doubled the number of A- and B-rated schools in just two years." (Houston Independent School District)

Beyond opposing the state takeover, CVPE advocates against mandatory STAAR testing and urges parents to boycott the exams. The group also calls for divesting from campus policing — ending student arrests except in severe cases such as murder — and encourages participation in walkouts and political protests.

TPPF contends that CVPE actively instructs parents on how to organize student demonstrations outside schools, while CVPE maintains that peaceful advocacy is essential to improving school environments and curricula.

"Some of the things they are advocating for is that parents should boycott the STAAR exam because the test allegedly supports racism and inequality," Bierly added. "Scrapping this testing removes a key pathway for low-income kids to access advanced academic tracks."
FAR-LEFT ACTIVIST CONFERENCE AT TEACHERS UNION HQ RAISES CLASSROOM CONCERNS

CVPE defends its platform, maintaining that restorative justice and expanded mental health resources foster safer learning environments than punitive measures, insisting "HISD students should be heard and not herded."

Ruth Kravetz, co-founder of CVPE, pushed back on both TPPF’s report and the state's academic claims. Speaking to Fox News Digital, Kravetz dismissed assertions that her group relies on DSA tactics, emphasizing that CVPE supporters span the political spectrum.
"Some of those parents are Republicans. Some are Democrats, some are socialists, and some are unaffiliated," Kravetz said.
POWERFUL TEACHERS' UNIONS SHARE STRIKING LINK WITH STATES STRUGGLING TO TEACH KIDS TO READ
Kravetz also criticized high-stakes standardized testing, arguing that it fails to improve student outcomes.

"It undermines educational quality," Kravetz said. "It narrows instruction and reduces deeper, more meaningful learning ... I don't think any parent ever said, ‘I hope my kid grows up to be able to fill in a multiple-choice test well.’"
Kravetz previously challenged the "Texas Miracle" touted by HISD Superintendent Mike Miles and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, alleging that recent test improvements were artificially-engineered.

"The truth is that HISD’s Mike Miles didn’t allow qualified students to even take Algebra I," Kravetz said. "This skewed the STAAR results and played a shell game with scores. Most importantly, they denied opportunities to countless kids just to make the numbers look better."
HISD did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: South Carolina fitness trainer's cause of death made public as coroner defends husband
summary: Elena Moore's autopsy revealed cardiac dysrhythmia with premature ventricular contractions, and her husband Brannon Slice was never a suspect.
story: Sondra Campbell, who was close friends with Moore, told Fox News Digital what Elena Moore said to her just weeks before a body matching her description was found.

Nearly four months after the body of a missing South Carolina fitness enthusiast was found, authorities have determined that 39-year-old Elena Katherine Moore died of natural causes stemming from a heart condition, ending months of speculation surrounding her disappearance.

Lexington County Coroner Margaret Fisher announced Friday that Moore died from complications of cardiac dysrhythmia with premature ventricular contractions, a condition involving an abnormal heart rhythm.
Fisher said the autopsy found no evidence of traumatic injuries, including broken bones, strangulation or sexual assault. Toxicology testing detected alcohol but no other substances.

title: Federal judge blocks deportation of Dominican illegal immigrant shot by ICE during NYC arrest attempt
summary: A Dominican illegal immigrant was shot by ICE officers in the Bronx after allegedly driving toward agents. Bodycam video captured the chaotic aftermath.
story: Body camera footage shows NYPD officers responding after a male was shot in Marble Hill on Thursday. The officers transported the individual who was shot to the hospital.

A federal judge has temporarily blocked the deportation of an illegal immigrant who was shot Thursday during a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation in New York City, as local and federal authorities on Friday released video surrounding the shooting.

In a two-page order, U.S. District Judge Paul Oetken, an Obama appointee, ruled that the man — whom police identified as Oscar Belgal but who was named in a court document as Oscar Bergal — cannot be removed from the United States without a court order while his petition challenging his detention remains pending.
The judge also barred federal authorities from transferring him to any facility outside the Southern or Eastern Districts of New York or the District of New Jersey without prior court approval.
MAMDANI DEMANDS TRUMP RELEASE ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE AGENT AS PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX

Law enforcement personnel tend to the suspect after he was shot by federal immigration officers on Thursday in New York. A 5-year-old boy was inside the car. On Friday, a judge blocked his deportation. (New York City Police Department via AP)

In a Friday court hearing, a judge dismissed a defense application for a temporary restringing order with prejudice because federal prosecutors didn't challenge Oetken's order that Belgal not be deported.

Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, was shot after refusing to comply with lawful orders while ICE officers were conducting a targeted operation to arrest him in the Bronx, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

During the encounter, the Belgal pulled his vehicle forward before at least one officer fired seven rounds, striking him below his left ear, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference near the shooting scene late Thursday.

ICE officers used their vehicles to block him as he attempted to drive away, but Belgal accelerated toward them, Marcos Charles, a senior ICE official, said Friday during a news conference in Washington alongside DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
"Our officers, using their training and believing that their life and the life of the partners and the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons," Charles said.
AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARKS FIGHT OVER VENEZUELAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S DEPORTATION

In this image taken from New York City Police Department body camera video, law enforcement personnel tend to the suspect, who was shot by federal immigration officers on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in New York, as he drove his car with a 5-year-old boy inside. (New York City Police Department via AP)
A 5-year-old boy inside the vehicle was unharmed. Belgal survived the shooting and was treated at a local hospital, Charles added.
He has since been released. However, his lawyers said he still has a bullet inside his body.

ICE agents were unaware that a child was inside the vehicle, but Charles said Belgal "was aware" and chose to put the boy at risk by attempting to evade law enforcement. In a statement, Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark said her office was working to establish the facts of the case and determine the next course of action.

"Any shooting in the Bronx is a matter of grave concern that impacts community safety," Clark said. "As District Attorney, it is my top priority to protect the well-being of everyone in the borough. We will continue to conduct a thorough investigation where our process is guided by the evidence and the law."
Outside the courthouse, Harold Solis, an immigration attorney with the nonprofit Make the Road New York, criticized the ICE officers' actions.

"Regardless of whether or not someone has a criminal history, it is not lawful and it is not OK to shoot a father in an afternoon with his son in the back seat," Solis told reporters Friday. "That is not how we resolve legal disputes in this country. We resolve them in buildings like these, in courtrooms."

Protesters and law enforcement officers clash close to the scene where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx borough of New York on October 8, 2026, according to local media and police.  (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)
On Friday, the NYPD released bodycam footage showing officers arriving at the scene following the gunfire. The NYPD was not involved in the shooting incident.
Video shows the suspect sitting handcuffed on the ground as officers arrive. In the background, a crowd can be heard voicing anger and dismay at the shooting.

According to DHS, Belgal has a prior grand larceny conviction and previous arrests for assault, robbery, drug possession, and weapons possession. Federal authorities also alleged that he has ties to the notorious Trinitarios street gang.
Hours later, the NYPD released surveillance video taken from two vantage points. The muted video shows one angle of the seconds right before the shooting and another angle right after the shooting.

title: Severe turbulence diverts New York City flight to Miami, 8 injured

story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

title: Charles Manson follower tied to Sharon Tate murders gets recommended for parole after 55 years in prison
summary: Patricia Krenwinkel's third parole recommendation in four years sets up another potential clash with Gavin Newsom over the Manson Family killer's release.
story: Former Sacramento DA Anne Marie Schubert is spearheading a lawsuit challenging new California Board of Parole Hearings guidelines that she warns will open a pathway to freedom for serial killers, mass shooters and more of the state's worst violent criminals.
Patricia Krenwinkel, a former follower of cult leader Charles Manson convicted in the 1969 Tate-LaBianca murders, has been recommended for parole after spending more than 55 years behind bars.

Krenwinkel, 78, was recommended for parole Tuesday for the third time in four years, setting up another potential showdown with California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has blocked her release twice over concerns that she remains a danger to the public.
The latest decision, confirmed by the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's inmate database, comes less than a year after Newsom reversed her previous parole recommendation.
CHARLES MANSON CULT FOLLOWER BRUCE DAVIS, CONVICTED IN TWO 1969 KILLINGS, DIES BEHIND BARS AT 83

In his October 2025 decision, Newsom found that Krenwinkel "lacks the requisite insight she needs to be safely released," despite acknowledging her efforts to rehabilitate herself while spending decades in prison.
Manson family members Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie van Houten. (Bettmann Archive)
"When considered as a whole, the evidence shows that she currently poses an unreasonable danger to society if released from prison at this time," Newsom wrote.
NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'
State records show Krenwinkel was previously recommended for parole in May 2022 and May 2025, but Newsom reversed both decisions, keeping her behind bars.
The decision does not guarantee Krenwinkel's release, as the parole board must first complete its review before Newsom can decide whether to let her go free or block her release for a third time.
MENENDEZ BROTHERS GRANTED 2027 PAROLE HEARING A YEAR EARLIER THAN EXPECTED
For now, she remains at the California Institution for Women in Corona, where she is serving a life sentence after entering the state prison system on April 28, 1971.

(L-R) Susan Denise Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel and Leslie Van Houten laugh after receiving the death sentence for their part in the Tate-LaBianca killing at the order of Charles Manson. (Bettmann Archive via Getty Images)

Krenwinkel was just 21 when she joined other members of Manson's so-called "Family" in two nights of killings in August 1969 that left seven people dead, including actress Sharon Tate, who was eight months pregnant.

According to Newsom's summary of the case, Krenwinkel and other Manson followers fatally stabbed Tate's friend Abigail Folger and helped attack several other victims. The following night, the group murdered Leno and Rosemary LaBianca, leaving bloody messages throughout their home.

title: Former Massachusetts police officer faces murder trial over pregnant woman's staged suicide

story: Phil Keith was Knoxville's chief of police in the 1990s, when Christa Pike and two friends tortured and killed a classmate named Colleen Slemmer.
The murder trial for a former Massachusetts police officer accused of killing his pregnant mistress and staging the scene to look like a suicide is kicking off after a brief 9 a.m. hearing Friday.

Once the jury is seated, the trial of former Stoughton Police Officer Matthew Farwell will kick off with opening statements followed by testimony from Stoughton Detective Heather Cheever and then from a local elementary school official.
The FBI arrested Farwell, 40, in August 2024 in connection with the death of 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore, which happened three years earlier.
EX-MASSACHUSETTS OFFICER ALLEGEDLY MURDERED PREGNANT WOMAN HE GROOMED AS A TEEN, STAGED IT TO LOOK LIKE SUICIDE

Sandra Birchmore pictured in a selfie she posted to Facebook in January 2021, about three weeks before she was killed in a scene prosecutors allege was staged to look like a suicide. Prosecutors have accused Farwell of grooming Birchmore since she was a teenager, maintaining a sexual relationship for years and then killing her when she told him she'd become pregnant and staging her death to look like a suicide.
Birchmore's death was initially deemed a suicide. But Farwell was charged following internal affairs and FBI investigations.
