What to know about Pope Leo’s surgery to remove a lung nodule

Lung cancer is more treatable if caught early. The deadly cancer is most often caused by cigarette smoking, but about 20% of lung cancer cases are diagnosed in people who have never smoked or used tobacco, according to the American Cancer Society.
However, finding a nodule on a scan doesn’t confirm a cancer diagnosis, Bharat said, and the surgery will reveal more information as doctors are able to put the nodule under a microscope.
Advances in the procedures mean they are generally less invasive and some patients begin walking within a day or two.
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement Sunday that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”
If the nodule is larger and more lung tissue is removed, meaning the surgery is more extensive, it may be three to four weeks before a patient is fully recovered.
“Given the pope’s age, his recovery could be slower than that of a younger, otherwise healthy patient,” Bharat said. Leo is 71.

The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s possible he could make the trip, doctors suggest, if the surgery is minimally invasive and there are no surprise findings. If the nodule is cancerous, doctors will determine whether he can be treated while traveling or the trip may need to be postponed.

title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire, but Zelenskyy says this is ‘news for me’
summary: President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict.
story: President Donald Trump claimed Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an “energy ceasefire” as part of the ongoing conflict. There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly said this “was news for me.”
Trump made a similar announcement a month ago, only for the two sides to continue their aerial attacks on each other’s energy facilities.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” He did not elaborate further on what the ceasefire might include.
Zelenskyy told Axios that he knew nothing about a ceasefire deal.

“But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire Ukraine will agree,” Zelenskyy said, according to Axios. “If President Trump negotiated it with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin — please tell us when the ceasefire begins — we are ready and we will accept it.”
NBC News has reached out to Zelenskyy’s office for further comment.

It follows a dramatic few days in which Trump agreed to a diesel deal with the Kremlin, demanded Kyiv halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced. The shift left Kyiv and its European allies reeling.

The U.S. agreed Friday to lift sanctions on Russian fuel in a deal that Trump said would see Russia “immediately” release 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and global marketplace,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.

title: Sen. Thom Tillis says he believes Trump’s fuel deal with Russia could be breaking the law
summary: Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia in order to allow Russia to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.
story: Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia to allow it to release diesel fuel to the global market may be breaking the law.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” Tillis said.

Trump announced in a Friday post on Truth Social that Russia would “immediately supply” hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the global marketplace, with more than 1 million additional tons soon on the way. The move drew sharp condemnation from Ukraine and critics of the Trump administration.

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, lawmakers took a series of steps to try to financially punish the Kremlin. In 2022, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to ban Russian oil imports, and Congress has not made changes to the law to reflect the president’s announcement.
Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether he believes the president is breaking the law with his Russia deal, Tillis said, “I believe that he may be.”
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor,” he added. “Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied.”
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the senator’s remarks.
Tillis referenced year-end congressional funding negotiations when asked what the Senate could do if Tillis believes Trump is breaking the law.

“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” he said.

Asked whether Trump’s deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin was putting American lives at risk, Tillis said, “It absolutely will,” pointing to Russian funding of mercenaries and the Kremlin’s relationship with Iran.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Tillis has just months remaining before his term expires. His retirement from the Senate created a high-profile battleground opening. Democrats are eyeing his seat as a prime target to flip as they seek control of the chamber.

Tillis has been highly critical of aspects of the Trump administration, including the performance of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Tillis, who voted for Hegseth’s confirmation, now says he regrets his vote.
Tillis on Sunday condemned the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 mass shooting in Fort Hood, Texas.
Tillis said that the livestream plans would radicalize people and be used by terrorist groups as a recruiting tool.

“The Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life,” he said.

“This is not who we are, and it’s another example of why Pete Hegseth, in all of his bravado, needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader, and we need strong leadership supporting President Trump right now,” he added.

title: Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off GOP election denial
summary: Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said his fellow Democrats need to “win by massive numbers” in the midterm elections so the result “is unquestionable.”
story: Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said his fellow Democrats need to “win by massive numbers” in the upcoming midterm elections so the result “is unquestionable.”
“Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” in an interview that aired Sunday.
Asked by NBC News on Saturday whether he would accept the results of the midterm elections no matter who wins, Trump said, “Of course I will. But we don’t want cheating.”

El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has also denied 2020 election results, El-Sayed told moderator Kristen Welker. “The guy I’m running against, he insinuates that he didn’t actually lose in 2020,” he said. “He talks about this mythical van that showed up in Detroit with a bunch of votes, as if he didn’t lose.”

Asked by Welker about whether he thinks Trump and Rogers would call his race into question if the results are close, El-Sayed said, “I am concerned that Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are not committed to the institution of our democracy.”

After Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election, Trump targeted Michigan with election fraud claims that were eventually shot down by a judge, who called them “nothing but speculation and conjecture.”

Michigan was also among a handful of states where Trump supporters in 2020 sought to submit a slate of so-called fake electors to the Electoral College to falsely declare that Trump won. Fifteen people were charged in the alleged scheme, but their cases were later dismissed.

Earlier this year, in a series of escalating inquiries about the state’s voter rolls, the Trump administration demanded that Wayne County, home to Detroit, give the federal government all of its ballots from the 2024 presidential election.

In the “Meet the Press interview,” which was taped on Friday, El-Sayed said he’s confident he can win over former Trump voters with his campaign’s economic focus. That includes making healthcare more accessible through “Medicare for All” and fighting corporate interests.

“Everywhere I go, I get somebody who comes up and says, ‘Look, I voted for Trump two, three times, and I’m voting for you.’ And I ask why. They say, ‘It’s because you really want me to have healthcare.’ I really want them to have healthcare. ‘It’s because you really are America first.’ I really am America first,” said El-Sayed, a former public health official.
He also hopes those economic messages resonate with Jewish voters who may otherwise be skeptical of him because of his criticism of Israel and his rhetoric.

“The things that unite us are so much bigger than the things that divide us, so much bigger. We believe in religious pluralism. We believe in the separation of church and state. We believe that more people deserve healthcare. We believe in reproductive rights. We believe that Donald Trump is an existential threat on our democracy. We believe that corporations shouldn’t be able to buy politicians,” he said.
For Subscribers

El-Sayed again expressed regret about his initial reaction to a March vehicle-ramming attack on a synagogue near Detroit. He condemned the attack at the time but added that “hurt people hurt people,” noting that some of the attacker’s family members had died days earlier in airstrikes in Lebanon.
For Subscribers

“If I step on somebody’s grief, of course I regret that. And I really wish I’d thought about how somebody would have felt hearing that and thought twice about making those comments,” El-Sayed told Welker.

“My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to my own kids,” he added. “And we need to be able to know that we can go to our schools, that we can go to our places of worship, and that nobody is going to attack.”
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supports pro-Israel candidates from both parties, targeted El-Sayed’s initial comments on the attack in mailers sent to voters this week.

A super PAC called “Together for Michigan” also began airing ads this week centered on the remarks. In one ad, a woman says her son was in the synagogue on the day of the attack, telling viewers that El-Sayed “gave an excuse to someone who wanted to murder children. I’m a lifelong Democrat, but this election, I’m voting for Mike Rogers.”

With the final push to the midterms underway, Welker asked El-Sayed about his plans to campaign with former President Barack Obama. In a 2012 HuffPost opinion piece, El-Sayed wrote that “Obama was not the right choice. He just wasn’t the wrong one. This leader has perpetrated war, violated our civil liberties, deported more people from our shores than any other president before him, and the list of his failures goes on.”
On Friday, El-Sayed said that time has changed his perspective on Obama.

“I think about eight years of President Obama’s leadership and you compare that to the 12 years we’ve lived since. You look back and say, ‘Man, that was a really capable leader, who led with a kind of belief in people and uncommon grace, even for people who disagreed with him,’” El-Sayed said.
He added that he considers Obama a “mentor” and that great mentors “let you grow up.”

title: To counteract a spooky economy, America prepares to spend on Halloween candy
summary: This Halloween, rising prices for groceries and gas are pushing many consumers to cut back. But they’re not giving up Halloween candy.
story: This Halloween, the fright isn’t just at the haunted house. Rising prices for everything from groceries to gas are driving many consumers to cut back.
“I’m walking to save a little bit of money,” said Lakisha Reardon, a legal assistant. “I’m bringing in my own lunch.”
Reardon said she has especially seen her electric bill spike this year. She said she is paying an extra $150 every month.
“I’m ready to invest in candles,” she said.
But one thing she won’t give up? Halloween candy.
Average prices for chewing gum and candy have soared 8.1% over the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Despite the higher prices, Americans are still buying treats.

“I remember being a little kid and being super excited when I would get Reese’s Cups,” said Abby Mynatt, a college student who lives in Knoxville, Tennessee. “I want to give that to some other children.”
Mynatt, 21, said she usually spends around $50 for Halloween candy. She is expecting to shell out a bit more money this year despite financial pressures.
“I certainly think there are a little more tense things with my budget right now,” she said. “But I still think that certain things, even just little pleasures, are still worth it.”
The price of nonchocolate candy items has averaged $3.31 this year, up 1.8% from last year, according to PwC. But Halloween chocolate prices have jumped 15.5%, to an average of $5.67 per package.
Industry experts attribute the rise in chocolate prices partly to a cocoa shock over the last couple years.

Extreme weather in key cocoa-producing countries like Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana sent global cocoa prices soaring — they quadrupled from January 2023 to January 2025, according to data from the International Monetary Fund.

“Because chocolate makers buy cocoa months, sometimes up to two years ahead, shoppers are paying for that spike now,” said Ali Furman, PwC’s consumer markets industry leader. “Cocoa prices have since fallen by about half, but lower costs take time to reach the shelf and won’t show up on shelves this Halloween season.”
The market research firm NIQ has seen a more muted increase in prices, with chocolate overall up 9.4% from a year ago but Halloween-specific chocolate just up 1.7%.
Analysts say tariffs this year aren’t helping, either. In July, the U.S. imposed tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 trade partners.

“Chocolate comes from elsewhere, so tariffs being added onto it have certainly increased costs that manufacturers are feeling as well,” said Chris Costagli, the leader of food and nonalcoholic beverage insights at NIQ.
Still, the National Retail Federation projects that Halloween spending will soar to $13.5 billion this season, with 96% of Halloween shoppers expecting to buy sweets.
For Subscribers
It’s part of a broader trend this year of consumers leaning into little luxuries like makeup and movie tickets as an antidote for economic gloom.
For Subscribers

A lot of that gloom stems from concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living. Consumer prices have jumped 3.4% over the last year in large part due to rising energy costs, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
With wages up just 3% over the same period, paychecks aren’t keeping up with prices.
It has led many people to forgo bigger purchases and cut back in small ways every day.
Leonard Smith is planning to buy Halloween candy this year, but says he may cut back.
“I don’t want to spend that much money because I need money for other things besides candy,” said Smith, 36, who lives in Delaware.
But he has a strategy to save: Smith buys candy after Halloween when many stores slash prices.

Ari Monahan, a nanny who describes herself as “like a Disney adult, but for Halloween,” said she may get candy that’s a little less expensive, but she still wants to treat the kids in her New York City neighborhood.
“I want to be the good house,” she said. “There’s not that many kids in my area, so I want to give them a little prize for coming.”
Monahan, 30, also buys little treats for herself. “Dark chocolate, a lot of coffees, anything pumpkin spice,” she said.

“If it makes me smile and I have a little money, I’ll pay for it because everything is so grim right now,” she added. “A pair of socks with dachshunds on it, I’m like, ‘You know what? I can do that. I could swing it today.’”
Monahan says rising prices are taking a big bite out of her paycheck, and she worries she might never be able to buy a house.

Home prices are near record highs, and mortgage rates have spiked over the course of the war with Iran — with the 30-year fixed rate topping 7.6% earlier this month, a nearly three-year high. It’s a double whammy that is putting a key pillar of the American dream further out of reach for many people.
And yet in an economy where the big things might seem far away, there are always little treats to get by.
“I’ve been in a real ‘buy yourself little treats’ mentality,” said Monahan. “I keep buying too much stuff for my dog. I guess I didn’t buy another dog. That’s saving, right?”

title: One month into the NFL season, referees are the biggest story
summary: Rare public suspensions, numerous flags and rescinded fines have made those who set and enforce the rules as much of a discussion topic as the NFL’s more visible stars.
story: When New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel cursed out an official last week for a defensive holding penalty he described as a “terrible ... effing call,” it was hardly the first time he’d complained to that level.
“I’ve said that 87 times since I’ve been a head coach,” Vrabel said. “It was nothing derogatory.”
It earned Vrabel an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty all the same and led him to call the official “a little sensitive.”

Tension between officials and those who must abide by their rules has existed since sports began and is so commonplace as to go mostly unremarked. But five weeks into the new NFL season, that’s no longer the case. Rare public suspensions, numerous flags and rescinded fines have made those who set and enforce the rules as much of a discussion topic as the league’s more visible stars.

Games have averaged 15 penalties, the third-highest leaguewide average through Week 4 since the 1970 merger, according to research by NBC Sports. The number of total fouls called per game, 16.86, is down from the 17.44 that were called at the same point of last season, according to a league spokesman. That still is higher than the number of fouls called through Week 4 in 2024 (15.52), 2023 (15.34) and 2022 (14.38).
Penalties are only one reason officials are in the spotlight.

The NFL this week took the rare public step of announcing suspensions of two officials after line judge Jeff Seeman was shown on camera cursing multiple times toward Arizona tight end Trey McBride, leading to a two-game suspension. Referee Adrian Hill also was suspended, for one game, for his contentious reaction to Minnesota’s Eric Wilson after accidental contact knocked Hill to the ground. The NFL said the instances reflected “unprofessional conduct,” while the union that represents NFL officials vowed to challenge the discipline, calling it “excessive and inconsistent with past precedent.”
Coaches including Minnesota’s Kevin O’Connell and Arizona’s Mike LaFleur complimented the work of Seeman and Hill.

“There’s a lot of verbal back-and-forth, or really one-way traffic, from the coaches, players to the officials, but we’ve always told the officials you cannot respond in kind,” former NFL referee Dean Blandino said this week.

Though the union disagreed with the level of punishment handed down, it did acknowledge that such verbal back-and-forth was not necessarily an outlier. In a statement, the referees’ union said it wanted to meet with the players’ union “to address on-field conduct and the growing levels of confrontation between players and officials.”
“It’s about time,” Super Bowl-winning former coach Bruce Arians said this week about the discipline. “You know, there’s finally some accountability in that department.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The NFL does not exempt officials from accountability. It just rarely publicizes it. Referees’ performances are judged using internal grades for which high performers are rewarded with high-profile postseason assignments, while consistently low scorers can lose their jobs.

A new and more visible accountability measure exists, as well. As part of a new, seven-year collective bargaining agreement between the league and its referees that was established in May, the NFL has created a “bench” of referees who can step in for in-game switches.

“They’re going to start working this weekend,” Blandino said. “So if you have an underperforming official on a crew, that official will sit down and you’ll have a bench official that will come in like that backup, that No. 2, that will come in and work for them.”

The NFL this week also walked back fines — ranging from $8,847 to $14,926 — it had issued multiple players for celebrations the league initially said showed them imitating chugging a beer, which it deemed an offensive demonstration. In one case, San Francisco’s Kyle Juszczyk said he was imitating drinking from a juice box, a play on his last name’s pronunciation and his “Juice” nickname.

“Even if it was beer, I don’t think that should be a problem with all the beer endorsements that we have in the NFL,” Juszczyk told reporters after the fine was issued. “We have everything. So even if it was beer, which it wasn’t, I still felt like it wasn’t an infraction.”

Confusion about what celebrations are allowed and which are not led the league and its players union this week to issue a joint statement clarifying the line that should not be crossed. Violations include gestures that are sexual or depict smoking, violence and using drugs, gang-related signs or weapons.

“Conversely, recent celebrations imitating drinking a beverage will not be considered violations or result in discipline,” the joint statement read. It added that “individual and team celebrations are part of the game.”
So, too, this season is the focus on the flags and the officials who throw them.

title: Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
summary: Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
story: Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will undergo surgery to remove an early-stage nodule on his lung.
The Vatican said the procedure was planned for this week.
“Recently, during some medical tests, doctors discovered a localized nodule in my lung,” the American pontiff, 71, said during his noon prayer at St. Peter’s Square.

“It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized,” Leo said from the window of the Apostolic Palace. “The doctors believe it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”
The pontiff said that surgery had already been scheduled “for the coming days,” and thanked onlookers for their support.
“I entrust myself to your prayers,” he said.
The news drew applause from the thousands gathered in the square, before he wished the crowd a “happy Sunday.”
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that “the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week.”
Leo announced the surgery at the end of his regular address, in which he appealed for an end to the war in Ukraine and the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea.
“The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, including weekly games of tennis.
The pontiff has a major trip scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November. It’s unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wished Leo well.
“I would like to express to the Holy Father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days,” she said in a statement.
“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it (today) ...are reassuring,” Meloni added.
Born Robert Francis Prevost, he became the first American pope when he was appointed in 2025.
Originally from the South Side of Chicago, he spent much of his career ministering in Peru and leading the Vatican’s powerful office of bishops.

Leo’s father, Louis Prevost, served in the Navy during World War II and worked as a superintendent of schools in the south suburbs of Chicago. His mother, Mildred Martinez Prevost, was a librarian with a master’s degree in education and two sisters who were nuns.
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died of a stroke last April at age 88 after a long hospitalization following a number of health issues.

title: Saudi airport struck again a day after deadly attack
summary: An unidentified projectile struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport Sunday, injuring people a day after a deadly missile attack at the same site raised questions about whether the United States would join another conflict in the region.
story: An unidentified projectile struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport Sunday, injuring people a day after a deadly missile attack at the same site raised questions about whether the United States would join another conflict in the region.

Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation confirmed injuries in the new attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh but did not provide a count. It said authorities were assessing damage and checking the safety of airport facilities.

The Saudi-led coalition said the projectile struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, causing a fire that authorities were working to control. It also reported intercepting and destroying a cruise missile near the airport.

Saturday’s strike killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The victims included one American as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said Sunday that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died. The embassy said it was in contact with the family and would help repatriate the remains.
Some of the wounded were in critical condition, authorities said, while airport operations remained suspended Sunday.
President Donald Trump said afterward that the U.S. was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” Trump told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Saturday’s strike drew widespread condemnation and intensified pressure on the kingdom and its allies to respond to the Houthi rebels. The attack was the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade and marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen-based Houthis’ campaign against the leading oil exporter, which has already rattled the global economy.

Saudi Arabia’s government and its allies blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s strike. The group did not immediately claim responsibility for the latest attack, although it renewed a warning to stay away from Saudi airports.
Washington also blamed the Houthis for Saturday’s assault, the latest of several on the busy facility in the past week. Three people were killed there in an attack on Thursday.

The attack has drawn fresh scrutiny of Washington’s response to the widening conflict, in which the Houthis have hit Saudi energy infrastructure and seized territory that gives them leverage over shipping in the Red Sea.
Trump responds to potential U.S. involvement after Saudi attack
The U.S. launched a three-month bombing campaign against the Houthis last year to stop them from targeting shipping through the critical waterway, an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudis will be looking to allies like Pakistan, Turkey, Syria, Egypt and the U.S. for help, said Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
“But I doubt very much whether there is an answer or even a military solution to the Yemeni conflict,” he told NBC News.

“The Houthis are determined to fight to the end,” Gerges said. “I suspect that the reason why the U.S. has been reluctant is not only because of the Iran war, but also because the U.S tried for several months to force the Houthis to stand down, and they did not succeed.”

At the same time, the Houthis are becoming “more nimble, more resourceful, more deadly by the day, and I think what we have seen in the past few weeks is that the targeting system of the Houthis has become much more effective,” he said.

Egypt said Sunday that it “stands firmly” with Saudi Arabia, expressing “strong condemnation” for the attacks.” Qatar called the missile strike “a grave violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security.”
Germany and Canada also condemned the attacks, with Prime Minister Mark Carney describing them as “abhorrent.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres blamed the Houthis, calling the attack “a violation of international law.” The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis called the attack a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowed a strong response.
Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport kill 3 Saudi nationals

The renewed fighting has developed alongside the broader war involving Iran, with the Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi territory as Saudi-backed forces battle the group inside Yemen. The latest violence follows the collapse of a truce in July and a renewed Saudi-backed offensive against Houthi positions.

The Houthis have expanded their operations along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb strait, a critical shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Disruption there threatens international trade and energy shipments, raising fuel prices and adding another source of instability to global markets.

Trump has focused intensely on energy prices ahead of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with the Kremlin that stunned Ukraine. But he has so far resisted deeper involvement in the Middle East.
After sweeping gains by Houthi forces last month, Trump said the group had contacted the U.S. to stress that they “don’t want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman urged Trump in September to take military action against the Houthis, a person familiar with the matter told NBC News.
“There is a whole lot that America can deliver,” said Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, a retired professor of political science from the United Arab Emirates.

“It doesn’t have to be in the form of going all out against the Houthis, but American sharing of intelligence, America providing the best of defense systems against Houthis’ drones and missiles is needed, and I think if that is delivered, Saudi Arabia and the rest can defend themselves,” he said.

Abdulla also called on Turkey and Pakistan to come to Saudi Arabia’s defense. The three nations signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca in August, a pact of Sunni Muslim U.S. allies alarmed at growing regional conflict.
“Now it’s the time to activate what this alliance treaty involves,” added Abdulla. “That an attack on one is an attack against all.”

title: Justice Department investigating major TV networks over suspending pool coverage of Trump
summary: The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.
story: WASHINGTON — The Justice Department said it is investigating five major TV broadcast networks for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, a department spokesperson said.

The investigation into the networks that make up the White House TV press pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — is underway, and the department sent out “civil investigative demands” on Friday, according to a Justice Department official.

“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” department spokeswoman Emily Covington said Saturday.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording the president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The network performing pool duty then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets.
The New York Times first reported the investigation.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ABC News said it has not received any notification from the Justice Department but expects to. Representatives for NBC, CBS and CNN declined to comment. Fox did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The investigation appears to be the latest move from the White House in its escalating feud against the press corps.

Last month, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, citing what he said was “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The other networks in the TV pool briefly declined to participate in pool duties after CNN was removed from its spot in the rotation.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to block the ban, claiming it was a violation of the First Amendment. They were reinstated about a week later after a judge ruled that the administration had to temporarily restore their access for 14 days. A federal judge this week extended the order to Tuesday.

The five major networks released a joint statement at the time, saying: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

The pool system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which include outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.

During the time the outlets declined to provide pool coverage, individual TV networks, including NBC News, continued to provide coverage of White House events that were open to the press, outside of the pool.

Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said in a statement that the First Amendment protects the decisions news organizations make about coverage and called the investigation “another and even more brazen attempt to try to intimidate journalists.”
Kelly O’Donnell reported from Washington, and Marlene Lenthang from Los Angeles.

title: Talking Shop with Angie Katsanevas from ‘The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’
summary: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’ star Angie Katsanevas shares her favorite Kérastase hair care and travel must-haves from Skims, SkinCeuticals and more.
story: Talking Shop is our series where we talk to interesting people about their most interesting buys.

She may have technically started as a “friend of,” but Angie Katsanevas has really always been a snowflake-holding member of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.” She never fails to make viewers laugh with her iconic one-liners and props (who could forget the scroll from season five), but she balances her humor with sincerity as she shares her Greek-American heritage, as well as her role as a caring friend, supportive mom and serious business woman. And this season, which is currently airing on Bravo every Wednesday, Katsanevas says she’s excited for viewers to get to know her even better.

“We never know what they’re going to show, but there’s a lot of things I get to share in my personal story this season,” says Katsanevas. Standout moments include spending time with her daughter, Elektra, and her dad, who’s about to turn 90, as well as going behind the scenes of her business, the Lunatic Fringe Salon franchise. Katsanevas, who’s been a hairdresser for decades, even went to Washington D.C. earlier this year to testify before Congress on behalf of small businesses, becoming the first Housewife to do so.
I recently caught up with Katsanevas, who shared some of her all-time favorite products, including a few that you’ll recognize from memorable moments on the show.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
Kérastase Chronologiste Overnight Youth Serum

One thing about Katsanevas is that her hair is always perfectly shiny, smooth and frizz-free — and she’s more than happy to tell you her secret to getting it that way. “I’m Kérastase girl,” she says, which all RHOSLC fans know — after all, the brand is mentioned in some of the show’s most famous scenes. “I love the products because they give you hold, softness and volume, but your hair can still move. I think we’ve gotten away from stiff hair — high body count hair, if you will,” says Katsanevas, referencing one of her most viral one-liners. “I’ve tried a million other things, and I’ve never been able to replace Kérastase to give you that timeless, beautiful blowout.”

Katsanevas’ salon, Lunatic Fringe, has carried Kérastase products and offered its professional treatments for about 30 years. She also personally works with the brand, and especially loves its Chronologiste line. “It’s a luxury hair care line that’s anti-aging,” she says. “It helps fight signs of aging like dryness, dullness and lack of volume or thickness, which a lot of women battle as their hair changes. I’m going to be 53, and to have these products is pretty incredible.” Her top pick is the Chronologiste Overnight Youth Serum, which she puts in her hair before bed to work while she sleeps, and her other must-have is Kérastase’s Mousse Bouffante.
Skims Sleep Long-Sleeve Button Up Set

Whether she’s traveling with family or her Housewives castmates, Katsanevas says packing her favorite things is essential to sleeping and resting well. Something that goes into her suitcase first is Skims pajamas, which you’ve seen her wear numerous times on the show. “I’m obsessed with them,” she says. “My daughter Elektra got me into them — she said, ‘Mom, they feel like a hug,’ and they do. They have the perfect weight to them, and now I can’t sleep without my Skims jammies.”
Slip Silk Pillowcase

“When I’m going on ‘Watch What Happens Live,’ I don’t want a crease in my face for having slept wrong and have my wrinkles on display, so I take my Slip Silk Pillowcase with me everywhere I go,” says Katsanevas. “It makes a huge difference for my hair and skin.” The machine-washable pillowcase is made from 100 percent pure mulberry silk, and it has a zipper closure to help it stay on your pillow as you move through the night.
SkinCeuticals C E Ferulic Serum

“I used to not travel with all my skin care because I didn’t want to pack everything, but I have to have certain products, and this is one of them,” says Katsanevas about SkinCeuticals’ vitamin C serum. She applies it every morning, and its main active ingredient, 15 percent L-ascorbic acid, helps correct the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, discoloration, loss of firmness and brightness, according to the brand. SkinCeuticals also says the serum is effective for at least 72 hours once it absorbs into your skin.
Peter Thomas Roth Water Drench Hyaluronic Cloud Hydra-Gel Eye Patches

These under eye patches are another one of Katsanevas’ skin care essentials. She uses them pre-glam to hydrate, de-puff and smooth out her skin, or she puts them on after taking off her makeup to reset her skin and feel refreshed before bed.
The patches are made with ingredients like hyaluronic acid, ceramides, collagen and caffeine, and after wearing them for about 15 minutes you remove them and pat the remaining serum into the skin.
Hermés Cheval d’Orient Soy Dish

Hosting is in Katsanevas’ blood. She has distinct memories of her parents, grandparents and aunts using their finest china whenever the family got together, and putting that kind of effort into hosting is something she’s always prioritized.

“When people come into my home, I treat them like family,” says Katsanevas. “I love beautiful dishes, and tea cups, and servingware and having flowers out  — I think it really adds to the experience. I know I go over the top, even if it’s just a little coffee date — like this season, when the women were coming over in the first episode, I went out and bought some really beautiful new appetizer plates. We’ve all gotten so busy, so people put out paper plates and cups, but the little details make it feel more beautiful. It’s fun when you have friends that notice it, like Mary [Cosby], and I want to teach Elektra to set the table, slow down and realize that it’s all part of the experience.”

Katsanevas says she plans to buy her daughter, an avid equestrian, Hermes dishes from the Cheval d’Orient line to start her collection of fine china. “You’re passing down something beautiful, and you’re also passing down a memory for generations,” she says.
Why trust NBC Selected?

I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who writes our Talking Shop series, interviewing people like Paris Hilton, Maureen Kelly, Lindsay Hubbard and Chase Crawford. To write this article, I talked to “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” star Angie Katsanevas about season seven of the show and her favorite products.
Catch up on NBC Selected’s in-depth coverage of tech and tools, wellness and more, and follow us on Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok to stay up to date.

title: To counteract a spooky economy, America prepares to spend on Halloween candy
summary: This Halloween, rising prices for groceries and gas are pushing many consumers to cut back. But they’re not giving up Halloween candy.
story: This Halloween, the fright isn’t just at the haunted house. Rising prices for everything from groceries to gas are driving many consumers to cut back.
“I’m walking to save a little bit of money,” said Lakisha Reardon, a legal assistant. “I’m bringing in my own lunch.”
Reardon said she has especially seen her electric bill spike this year. She said she is paying an extra $150 every month.
“I’m ready to invest in candles,” she said.
But one thing she won’t give up? Halloween candy.
Average prices for chewing gum and candy have soared 8.1% over the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Despite the higher prices, Americans are still buying treats.

“I remember being a little kid and being super excited when I would get Reese’s Cups,” said Abby Mynatt, a college student who lives in Knoxville, Tennessee. “I want to give that to some other children.”
Mynatt, 21, said she usually spends around $50 for Halloween candy. She is expecting to shell out a bit more money this year despite financial pressures.
“I certainly think there are a little more tense things with my budget right now,” she said. “But I still think that certain things, even just little pleasures, are still worth it.”
The price of nonchocolate candy items has averaged $3.31 this year, up 1.8% from last year, according to PwC. But Halloween chocolate prices have jumped 15.5%, to an average of $5.67 per package.
Industry experts attribute the rise in chocolate prices partly to a cocoa shock over the last couple years.

Extreme weather in key cocoa-producing countries like Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana sent global cocoa prices soaring — they quadrupled from January 2023 to January 2025, according to data from the International Monetary Fund.

“Because chocolate makers buy cocoa months, sometimes up to two years ahead, shoppers are paying for that spike now,” said Ali Furman, PwC’s consumer markets industry leader. “Cocoa prices have since fallen by about half, but lower costs take time to reach the shelf and won’t show up on shelves this Halloween season.”
The market research firm NIQ has seen a more muted increase in prices, with chocolate overall up 9.4% from a year ago but Halloween-specific chocolate just up 1.7%.
Analysts say tariffs this year aren’t helping, either. In July, the U.S. imposed tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 trade partners.

“Chocolate comes from elsewhere, so tariffs being added onto it have certainly increased costs that manufacturers are feeling as well,” said Chris Costagli, the leader of food and nonalcoholic beverage insights at NIQ.
Still, the National Retail Federation projects that Halloween spending will soar to $13.5 billion this season, with 96% of Halloween shoppers expecting to buy sweets.
For Subscribers
It’s part of a broader trend this year of consumers leaning into little luxuries like makeup and movie tickets as an antidote for economic gloom.
For Subscribers

A lot of that gloom stems from concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living. Consumer prices have jumped 3.4% over the last year in large part due to rising energy costs, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
With wages up just 3% over the same period, paychecks aren’t keeping up with prices.
It has led many people to forgo bigger purchases and cut back in small ways every day.
Leonard Smith is planning to buy Halloween candy this year, but says he may cut back.
“I don’t want to spend that much money because I need money for other things besides candy,” said Smith, 36, who lives in Delaware.
But he has a strategy to save: Smith buys candy after Halloween when many stores slash prices.

Ari Monahan, a nanny who describes herself as “like a Disney adult, but for Halloween,” said she may get candy that’s a little less expensive, but she still wants to treat the kids in her New York City neighborhood.
“I want to be the good house,” she said. “There’s not that many kids in my area, so I want to give them a little prize for coming.”
Monahan, 30, also buys little treats for herself. “Dark chocolate, a lot of coffees, anything pumpkin spice,” she said.

“If it makes me smile and I have a little money, I’ll pay for it because everything is so grim right now,” she added. “A pair of socks with dachshunds on it, I’m like, ‘You know what? I can do that. I could swing it today.’”
Monahan says rising prices are taking a big bite out of her paycheck, and she worries she might never be able to buy a house.

Home prices are near record highs, and mortgage rates have spiked over the course of the war with Iran — with the 30-year fixed rate topping 7.6% earlier this month, a nearly three-year high. It’s a double whammy that is putting a key pillar of the American dream further out of reach for many people.
And yet in an economy where the big things might seem far away, there are always little treats to get by.
“I’ve been in a real ‘buy yourself little treats’ mentality,” said Monahan. “I keep buying too much stuff for my dog. I guess I didn’t buy another dog. That’s saving, right?”

title: Ben Affleck Reveals Hilarious Reason Why Matt Damon Passed Up Lead Role in ‘Animals’
summary: Ben Affleck reveals why his best friend, Matt Damon, couldn’t take on the leading role in his new Netflix thriller “Animals” as he had once hoped.
story: Ben Affleck reveals why his best friend, Matt Damon, couldn’t take on the leading role in his new Netflix thriller “Animals” as he had once hoped.

Affleck, who directed and starred in the new movie joined the Oct. 11 episode of Sunday Sitdown to chat about the film. And he revealed that Damon, initially his top pick to star in flick, had some other plans instead.
“I’m sure you’re aware, Ben, you were not the director’s first choice to star in this movie,” host Willie Geist joked.
Affleck confirmed the detail, explaining that Damon got another professional opportunity.

“Matt then ended up getting offered this little, kinda s----- little movie, ‘The Odyssey’ that bombed. And he was very embarrassed by it, of course.” Affleck said, laughing. “It just didn’t work at the box office, or with the critics, which happens sometimes.”
The “Animals” star went on to praise his friend, he played titular character Odysseus.
“He was really as happy as I’ve ever seen him the day that he got that job,” Affleck told Willie of Damon.
Damon and Affleck have been well-known besties, going through their first massive Hollywood moment together as they won the best screenplay Oscar in 1998 for “Good Will Hunting.”
“The whole idea of even being there was absurd,” Affleck recalled to Willie of attending the Oscars. “The year before, we’d watched the show from an apartment in Somerville, Massachusetts.”
The two have since acted in multiple films together including “The Last Duel” in 2021 and “Air” in 2023.

Additionally, Affleck has launched multiple production companies with Damon including Artists Equity, founded in November 2022. The company is behind a number of titles including “Air” and new film “Animals.”

The crime thriller, released Oct. 9, follows a high-profile Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped, forcing the hopeful and his wife, played by Kerry Washington, into coming up with the $7 million ransom amid a financially stressful time in his campaign.
“I make movies mindful of the audience. But also, I did some things I really wanted to do in this that I think were really interesting,” the actor and director said of the new film.
Affleck beamed over his newest project, “I love this movie, ‘Animals.’ I really want people to see it.”

title: Mike Ditka’s Perfectly Unhinged Version of ‘Take Me Out To The Ballgame’ Resurfaces After Death
summary: A resurfaced video of Chicago Bears icon Mike Ditka singing during the seventh inning stretch at a baseball game is giving many fans something to smile about as they grieve the football giant’s death.
story: A resurfaced video of Chicago Bears icon Mike Ditka singing during the seventh inning stretch at a baseball game is giving many fans something to smile about as they grieve the football giant’s death.
The video features Ditka singing the classic “Take Me Out To The Ballgame” during a July 1998 match at Chicago’s Wrigley Field. And he definitely puts his own twist on the song.

In the clip, shared by MLB, Ditka raucously belts out the words, losing his voice several times throughout the song. Adding to his undeniable aura, Ditka also speeds up, leading the organist to attempt to match his pace.
It’s controlled chaos — just like the beloved football icon himself.
Ditka’s family announced his death Oct. 9. He was 86.

The Bears icon, who led the team to its only Super Bowl victory in  1986, was known for his big personality as much as he was for his gridiron prowess. And that charisma certainly shined during that 1998 Chicago Cubs game against the Pittsburgh Pirates.

That wasn’t even Ditka’s only famous rendition of the ballpark song. During a 2005 game at Wrigley Field between the Cubs and the Philadelphia Phillies, Ditka was joined by comedian Will Ferrell to lead the stadium in the song. The pair, who starred in comedy “Kicking & Screaming,” don’t exactly sing in-sync.

Ditka, who was inducted into the pro football Hall of Fame in 1988, has long been a source of comedy fodder. He even became the focus of a recurring sketch on “Saturday Night Live” in which a group of superfans, who look just like Ditka himself, hail the legendary coach as something of a god.

title: Alexander Skarsgard’s See-Through Dress Shoes Are Causing Chaos Across The Internet
summary: Actor Alexander Skarsgard showed up in a pair of see-through shoes to the annual BFI London Film Festival for an Oct. 8 screening of his upcoming romantic fantasy movie “Wicker.”
story: To call this a bold fashion choice would be an understatement.

Actor Alexander Skarsgard showed up to the annual BFI London Film Festival for an Oct. 8 screening of his upcoming romantic fantasy movie “Wicker.” But his look quickly became a focus of the event as he rocked a pair of see-through oxford shoes on the red carpet.
The shoes unsurprisingly elicited a range of responses from disgust to extreme lust.
Skarsgard’s transparent black shoes, which featured vinyl laces, were paired with a gold, metallic suit.
The oxfords, from fashion house Saint Laurent’s spring 2027 collection, made waves earlier this year when they debuted on the runway at  men’s Paris fashion week in June.

Corrado De Biase, the brand’s freelance design director of shoes, explained that the look is called “O. Fan,” after adult online platform OnlyFans. The shoes, he told Women’s Wear Daily, are a celebration of sexuality in the gay community.

“Because Monsieur Saint Laurent himself was really linked to those young community people when he was young,” De Biase told the outlet. “So it’s normal that a brand like us looks at that kind of thing. It’s been part of the house from the beginning.”
Saint Laurent creative director Anthony Vaccarello had a snarkier explanation for the footwear.
“I asked myself: ‘Why torture women with plastic shoes, but not men?’” Vaccarello said, according to WWD.
People across the internet had their own interpretations of the look. Some couldn’t help but wonder how Skarsgard was faring in the no-doubt sweaty shoes.
Others were just thirsting over the fashion choice.
“Oo our steak is too juicy, our lobster is too buttery, Alexander Skarsgaard is showing too much foot,” one commenter wrote on Instagram.

Well, 2026 appears to be the year of the gutsy red carpet footwear. Margaret Qualley sported a pair of Chanel’s “shoeless shoes” to the world premiere of “The Dog Stars” in August. The shoes were essentially black heels that were strapped to Qualley’s feet with two sets of laces and no soles.
While some deemed the shoes as chic, others joked that the barely-there footwear was a sign of “shrinkflation.”

title: Ben Affleck Admits He Trash Talks Kids Online While Playing ‘Fortnite’
summary: Ben Affleck recently revealed on the “New Heights” podcast that he sometimes gets into squabbles with kids on the internet while playing popular multiplayer open-world survival game “Fortnight.”
story: Gamer rage gets to everyone — even celebs.
Ben Affleck recently revealed on the “New Heights” podcast that he sometimes trash talks kids on the internet while playing popular multiplayer open-world survival game “Fortnight.”
Affleck, it appears, has a tough time taking the heat.

“Twelve-year-olds just f--- you up,” Affleck lamented to hosts Travis Kelce and Jason Kelce on the Oct. 7 podcast episode. “I get killed right away and they taunt you and s--- like ‘You suck! F--- you!’”
Affleck acknowledged that he ends up “getting in arguments” with the kids in the game’s chat.
“F--- you! I don’t suck,” he says in response to the taunting, Affleck told the podcast hosts. “I’m a grown man.”

Affleck, who’s currently promoting crime-thriller film “Animals,” joined the podcast to discuss the project. He explained that the costumes in the film are inspired by some of the outfits, referred to as skins, in “Fortnite.” The video game famously features different skins that can be upgraded through milestones, challenges and more.
As Affleck points out in the podcast, the game has also dropped exclusive and limited edition skins that have become some of the most coveted aspects of the game.
“My son and he’s like ‘For Christmas, can you get me these real skins for Fortnite?’ But they’re 300 bucks,” Affleck tells the podcast of the virtual costumes.
Affleck has long been an avid gamer. On the podcast, he explained that in addition to first-person shooter games, he’s a fan of sports games like football game “Madden” and basketball game “NBA 2K.”

The actor has also been open about his love for “Valorant,” a first-person tactical hero shooter video game. He’s been spotted at major tournaments and even joined a watch party livestream last year with esports team Sentinels.

title: ‘Pretty Little Liars’ Actor Says He Was Held At Gunpoint and Knifepoint in Mugging Attack
summary: Actor Keegan Allen, best known for his role in teen drama series “Pretty Little Liars,” alleges in an Oct. 9 video that he was violently mugged in West Hollywood by two masked men.
story: Actor Keegan Allen, best known for his role in teen drama series “Pretty Little Liars,” alleges in an Oct. 9 video that he was violently mugged in West Hollywood by two masked men.

In the video that was posted to his Instagram account, Allen, who appears to be bleeding from his head, says that he was robbed outside of Laurel Supply, an upscale grocery store in the Los Angeles neighborhood.

“These two dudes hit me in the head and pointed a gun at me with a knife, and then took off,” a visibly bloody Allen, catching his breath, says in the graphic video. He adds that the attackers took his watch.
Responding to comments under his video, the 37-year-old told fans that he went to the hospital following the incident and was “def concussed.”

The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department shared a statement in response to an NBC News request for comment on the incident. The department said that the LAPD’s Major Crimes Bureau is investigating the reported Oct. 8 armed robbery.
In the Instagram video, Allen shared footage of the alleged attack, which shows two men pointing a gun at a victim. One of the men bashes the victim over the head.
“Robbed at gunpoint and knifepoint by two young men that threatened to KILL me over my watch and would have! God said no tonight. My life for a watch,” he wrote in the caption of his post.
Allen wrote in response to a comment that one of the attackers also demanded a bracelet the actor was wearing, which led to the beating.
“I was trying to tell him it’s not easy to take off and said ‘you can take it off’ and he pistol whipped me,” Allen wrote.

The sheriff’s department said in the statement that deputies responded to the incident around 9:05 p.m. and spoke to a victim who reported being approached by two male suspects in black clothing. The victim told deputies that one suspect pointed a handgun at him while the other brandished a knife.
Actor Keegan Allen describes violent mugging incident

“During the incident, one of the suspects struck the victim in the face with the handgun, causing a laceration to his forehead,” the statement said. “The suspects took the victim’s watch and fled the location in an unknown vehicle.”
Personnel from the Los Angeles County Fire Department responded to the scene and medically evaluated the victim, who was not transported to the hospital, the statement said.
In his post, Allen called out Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass and California governor Gavin Newsom.
“Let’s hope all these flock cameras that @karenbassla @gavinnewsom and everyone thinks will stop crime can find these very dangerous criminals,” Allen wrote on Instagram.

In a statement sent to NBC News, Bass called the incident “egregious.” She also pointed out that West Hollywood is an independent city and that the LA County Sheriff’s Department is leading the investigation. It is technically not part of the city of Los Angeles.
“No one should have to experience something like this,” Bass said.

According to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, serious crimes in the area have decreased nearly 10% from January through August. Additionally, robberies have been on the decline. Statistics show that through August, there were 49 reported robberies. That’s a 21% decrease from the 62 incidents during the same period in 2025.
In response to recent October incidents, a department spokesperson said that the agency is increasing the number of deputies conducting patrols throughout the city.
“While these declines are encouraging, they do not diminish the seriousness of recent robberies or the fear felt by our community,” a spokesperson for the department said.

title: There’s a New Britney Spears Song. Listen to ‘She’ll Never Be Me’
summary: Britney Spears fans got an unexpected surprise in the form of a previously unreleased song from the pop icon.
story: Britney Spears fans got an unexpected surprise in the form of a previously unreleased song from the pop icon.
On Oct. 9, Spears and her team dropped the song “She’ll Never Be Me,” which was recorded for her 2001 self-titled third album “Britney.”
The song comes weeks before the album celebrates its 25th anniversary with a special edition re-release, “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition),” that includes songs from the vault.
“She’ll Never Be Me” is a quintessential Britney Spears track with its bubblegum pop, early aughts sound, girl power lyrics and the singer’s signature girlish and gritty vocals.
The 3-minute track talks about a former lover who is now with someone that looks just like her.

“You know I’m one of a kind/Boy, what’s this I see/Your girl, she looks just like me/Blond hair and dressed to a T,” she begins. “You tell me how can this be/Does she know I was the one/Who used to turn you on/But you don’t want to talk about it.”
According to the song’s YouTube description, Spears is credited as the lyricist, associated performer and composer.
Her ex Justin Timberlake is also featured as a lyricist and composer, along with Bradley Daymond and Alex Greggs. Riprock ‘n’ Alex G is a producer.

“She’ll Never Be Me” is one of five new songs included in the “Britney” re-release, including “Am I a Sinner,” “When I Say So,” “My Big Secret” and “Right Now (Taste The Victory)” from her 2002 Pepsi commercial.
Fans will get to hear the songs when “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition)” is released on Nov. 6.
The last time Spears shared a new song was 2023’s “Mind Your Business” with Will.i.am. In 2020, she also dropped a never-before-heard collaboration with the Backstreet Boys titled “Matches.”
The song was featured in a deluxe edition of her 2016 album “Glory.”

title: Crystal Harris Posts Message She Sent Jessica Biel With Plea to ‘Reconsider’ Playing Hugh Hefner’s Wife in Movie
summary: Hugh Hefner’s widow, Crystal Harris, is asking Jessica Biel not to portray a fictional version of the Playboy founder’s wife in the upcoming movie “Playmates.”
story: Hugh Hefner’s widow, Crystal Harris, is asking Jessica Biel not to portray a fictional version of the Playboy founder’s wife in the upcoming movie “Playmates.”

Harris, who was married to Hefner from 2012 until his death in 2017, posted a screenshot of a text on Instagram on Oct. 8 that she sent Biel, urging her to pass up the role of Hefner’s fictional wife.
“Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner’s ‘wife’ if this film intends to romanticize him or the Playboy world,” Harris wrote in a message to Biel, according to the screenshot she shared on Instagram.

“I was actually his wife, and I experienced sexual, emotional, financial and physical abuse in that relationship. Many other women have come forward with allegations of rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation as well.

“There are also deeply troubling concerns involving minors. I hope everyone involved in this film takes the time to listen to the women who lived it before helping Hollywood turn it back into nostalgia.”
TODAY.com has reached out to Biel for comment about Harris’ post, as well as Harris for any further comment about what she wrote. Neither responded.
TODAY.com also reached out toHefner’s estate for comment about Harris’ allegations of experiencing “rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation,” but did not hear back.
The film is being made by Searchlight Pictures, which not did reply to TODAY.com’s request for comment about Harris’ post or Biel’s casting in the movie.

Variety reported Oct. 6 that Biel has joined the cast of “Playmates,” a coming-of-age story about a 13-year-old girl who befriends a woman competing with other hopefuls to become Playmate of the Month. Bill Pullman, Lily-Rose Depp and Indiana Elle are also attached to star in it.
Biel is slated to play Hefner’s wife in the movie. According to Variety, the character is fictional and not based on a real person.
Hefner was married two other times, to Kimberley Conrad from 1989 to 2010 and Millie Williams from 1949 to 1959.
Harris followed up her post with another one, in which she showed appreciation for the “overwhelming response” she received.
“So many women are speaking up, sharing their experiences, and expressing that they’ve simply had enough,” she wrote.

“Victim blaming is still far too common, especially when it comes to narcissistic and emotional abuse. I know that not everyone has experienced these dynamics firsthand, and I’m genuinely glad for those who haven’t. But I also hope we can listen to and support the women who have, even when their experiences are difficult to understand.”

Harris also said she wants “to support women” and express her hope that the movie is “not something that will glorify Hugh Hefner. With women in the leading roles, my hope is that the film ultimately delivers a message of empowerment: that women can find fulfillment, independence, and a sense of self beyond Playboy.”
In 2024, Harris penned a memoir, “Only Say Good Things: Surviving ‘Playboy’ and Finding Myself,” in which she wrote that living in the famed Playboy Mansion was like living in a prison.

“I always had to be home by six o’clock. If I wasn’t, it was a problem. He would be upset. He would be yelling my name through the house,” she says of Hugh Hefner, writing that she felt like Rapunzel locked in a tower.
“I didn’t know then that I could rescue myself. I didn’t always know I needed to be rescued, but I knew I was trapped,” she added.
Harris also said Hefner was a “narcissist” and had a need to control the women who lived in the mansion.
“It’s like he wanted us to beg him for something, so he could feel even more powerful and probably have us feel small,” she told TODAY.com in 2024.
“It was weird and it was hard. Looking back, he did use me and manipulate me for his own gain in every way,” she continued.
In August, Harris said Hefner was “very abusive” and that she was “brainwashed” when she appeared on the “No One Asked Her” podcast.

“So I just thought I was the crazy one because all of the media put Hef on such a pedestal that I’m like, ‘OK, if they all see him as this larger-than-life amazing human, there must be something wrong with me,” she said.
Hefner has been accused of sexual misconduct before, with multiple allegations leveled against him in the 2022 A&E series “Secrets of Playboy,” released five years after he died in 2017.

“This series contains allegations of wrongdoing over decades by Hugh Hefner and others associated with him,” read a statement at the end of each episode. “The vast majority of allegations have not been the subject of criminal investigations or charges, and they do not constitute proof of guilt.”

title: How Realistic Is ‘War’? A Divorce Lawyer Says this 1 Move Would Get Characters Disbarred
summary: A UK divorce lawyer reacts to the HBO drama “War” including the mole and serving papers on the red carpet.
story: “Take It From Me” is a TODAY.com series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this story, a U.K. divorce lawyer weighs in on “War.”

HBO’s new legal drama “War” gives viewers an unflinching look behind the scenes of a nasty, high-powered divorce. The series focuses on the lengths divorce lawyers from rival law firms in London will go to score a profitable win for their clients.

The depiction of ruthless attorneys scheming to gain the upper hand in a pending divorce “heavily dramatized for viewing public consumption,” and not necessarily realistic, said Daniel Sugaré, the head of family law department at Sugaré & Co. Solicitors in the U.K.

Set in London, “War” tells the story of the shattering end of the decade-long marriage between tech billionaire Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and his Hollywood star wife, Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), resulting in divorce.
Morgan and Carla hire lawyers from rival London law firms, Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne, respectively, to take each other down in court.
Here’s what a real divorce lawyer thinks of the show’s pilot.
Hiring a Lawyer As a Mole? That’s a Big No-No
One of lawyers’ most egregious antics would cause them to lose their law licenses in real life, Sugaré said.
Specifically, Cathcarts & Sons’s move to send struggling young lawyer Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) to Taylor & Byrne to act as a mole for their case.
“(Johnny) would be struck off immediately by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA),” Sugaré said of the mole.
“You’ve got a duty to your clients to act confidentially, act in their best interests, and by sharing information like in that manner, that they would be bound for disciplinary procedures,” he added.
The higher-ups at Cathcarts & Sons who orchestrated the scheme “would also face significant legal consequences from the SRA and potentially criminal proceedings,” he said.
The bad behavior of the lawyers on the show veers far from what real-life attorneys aim to do: help clients remain calm and focused so they can come to an agreement.
“In certain cases, you have to act in an aggressive way to protect your client’s interest,” said Sugaré. “But in the show, it seems like they’re doing that more than what is necessary.”
Carla’s Cheating Scheme

The show starts with Morgan sleeping with a young woman named Flora (Rose Williams). Turns out the moment has been orchestrated by Carla. She wants to prove that Morgan is unfaithful, and in doing so, exploit the prenuptial’s infidelity clause.
But will Carla’s scheme actually work? Not so fast, Sugaré said.
“An affair is not ordinarily a legal escape route from a prenuptial agreement,” Sugaré said.
Sugaré said infidelity clauses are “unusual” in England, as prenups generally deal with financial agreements rather than penalties for cheating.

“Even if this agreement contains an infidelity clause, Carla could not assume that the court would enforce it. While these cases are fact specific, proof of an affair would not ordinarily invalidate the agreement or entitle her to a larger settlement,” he said.
Serving Papers on the Red Carpet
Morgan and Carla race to be the one to serve the other with divorce papers. Morgan ultimately Carla divorce papers on a red carpet.
It’s a biting and humiliating moment, but not necessarily a tactic that gives Morgan an edge, according to Sugaré.
“The race to start divorce proceedings makes good television, but being the applicant does not give Morgan priority over the assets or make the judge more sympathetic to him,” Sugaré said.
And while serving a divorce application on a red carpet is “legally permissible,” it’s normally facilitated via email, Sugaré says.
So, Is Divorce Really ‘War’?
As for the show’s title? Sugaré said war is an apt metaphor for the potential brutality of divorce.
“It can get aggressive. It can be vicious. It can be personal, and the job of the lawyer is to try and rein your client in,” Sugaré said.

He explained a good lawyer tries to help clients stop ruminating about their emotions and the end of the marriage and instead prepare to “reach sensible agreements or make big decisions about (their) future,” he said.
His advice for anyone entering into a marriage? At the risk of sounding like an “anti-love guy,” Sugaré suggests both parties sign a prenuptial agreement.

“In the right circumstances, a prenuptial agreement can give both parties clarity and certainty. It may not be the most romantic conversation before a wedding, but being open about finances at the outset can prevent far greater conflict later.”

title: 4 Biggest Takeaways From Michael Douglas’ Explosive Memoir
summary: Actor Michael Douglas, who cemented his legendary status after a decadeslong career in Hollywood,” reflects on his wildly eventful life in new memoir “One Helluva Ride.”
story: Actor Michael Douglas, who cemented his legendary status after a decadeslong career in Hollywood,” reflects on his wildly eventful life in new memoir “One Helluva Ride.” And that includes some pretty explosive confessions.

Douglas, best known for his roles in blockbuster films “Wall Street” and “Basic Instinct,” details his personal sagas involving everything from infidelity to struggles with parenting in what many readers have already considered a bombshell of a book.

Now 82, the actor writes that he is refusing to shy away from any aspect of his life, and that includes some of the more unsavory elements, acknowledging that he spent a large part of his career portraying the “modern, flawed, American male.” And that archetype, he adds, “wasn’t exactly a stretch for me.”

With eight decades of drama — literally and figuratively — to unpack, Douglas says in the sprawling, 500-page memoir released Oct. 6, that the account reveals “who I became and the choices I made along the way.”
“I’ve lived a large part of my life in the public eye, but I’m a very private person,” Douglas writes. “Fame can blur the truth. Now it’s time to finally bring it all back into focus.”
Here are some of the most eye-opening highlights from “One Helluva Ride.”
He Had a Complicated Relationship With His Father, Screen Legend Kirk Douglas
Michael Douglas had a complicated, sometimes tenuous relationship with his father Kirk Douglas. And it was one that ended up shaping much of his professional and personal life, he wrote.

Kirk Douglas, who was born Issur Danielovitch Demsky, was the child of Russian Jewish immigrants and had spent much of his upbringing enduring poverty and domestic violence, the memoir says. Aspects of his difficult beginnings bled into the way in which Kirk Douglas parented — a role that, the younger Douglas wrote, involved violence and rage that at times were rationalized as “care.”

But against a backdrop of family tensions were also professional pressures, Michael Douglas wrote. In the book he recounted the way in which he’d struggled to make a name for himself, independent of his father, often having to contend with inevitable comparisons between the two. It was difficult, Michael Douglas wrote, as someone whose Hollywood dad had become synonymous with an iconic gladiator hero.
“I should have been born Mikhail Danielovitch, grandson of a ragman,” he wrote in the memoir. “Instead, I was born Michael Kirk Douglas, son of Spartacus.”

They also experienced some frictions in the field, made all the more complicated by their family dynamic. In one standout experience, Michael Douglas recounted working on “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” as a producer and having to reject his own father for the lead role of Randle Patrick “Mac” McMurphy, a character that Kirk Douglas had already portrayed on Broadway. The studio head and director of the project felt that Kirk Douglas was too old for the role, so it went to Jack Nicholson, whose performance would land him an Oscar.

“I saw a flash of my father’s rage, then he was silent. Just as I’d feared, Dad blamed me. He said I had betrayed him. I was crushed,” Michael Douglas wrote, adding that the incident put “a distance between us that would take years to overcome.”

While the father-son duo had their ups and downs throughout the decades, it was a 1991 mid-air helicopter crash that left two dead and Kirk Douglas severely injured that kicked off a strong transformation in the pair’s relationship, Michael Douglas wrote.

“It dramatically changed him — from an actor desperate to find his next role, into a more reflective person who embraced his Jewish roots, his family, and his legacy,” Michael Douglas wrote. “All of us in the family knew he had become a much better man after being given his second chance.”
He Had An Affair With Co-Star Kathleen Turner That He Kept Under Wraps For 40 Years

Among the most shocking revelations in the memoir is the truth behind his long suspected, but never confirmed, affair with co-star Kathleen Turner, with whom he starred in 1984 film “Romancing the Stone.” At the time, Michael Douglas was married to producer Diandra Luker, but wrote that the two were separated.
Though for decades, he and Turner maintained to the public that their on-screen chemistry was just that. Douglas wrote in the memoir that they’d been stretching the truth the whole time.
“It was a lie meant to protect my wife and son, a lie we told the world for 40 years,” Douglas said.

Douglas wrote in the memoir that the pair did indeed fall for each another during production, building a close relationship as they navigated the pressures of the film along with their mutual attraction while shooting in Mexico.

“Following an exhausting day of shooting in the jungle, we’d go out and have a meal, or head out with the group and afterward I would sneak into her hotel room after everybody was asleep,” Douglas said, before referencing their characters. “There were no cameras in elevators, no assistants using cell phones to take pictures. As Jack and Joan were falling in love, Kathleen and I were keeping the chemistry alive.”
Things took a turn, Douglas wrote, when Luker brought their son Cameron Douglas to visit. He recounted that Luker was growing suspicious.

“At some point, she was alone with Kathleen and made it clear to her that we were still married,” he wrote. “Her view of the terms of our separation was different from mine. This gave Kathleen pause. She didn’t want to interfere.”

He wrote that after the visit, he and Turner ended their affair and he went back to Luker. The decision, he explained, was made with his son in mind. Michael Douglas himself was a child of divorce and had been deeply impacted by his parents’ separation, he wrote. But the choice to stay with Luker “may have done more harm than good,” he wrote.
“Even if you are the child of divorce, you still forget that all your kid wants is a peaceful, happy home, and sometimes the best way to do that is to give your kid two homes,” he wrote.

Douglas’ book also mentions other affairs including a brief fling with “Romancing the Stone” screenwriter Diane Thomas and another extramarital relationship with Jeanne Tripplehorn, his co-star in the 1992 film “Basic Instinct,” for whom he was “ready to officially leave my wife.”
He Had to Break Things Off With Five Different Women Before Dating Now-Wife Catherine Zeta-Jones
Catherine Zeta-Jones would become Douglas’ great love in life, however the two had a rather unusual start.

Zeta-Jones was long aware of Douglas’ playboy reputation and made that clear the very first night they met, he said. But he was intent on playing the long game with the actor, who was 25 years his junior.

After months of wooing her — and one pivotal visit to Mallorca, Spain — Douglas finally won over Zeta-Jones. But before they could officially get serious, she laid down the law, telling him that he’d need to commit to a monogamous relationship with her in order for things to work out, Douglas wrote.
“I told her, ‘Wait here, I have to make five quick calls,’” Douglas recounted.
Douglas explained that after his separation from his wife, he began seeing five different women who all lived in different cities.
